"Shut up."

She pulled him over on top of her, which required a coordinated maneuver, his elbow finding the ground next to her ribs, her foot pressed flat against the tent wall — she felt the cold condensation on the fabric print itself against her sole, the whole wall bowing outward. The dome shuddered. Somewhere above them the rain fly shifted and dumped a little collected water down one side with a sound like someone pouring out a glass.

They both froze.

Nothing. The creek going on the way it had all night. Some insect. The particular ringing silence of a campground at eleven-thirty on a Tuesday.

"Okay," she breathed.

She had a brief, bright, disembodied thought about how the tent must look from outside — the flexing dome, the shadow of it against the trees — and then she stopped being able to think in that direction at all.

She could hear his breath and her own breath and the crinkle of the sleeping bag and beneath all of it that steady slick rhythm, and she turned her face into his shoulder and made a noise anyway, a thin desperate one, and he said "*shh*" in a tone that was mostly wonder.

She got a hand in his hair and pulled, and he lost the rhythm, and his forehead came down against her collarbone, and for a second he just breathed against her skin, hot and ragged. "Do you think they heard?" she said.

"No."

"You said that before."

"I have less confidence now."

# The Weight of It

The saloon in Bitter Creek had emptied out like water through a cracked jug, and Marion Teague couldn't say when it happened. One minute there'd been a piano and a card game and a woman laughing too loud near the stove. Now there was just the sound of the wind pushing at the shutters, and Ansel Pike sitting across the table with his hat pushed back and his hands flat on the wood, and between them the canvas sack with its corner gone dark where the gold had worn through.

"Forty pounds," Ansel said. "You want to talk about halves, we can talk about halves. But I carried it eleven miles up that draw while you sat with the horses."

"I shot the express man."

"That wasn't in the plan."

"Nothing was in the plan after the second charge blew wrong." Marion turned his glass a half-circle on the table, leaving a wet ring. "Don't sit there and act like you've got clean hands. Yours are the same color as mine."

The stove ticked. Somewhere upstairs a bed frame complained and went quiet.

"I'm taking it to Denver," Ansel said. "I've got a man there who'll break it down without asking. You come along, you get your cut when it's cut. That's the whole of my offer."

"That's not an offer. That's you telling me what's going to happen."

"Then it's that."

Marion looked at him a long moment — at the sunburn peeling off the bridge of his nose, at the gray coming in at his temples, at the small nick in his left ear from a fence wire in Kansas eight years back that Marion himself had pulled him off of. Eight years. It struck him as strange that a man could know another man's ear and not know him at all.

He reached for the sack.

Ansel's hand came off the table faster than seemed possible for a man that tired, and there was the knife — the same bone-handled thing he used to clean rabbits, the blade honed down narrow from years of the whetstone. He didn't stab with it. He came across, backhanded, the way you'd swat at a wasp, and the edge went over the back of Marion's forearm.

There was no pain at all. That was what Marion would remember. Just a cold line, like being touched with the flat of a spoon, and then his sleeve went heavy.

He got his other hand on Ansel's wrist and they went over sideways, the chair splintering under them, Marion's shoulder taking the floor and the breath going out of him in a grunt. Ansel was on top and had his weight on the knife arm, driving down, and Marion could feel the tendons in that wrist standing up like cable under his fingers. He hooked a boot heel behind Ansel's knee and heaved and the man's balance went and the knife came down anyway, wide, and buried itself in the floorboard an inch from Marion's ear. Marion heard it go in. It sounded like a nail.

He hit Ansel in the throat with the heel of his hand.

Ansel made a sound like a boot pulling out of mud and rolled off, both hands going up to his neck, and Marion got a knee under himself and stood and immediately had to catch the bar to keep from going back down. The room tilted. He looked at his arm.

The cut ran from the knob of his wrist bone up the outside of the forearm, six inches, maybe seven, and it had opened wide the way a cut does when it's clean and crosses the grain of the muscle. The edges had pulled back. He could see the pale bluish sheath over the muscle and, in one place near the wrist, something white and glistening that shifted when he moved his fingers, and his stomach went to water when he understood that he was watching a tendon slide in its groove. The blood wasn't spurting. It came in a steady heavy welling, filling the cut and spilling over both sides at once, running down over his palm and off the ends of his fingers and hitting the floorboards in a sound like someone flicking water off their hands. It was darker than he expected. Almost brown in the lamplight.

His fingers wouldn't close. He told them to and they curled halfway and stopped, the little finger and the ring finger hanging slack, and there was a numbness spreading over that side of the hand like the arm had been sat on wrong.

"Ansel," he said. His voice came out reasonable, conversational, which frightened him more than the wound did.

Ansel was on his knees by the overturned chair, breathing in long ragged pulls with his chin up, one hand still at his throat, the other reaching back for the knife in the floor without looking.

Marion pulled the bar towel down off the rail and wrapped it around his forearm and pinned the end with his teeth and drew it tight, and the pain arrived all at once then, arrived the way weather arrives, and he leaned his forehead against the cool brass of the bar rail and breathed through it while his hand went hot and thick inside the towel. The cloth darkened in bands, wick­ing through, and he thought without any particular feeling about it that he'd want that arm sewn tonight or he'd be a one-handed man for whatever was left.

When he lifted his head, Ansel had the knife again and was standing, unsteady, the blade held low and loose.

Between them, still on the table, the sack hadn't moved.

"You could just let go of it," Marion said. His mouth had gone dry as ash. "Both of us. We could just set it down and walk out different doors and it'd be like it never came out of that car."

Ansel wiped his mouth with the back of his knife hand. Considered it, or seemed to.

"Forty pounds," he said hoarsely. And came on.

# CHAPTER ELEVEN: THE YELLOW PAGES

The room was eight feet by ten and smelled like every bad decision ever made in this city. Sweat soaked into plaster. Mop water gone sour in the bucket. And underneath it all, cutting through like a rusty blade, the sweet rotten stink of Cavalier cigarettes — the kind they sell three packs for a quarter down at the docks, the kind that taste like somebody burned a mattress and rolled the ashes in newsprint.

Nardo smoked them. Nardo smoked them like he was trying to prove something to his lungs.

"Let's go again," he said.

"Let's not."

The other one — Kessel, the young one with the bad haircut and the good suit, and you should always wonder how a flatfoot on eighty-two a week affords a good suit — leaned against the door with his arms folded. He hadn't said much. He was the one I was worried about.

Nardo had the phone book. He'd carried it in under his arm like a deacon with a hymnal, and he'd set it on the table between us with a thump that meant business, and for the last forty minutes he'd been picking it up and putting it down and picking it up again, the way a man does with a card he's not sure he wants to play.

"You were on Dermott Street," he said. "Eleven forty, eleven forty-five."

"I was in bed."

"Whose?"

"Ask your wife."

I saw it coming and I still couldn't do a thing about it. That's the whole trouble with being handcuffed to a radiator pipe. The book came around flat and wide, two thousand pages of every Angelo and Zbornik in the county, and it caught me across the ribs on the left side.

Here's what nobody tells you about the phone book. It doesn't cut you. Doesn't split the eyebrow, doesn't loosen a tooth, doesn't leave anything a public defender can wave at a grand jury. What it does is spread the hurt out flat, like butter over too much toast, so there's no one spot for your brain to hold on to. A fist you can file away. A fist has an address. This was just a wall of white noise going off inside my body, a hurt with no center and no edges, and my nerves ran around in there like tenants in a burning building looking for a door.

I made a sound. I'd have preferred not to.

"Look at that," Nardo said. "He's got a voice after all."

"You should hear me sing."

The second one caught me in the same place, and the flame in my side went from white to something with color in it. I let my chin drop and studied the floor. Linoleum, once green, worn through to the black tar in a rough oval right where my chair was. A lot of men had put their feet where my feet were. The vacuum's handle pressed into her spine, and Nora didn't dare shift.

She had counted eleven seconds between the sound of the back door glass breaking and the moment she'd folded herself into the hall closet, and in those eleven seconds she had made every decision that mattered. Not the bedroom — no lock. Not the bathroom — no exit. Not the front door, because the front door had a deadbolt that stuck in humid weather and it had been raining since Tuesday.

So: the closet. Winter coats she hadn't touched since March. A shoebox of Christmas lights. The smell of cedar and mothballs and, faintly, her own sweat.

Her phone was in her hand, screen pressed flat against her thigh to hide the glow. Four percent. She had typed the address into the message box and hit send and watched it try, and try, and fail, because the cell signal in this house had always been a joke, a thing she complained about at dinner parties.

Footsteps in the kitchen. Unhurried. That was the part that turned her stomach to water — the *unhurriedness*. A person in a rush was a person who wanted something and would leave with it. This one walked like a man reading a menu.

Glass crunched. A cabinet opened, and closed.

"Kettle's still warm," he said.

Nora stopped breathing.

His voice was ordinary. Mid-range, a little nasal, the voice of someone who'd read your meter or delivered your couch. He wasn't shouting a threat or making demands. He was talking the way people talked when they were alone and comfortable.

"So you're home." A drawer slid open. Silverware shifted, a bright domestic clatter. "That's fine. That's actually easier."

Something metal set down on the counter. Something heavier than a spoon.

"You know what's hard?" he said. "Coming back. Having to come back because you were sloppy the first time. I hate coming back." The refrigerator door sucked open; the light would be spilling across the tile now, across the puddle by the door where the rain had come in with him. "I've done that twice. Twice in eleven years. Both times because I told myself, *ah, she's not going to say anything.* And then there's a sketch on the news that looks like my brother."

The fridge closed.

"No survivors," he said, mild as weather. "That's the whole discipline. Everything else is details."

Nora's jaw had locked. Her back teeth ground together with a pressure she could feel in her ears. Somewhere in the dark against her ankle, a hanger she'd knocked loose was resting on her shoe, and she understood with total clarity that if it slid to the floorboards she would die.

The footsteps moved. Kitchen to dining room — she tracked him by the change in the sound, hollow over the hardwood, then the small squeak of the loose board by the china cabinet that she'd been meaning to fix for three years.

"Nice house," he offered. "Lot of photographs. That's brave."

A pause.

"Nobody in the pictures but you and the dog."

The dog. Milo was at the vet overnight, and for one hysterical instant Nora felt grateful, and then she thought: *he knows there's no dog. He knows I'm alone. He's been watching.*

She began, very slowly, to lower her phone into the pocket of her cardigan. Four percent. If it rang — if her sister, three time zones away and always awake, decided tonight was the night to call about their mother's medication —

The screen brightened as she moved it, throwing pale light up the wall of coats, and she jammed it into the wool and held it there.

"Living room," he narrated. "Blanket on the couch. Wine glass. One glass." He laughed a little, not cruelly. "You were having a nice night."

The floor creaked closer. Hallway now. He was in the hallway.

"Here's what I want you to think about," he said, and his voice had changed — it had turned outward, aimed, no longer talk but address. "Whatever's in your head right now about waiting me out? It doesn't work. I've got until morning. I've got all the doors. I've got the only set of keys, which were in your purse, which was on the table by the front door, which is a *terrible* place to keep a purse."

Nora's eyes burned. She let them.

"Bathroom," he said. The shower curtain rattled on its rings, one long shriek of metal. "No."

Her heart was so loud she was certain it was audible through the door, a wet drum in the dark.

"Bedroom." Closet doors sliding, the *shush-thunk* of them meeting the frame. The bed frame groaning as he checked beneath it. "No, no, no."

Then nothing.

The silence went on. It stretched past the length of a breath, past the length of a thought, until she began to hope, absurdly, that he had simply evaporated, that she had imagined all of it, that she would open the door onto an empty house and a broken window and a story she'd tell for the rest of her life.

The board by the linen cupboard creaked.

Six feet away.

"You know," he said, so close now that she could hear the smile in it, "there's really only one place left."

Nora pressed her spine into the vacuum handle until it hurt, gripped the mothball-smelling hem of a coat she had bought for a trip she never took, and squeezed her eyes shut.

The knob turned with a small dry click.

And the closet door began, very slowly, to creak open.

# Redline

The starting line is a strip of chalk dust on cracked asphalt beneath the Delaney Street overpass, and there are maybe four hundred people crowded behind the concrete K-rails, all of them holding their phones up like votive candles.

I can taste the money in the air. Forty grand in a canvas bag, held by a kid named Tobias who doesn't blink much. Winner takes it. Loser gets nothing but the drive home and whatever their pride can still carry.

My hands are wet inside my gloves.

---

The Skyline idles like something with a fever, that lumpy off-beat stagger of a cam that was never meant for civilian roads. I've got the window down because I want to hear the other car — a Mustang, blown, so loud it makes the overpass columns hum — and because I want the smell. Race night has a smell. Unburnt fuel, sharp and sweet, so rich it goes straight past your nose into the back of your throat. Cooked brake dust. Tire warmers and cheap cologne and someone's blunt drifting from the crowd. It's the smell of the best and worst nights of my life, and my body knows it: my pulse is already at 140 and I haven't moved an inch.

Marisol leans in through the passenger window, hair stuck to her forehead. "Kellan checked the car twice," she says. "It's dialed."

"Where is he?"

She looks back over her shoulder at the crowd. Shrugs. "Bathroom. Somewhere."

The flag girl steps between us. She's maybe nineteen, silver dress, arms out like she's blessing us both.

I bring the revs up. The turbo spools into that hollow *whooooo* that lives somewhere behind my sternum, and the whole chassis leans into itself, and I stop thinking about Kellan or the money or anything except the six hundred meters of ruined industrial street stretching out into the dark.

Her arms drop.

---

The clutch dumps and the world compresses.

First gear is chaos — the tires break loose and I catch them, feather it, and the smoke comes up around the mirrors thick and white and smelling like a hundred pencil erasers burning at once. Second gear hits and the boost comes in all at once, a fist in the middle of my back, and the streetlights start arriving faster than my eyes can sort them.

The Mustang is beside me. Then behind me. Then beside me again, its exhaust punching at my door like a physical thing.

Third. The needle sweeps. Ninety. Warehouse doors strobe past on my right, ninety-eight, and I can see the crowd at the far end already, phone lights, that stupid brave stupid mass of people standing thirty feet from cars doing a hundred and twenty miles an hour.

Fourth gear. One-eighteen. The steering has gone light and honest, and I am, for about four seconds, the happiest I have ever been.

The finish tape is a line of orange spray paint. I cross it a car length up.

I lift.

I brake.

---

The pedal goes to the floor.

Not soft. Not spongy. *Gone.* All the way down, no resistance, like stepping into an open elevator shaft, and the sound my mouth makes isn't a word.

I pump it. Once, twice, three times, fast — and there's nothing, no pressure building, just that awful weightless travel and the smell hitting me now, hitting me *now* when it's far too late: brake fluid. Hot, oily, faintly sweet, blowing up through the firewall vents. It's been on the air since third gear and I mistook it for the night, for the smell of everything else.

*Someone cut the line.*

The thought arrives whole and complete. Someone knelt beside my car tonight with a blade and opened the rear line just enough that pressure would bleed out under load, so it'd hold at idle, so it'd hold when Kellan pressed the pedal in the pits, so it would only fail out here at the end of the straight with a hundred and ten miles an hour in my lap—

*Kellan wasn't in the bathroom.*

One-ten. The overpass abutment is coming.

Downshift. I get it into third and the engine screams past redline, the tach needle slapping against its stop, and it slows me — twenty miles an hour, maybe — and the rear steps out and I catch it and I'm using every inch of road now, both hands locked, and the crowd is *moving*, I can see them coming apart like water around a stone, people falling over each other to get behind the K-rails, and I understand with a clarity that feels almost peaceful that I have to go anywhere they aren't.

Handbrake. The rear locks, the tires start to scream, and the car swaps ends so fast the world turns into a smear of orange sodium light.

Then I'm going backwards at eighty miles an hour and there is nothing left to do but wait the half second out.

---

Impact isn't a sound. It's a subtraction — everything is taken out of the world at once, all the noise, all the air, all the up and down. The concrete barrier comes through the trunk and into the back seats. The seatbelt turns into a steel bar across my collarbone. Something in my chest goes *crack* like a green branch.

The Skyline pirouettes off the barrier, catches its nose on the curb, and rolls. I remember the second impact more than the first — the roof pillar folding down toward my head, the windshield turning to white crystal and coming in on me like weather. Then I'm upside down and there's a long, ringing, ticking quiet.

Fuel. That's what brings me back. Gasoline, raw and unmistakable, pooling somewhere I can hear it. Steam hissing off the exhaust manifold. The smell of hot metal and rubber that's still burning, laying its rich black smoke sideways along the asphalt.

Somebody is screaming my name from a long way off. My hands don't work right. Blood is running up my forehead into my hair, which is when I really understand that I'm hanging.

Through the shattered spiderweb where my window used to be, I can see legs running toward me. And past them, way past them, up on the overpass, one figure standing alone at the railing — not running, not filming. Just watching. Hands in his pockets.

I know that jacket.

I try to say his name and get only a mouthful of copper.

Then the hands are on me, six of them, ten, hauling at the door frame, and Marisol's voice is right at my ear saying *don't you dare, don't you dare, don't you dare,* and the whole ruined car groans as they drag me out across the glass while the gasoline keeps spreading, patient and bright, toward the heat.

I can taste the money in the air. Forty grand in a canvas bag, held by a kid named Tobias who doesn't blink much. Winner takes it. Loser gets nothing but the drive home and whatever their pride can still carry.

My hands are wet inside my gloves.

The Skyline idles like something with a fever, that lumpy off-beat stagger of a cam that was never meant for civilian roads. I've got the window down because I want to hear the other car — a Mustang, blown, so loud it makes the overpass columns hum — and because I want the smell. Race night has a smell. Unburnt fuel, sharp and sweet, so rich it goes straight past your nose into the back of your throat. Cooked brake dust. Tire warmers and cheap cologne and someone's blunt drifting from the crowd. It's the smell of the best and worst nights of my life, and my body knows it: my pulse is already at 140 and I haven't moved an inch.

Marisol leans in through the passenger window, hair stuck to her forehead. "Kellan checked the car twice," she says. "It's dialed."

"Where is he?"

She looks back over her shoulder at the crowd. Shrugs. "Bathroom. Somewhere."

The flag girl steps between us. She's maybe nineteen, silver dress, arms out like she's blessing us both.

I bring the revs up. The turbo spools into that hollow whooooo that lives somewhere behind my sternum, and the whole chassis leans into itself, and I stop thinking about Kellan or the money or anything except the six hundred meters of ruined industrial street stretching out into the dark.

Her arms drop.

The clutch dumps and the world compresses.

First gear is chaos — the tires break loose and I catch them, feather it, and the smoke comes up around the mirrors thick and white and smelling like a hundred pencil erasers burning at once. Second gear hits and the boost comes in all at once, a fist in the middle of my back, and the streetlights start arriving faster than my eyes can sort them.

The Mustang is beside me. Then behind me. Then beside me again, its exhaust punching at my door like a physical thing.

Third. The needle sweeps. Ninety. Warehouse doors strobe past on my right, ninety-eight, and I can see the crowd at the far end already, phone lights, that stupid brave stupid mass of people standing thirty feet from cars doing a hundred and twenty miles an hour.

Fourth gear. One-eighteen. The steering has gone light and honest, and I am, for about four seconds, the happiest I have ever been.

The finish tape is a line of orange spray paint. I cross it a car length up.

I lift.

I brake.

The pedal goes to the floor.

Not soft. Not spongy. Gone. All the way down, no resistance, like stepping into an open elevator shaft, and the sound my mouth makes isn't a word.

I pump it. Once, twice, three times, fast — and there's nothing, no pressure building, just that awful weightless travel and the smell hitting me now, hitting me now when it's far too late: brake fluid. Hot, oily, faintly sweet, blowing up through the firewall vents. It's been on the air since third gear and I mistook it for the night, for the smell of everything else.

Someone cut the line.

The thought arrives whole and complete. Someone knelt beside my car tonight with a blade and opened the rear line just enough that pressure would bleed out under load, so it'd hold at idle, so it'd hold when Kellan pressed the pedal in the pits, so it would only fail out here at the end of the straight with a hundred and ten miles an hour in my lap—

One-ten. The overpass abutment is coming.

I get it into third and the engine screams past redline, the tach needle slapping against its stop, and it slows me — twenty miles an hour, maybe — and the rear steps out and I catch it and I'm using every inch of road now, both hands locked, and the crowd is moving, I can see them coming apart like water around a stone, people falling over each other to get behind the K-rails, and I understand with a clarity that feels almost peaceful that I have to go anywhere they aren't.

Then I'm going backwards at eighty miles an hour and there is nothing left to do but wait the half second out.

Impact isn't a sound. It's a subtraction — everything is taken out of the world at once, all the noise, all the air, all the up and down. The concrete barrier comes through the trunk and into the back seats. The seatbelt turns into a steel bar across my collarbone. Something in my chest goes crack like a green branch.

The Skyline pirouettes off the barrier, catches its nose on the curb, and rolls. # The Ledger

The rain had been at the window for three hours, and the man at the desk had not once looked up at it.

He worked under the lamp with the shade tilted low, its light pooled on a bath towel he had taken from the rack and laid out square with the edges of the desk. Everything on the towel had a place. Everything in its place had a purpose. Solvent bottle, capped. Jar of patches. Cleaning rod broken into sections. A brass jag, a chamber brush worn to the nub of its usefulness. The rifle itself lay disassembled along the towel's long axis like a diagram of itself.

On the television, mounted too high on the wall, a woman with careful hair was saying the word *tragedy*.

He heard it the way he heard the rain.

---

He began, as always, with the bore. The barrel came free of the receiver and he set it in the cradle he had improvised from two folded washcloths, muzzle canted downward so the solvent would run out and not back into the action. He threaded a patch onto the jag, wet it, and pushed it through from the chamber end in one unhurried stroke. It emerged dark. He did not look at it long. Carbon fouling, a little copper wash streaking the white cotton green where the jacket material had smeared itself into the lands and grooves. Ninety-one rounds since the last full strip. He knew the number the way other men knew their children's ages.

Second patch. Third. The rod slid with a dry whisper.

"—was pronounced dead at the scene at approximately 8:40 this evening—"

Eight thirty-eight, he thought, without heat, without correction. Reporters worked from the timestamp on the ambulance log. He worked from the second hand of a watch he had synchronized that morning to the atomic clock signal. The discrepancy was two minutes and it did not matter and he noted it anyway, because noting things was the whole of him now, the way a carpenter cannot stop measuring doorframes.

He set the barrel aside to sit and let the solvent do its slow work, and took up the bolt.

This was the part he liked, if *liked* was a word he still had a use for. The bolt was a small machine of terrible simplicity. He rotated the extractor out of its slot with the tip of a punch and thumbed the plunger free, catching the spring before it could travel. The firing pin came out next, a pin of hard bright steel with a hemispherical tip, and he held it up to the lamp and turned it and found the tip unmarred, no mushrooming, no burr. A pin was a consumable item. It would fail eventually, and when it failed it would fail without warning, and so he replaced them on a schedule rather than on evidence. This one had eleven firings left in its service life. He would swap it out in Rotterdam.

He laid the pin on the towel, parallel to the bolt body, one centimeter of separation. Then he laid the extractor beside it, and the plunger, and the spring.

"—leaves behind a wife and two daughters—"

The anchorwoman's voice went soft on the word *daughters*, a professional softening, the vocal equivalent of a black armband. He recognized the technique. She was very good at it. They were both technicians.

He wet a cotton swab and worked it into the bolt face, into the recessed crescent where the case head sat during ignition, where the pressure of forty-odd thousand pounds per square inch was contained and directed and made into a single event lasting somewhat less than two milliseconds. Powder residue had baked into a grey lacquer there. He scraped at it patiently with a dental pick, and the grey lacquer came away in flakes the size of dust.

---

He did not think of the man on the television as a man on a television. He thought of him as a clause.

That was not cruelty. Cruelty required appetite, and appetite required that you want something from the person, and he wanted nothing at all. He had never known the name until the file, and he had already begun the discipline of forgetting it. There was a party of the first part and a party of the second part, and between them a set of specified conditions: a place, a window of hours, a required outcome, a schedule of remittance. He had reviewed the conditions. He had satisfied the conditions. Somewhere in a city he had no plans to visit, a ledger line balanced.

Contractual obligation. That was the phrase he used with himself, in the small hours, on the rare nights when something in him stirred and lifted its head and had to be spoken back to sleep. *You entered into an obligation and you discharged it.* Obligations were clean. Obligations had beginnings and ends. A man who works only within the four corners of an obligation cannot be accused of wanting anything, and a man who wants nothing cannot be reached.

He had believed this for nineteen years. He inspected the belief the way he inspected the firing pin — regularly, in good light, looking for hairline cracks — and reported to himself each time that the belief was serviceable.

The two daughters were not in the four corners.

He returned to the barrel.

---

Dry patches now, three of them, until the cotton came out only faintly grey. Then a patch with a whisper of oil, drawn through once, no more; a wet bore threw its first shot wide, and the first shot was the only shot that had ever been asked of him. He inspected the crown at the muzzle for nicks. He inspected the chamber with a small light and found it bright. He held the barrel up and looked down the bore at the lamp and saw the rifling turn away from him in its long unhurried spiral, a helix of shadow and light, clean as a snail shell.

Reassembly. The bolt body, the pin, the spring compressed and captured, the extractor snapped home under the plunger. He worked the bolt in his hands with his eyes closed and felt the lockup — the small solid *seat* of it, no grit, no hesitation. Barrel to receiver, torqued by feel to the setting his hands had learned years before his mind could have named it. The trigger group he only brushed and left dry; oil in a trigger group collected dust and dust changed the break, and the break was the last honest thing between intention and event. He set the sear with his thumbnail and let it off twice, listening.

The optic he did not touch. Turrets were set. Elevation and windage had been confirmed at a quarry outside the city eleven days ago and would not be disturbed for anything short of a fall.

Last, the buttstock, the cheek riser, the folding bipod with its legs collapsed. He laid the assembled rifle in the case, into the foam cut to its exact silhouette, and the foam took it without a gap anywhere, and he closed the lid and heard the latches seat.

Eleven minutes over his usual time. He noted this.

On the television the woman with the careful hair had moved on to a mudslide in another country. The rain kept up its patient work at the window.

He gathered the used patches, the black-grey wads of them, and counted them into the ashtray — eleven — and set them alight, and watched the solvent flare up blue and go out. He rinsed the ash. He wiped the desk. He shook out the towel, folded it in thirds, and returned it to the rack with the seam facing the wall, exactly as he had found it.

Then he sat on the edge of the bed in the dark with his hands on his knees, a clean man in a clean room, obligations discharged in full, and waited to see whether tonight would be a night he could sleep.

The vat took him the way water takes a stone — without ceremony.

First there was only the shock of temperature, which was not cold. Heat bloomed across his cheek where the surface met it, an intimate, spreading warmth like a hand pressed too hard, and for one full second that was all: warmth, and the sharp mineral stink rising off the liquid, and the thought *this isn't so bad* forming and dying in the same breath.

Then the reaction found its footing.

His skin went white. Not pale — *white*, the flat chalk-white of boiled bone, as the outer layer surrendered its water in a rush and the proteins beneath seized and knotted, cooking without fire. The color came up his jaw in a tide line, and where it passed, the surface bubbled fine and dense, a lather of gas working out from under him. The lather turned yellow. Then brown. Then a wet black that sloughed away in ribbons, curling off the muscle beneath like paper lifted from a wall.

The eyelashes went first among the details — a whisper of keratin, gone in an instant, taking the eyebrow with it. Then the lips, which had been open, simply were not lips anymore. They thinned, retracted, drew back from the teeth in a grin that widened past any grin a face could make, and the teeth stood exposed and startlingly clean, the whitest thing left, until the acid found the roots and they loosened in their sockets and shifted like fenceposts in soft ground.

The nose collapsed inward. There was cartilage there, and cartilage is patient, but it is not stone; it softened, sagged, folded, and the two dark openings behind it ran together into one ragged hollow. Fat beneath the cheeks turned rank and soapy, slipping loose from its scaffolding, so that the architecture of the face — the bones that had made him recognizable, the particular angle of him — emerged, then blurred, then emerged again, as if the vat were sketching him and erasing him by turns.

The eyes stayed longest, and worst. They clouded from the outside in, the clear windows going milky, then gray, then flattening as the fluid behind them boiled away and the globes sank slowly back into the orbits like ice retreating in a glass. Whatever expression they held was undone in stages: alarm, then absence, then only the shape where a look used to sit.

Steam came up off the surface, thick and acrid, carrying the smell of hot metal and scorched hair and something faintly, horribly like caramel. It fogged the tiles. It stripped the varnish from the beam overhead.

He went under. Bubbles rose in a slowing rhythm — a rush, a scatter, a last few — and the liquid closed and smoothed itself, darker now, clouded with a suspended haze that turned in slow spirals under the light. Somewhere in that haze the mineral parts of him, the enamel and the calcium, drifted down toward the bottom in a fine gray snow.

The surface stilled. It gave back the ceiling lamps in perfect, undisturbed circles, and there was nothing in it to suggest a face had ever been.

The stairs gave under her weight with a sound like a knuckle cracking, and then she was standing on packed earth, and the smell arrived.

It came in layers. First the wet-penny reek of blood, so thick it seemed to have texture, something she could feel settling on her tongue and the back of her throat. Under that, sweeter — the rotting-fruit smell of a garbage bag left in August sun, of the crawlspace where the possum had died the summer she was nine. And under *that*, faint and domestic and somehow the worst of all, the smell of Aubrey's coconut hair oil.

Jess put the back of her wrist against her mouth and swept the flashlight left.

The beam was too narrow. That was the cruelty of it — she could only see the basement in pieces, a two-foot circle of yellow that she had to move herself, choosing each time what to look at next, so that every horror was something she had gone and found on purpose.

Cole was closest, propped in the angle of the wall where the foundation stones met the floor, and for a moment she thought he was alive because he was sitting up. His head was tipped back against the mortar, chin lifted, throat presented. The throat was open. It was open the way a mouth is open, the edges pursed and dark and glistening, and the front of his sweatshirt had gone stiff and black-brown and cracked like drying mud where it had soaked and then begun to dry. His hands lay palms-up on the dirt beside his hips, fingers loosely curled. Relaxed. The hands of a man asleep in a lecture hall. Under his left thumbnail was the green paint from the boathouse door he'd helped her fix three days ago, and it was that — the paint, the stupid ordinary paint — that made her legs go soft, and she had to put a hand on the cold sweating stone to stay up.

The flashlight jerked and found the beam overhead.

Dana was hanging from it, upside down, ankles bound to the joist with the yellow nylon rope from the boat shed. Her hair hung straight down and swayed slightly, though there was no wind in the basement, no reason for it to sway. Blood had run down her body against the grain of things — up her stomach, up her chest, over her jaw, along her cheekbones — and dried in long brown deltas, following contours it should never have followed, so that her face was mapped with it, veined like a leaf. Her eyes were half open and clouded, the shine gone off them, dull as pond ice. Beneath her the earth had gone dark in a wide, soaked oval, and at the center of the oval a slow, patient *tap* — a single drop every few seconds, falling from her fingertips into the mud she had made. That sound had been going on the whole time Jess had been down here. She had been hearing it since the fourth step and had told herself it was a pipe.

She made a noise. Not a scream. Something smaller and more terrible, the sound of air being pressed out of her.

The beam swung and skidded across the far wall, and there was the workbench, and on the workbench something folded.

She didn't want to understand it. Her mind offered her alternatives: a tarp, a bundle of dropcloths, a deer, a deer, please a deer. But the shapes resolved the way a word resolves when you stare at it too long, and it was Wes, or the parts of him that had been kept, laid out in a careful row with a hand's width between each, the way a mechanic lays out the pieces of a carburetor so he can put it back together after. The cuts were not ragged. They were flat and clean and pale at the edges, and the marrow in the long bones was a soft, awful pink, the pink of the inside of a shell. His boots were still on. Both of them. Laced. He'd double-knotted them every morning, tugging hard, always the same two hard tugs, and she had never once thought about it until now and would think about it every day for the rest of her life.

The oldest one was in the corner, and she knew it was the oldest because it had stopped being anyone. It had gone dark and slack and settled, sunk in on itself, cheeks fallen away from the teeth so that it seemed to be laughing at some joke it had heard days ago. Not one of hers. Someone else's friend. Someone from before, from another summer, another vanload of kids who had turned off the highway because the sign said *CABINS — VACANCY*. There were flies at the eyes, unhurried, and a soft shifting sound coming from the folds of the sweatshirt, a sound like rice pouring, and she understood what was making it and turned her light away fast, fast, too late.

Cold on her cheeks. She was crying. She hadn't noticed starting.

Something moved in the dark at the top of the stairs, and the boards up there sang out under a weight much greater than hers, and the smell of coconut oil rose stronger, as if it were being carried, as if someone had been sitting a long while in the dark with their hands in Aubrey's hair, waiting for the last one to come down and find them all.

Jess switched off the flashlight.

She made herself breathe through her mouth. She made herself remember that behind Cole, low in the stone, there had been a coal chute with a rusted hasp, and that she had seen it, and that seeing it was the only thing down here she had chosen to look at that could still save her.

Then she began, very slowly, to move toward the body of her friend.

The sound arrived before anything else, and Marek mistook it for rain.

He was wedged eleven feet down in the limestone crevice, left leg folded the wrong way beneath him, and the sound came from the dark seam at the bottom of the shaft — a dry, whispering patter, like a light shower moving across dead leaves. It was the wrong season for rain. It was the wrong place; he was underground.

He clicked his headlamp on.

The floor of the crevice was moving. Not crawling — *pouring*, a glossy brown current welling up out of a crack no wider than his hand, spreading in a fan across the stone, folding over itself in ripples the way water does when it finds a level. The pattering was the sound of their bodies. Millions of small hard shells brushing over rock and over one another, and beneath that, quieter, a sound he would come to know intimately in the next four minutes: a papery *snip-snip-snip*, arrhythmic, ceaseless, like a hundred people clipping their nails in a small room.

They came up his boot without hesitation. He felt the weight of them first, a warm sandbag pressure climbing his shin, and then the first bite.

It was nothing. A spark of nettle-sting on the ankle, so small it was almost interesting. Then a second, an inch above it. Then eleven, then forty, and the arithmetic ran away from him. Each one was a tiny bright pinch, a needle of heat, a pin pushed just past the surface and twisted out again with a crumb of him in it. Individually they were beneath pain. Together they became something else — a sensation with no name, a sheet of fire laid over his skin and pressed down, and underneath the fire the terrible sense of *subtraction*, of being taken away in grains, the way a beach is taken.

He beat at his legs with both hands. His palms came away wet and the bodies burst like dry seed pods and it made no difference at all; the current simply closed over the gap he'd made. They went up under the cuff of his trousers, up the inside of his thigh, and the fabric came apart at the seams — not torn, *dismantled*, threads clipped one at a time by ten thousand mouths working with the patience of a machine.

The sound was in his clothes now. That was the worst of it, in those first seconds. The chittering had been out there, in the dark, an outside thing, and now it was inside his shirt, at his collarbone, and he could hear the mandibles working at close range: a fine crisp *ticking*, wet at the edges, like a mouthful of eggshells being chewed slowly. It came up through the bones of his chest and into his skull, so that he heard it not with his ears but with his teeth.

He screamed. They went into his mouth. He learned very quickly not to scream.

The mathematics of it was what undid him, in the last coherent stretch of his mind. He understood suddenly that there was no fighting this because there was nothing to fight — no jaws to pry, no throat to reach for, no single animal to hurt. It was a weather system. It was erosion. Each mouth took less than a mustard seed of him and gave it to the dark, and there were so many mouths that he could feel himself going, could feel the outline of his own body becoming vague and negotiable, the way a word repeated too many times stops being a word.

The pain crested and then, mercifully, stopped being pain. Something in the wounds — a compound in the saliva, he thought distantly, some clever chemistry a hundred million years old — turned the fire down to a cold, buzzing numbness, and after that he mostly felt pressure. Weight. A great living blanket, blood-warm, shifting in slow waves. It was almost restful. His hands lay open at his sides and he watched a black mitten of insects form over his right wrist and he could not persuade his fingers to close.

His headlamp went out — they had found the wires, or the battery housing, or the light simply drowned. In the darkness the sound became everything. It filled the crevice from floor to lip, that vast dry rustling with its infinite small scissors inside it, and Marek lay in the middle of it and listened, and thought, with the last surprised clarity left to him, that it sounded like applause.

Then like static.

Then like nothing, going on and on.

He had known for six passes that he could not win by fencing. Kestrel was faster in the wrist, longer in the arm, and worse, she was patient—she had already learned not to chase him, and she was letting the sand and the sun do her work.

So Hallam changed the question. Not *how do I avoid her point,* but *what will her point cost me,* and *what can I buy with it.*

He watched for the tell. She had it in the left shoulder: a small dip before the lunge, like someone leaning to look past a curtain. Three more exchanges to be sure. On the fourth, he opened the line.

It was not a feint. That was the whole of it. A feint she would have read; she read everything. He simply let his guard drift wide as though his arm had gone dead, as though the heat had finally found him, and he stepped in on the beat of her shoulder-dip and gave her his belly.

The shoulder dipped. She came.

The entry was not pain. That was what surprised him, even having planned for it. It was pressure, enormous and specific, a thumb pushed hard into a bruise the size of his whole torso, and then a bright cold line drawing itself through him, and a sound he felt rather than heard—a small deep *tick* as the point found something and went past it. His body understood before he did. Everything below his ribs turned to water. His knees tried to fold and he refused them, because folding was the one thing he could not do, not yet, not for four more heartbeats.

She was very close now. That was the purchase. Her arm was extended to the limit, her weight forward and committed, her guard nowhere, her face six inches from his—and her blade was inside him, which meant it was *his*, held fast by muscle and meat and the suck of his own flesh, and she could not withdraw it faster than his hand could move.

Her eyes changed. He saw the whole shape of it arrive in her: the recognition, then the arithmetic, then the wide black understanding that she had spent her only sentence on a man who had already read the last line.

He clamped his left hand over her sword hand, pinning it to the hilt, pinning the hilt to himself. There was a slippery warmth already coming out around the blade and running down into his boot.

His own weapon was too long for this. He dropped it. There was no time to be elegant, and elegance had never been what he was good at.

The dagger came off his hip. It came off his hip because he had spent the last six passes moving his hip closer to his hand, one inch at a time, the way you move a stone in a river without letting the water notice. The draw was awkward and it was low and it did not need to be anything else. He put it in under her arm where the plates gapped for the shoulder, and he did not stab so much as lean, letting his failing weight do it, driving the point up and in toward the place where everything in a person converges.

She made a sound like a door opening.

They went down together, which was the only way they could go down, joined at two points, her steel in his gut and his in her chest, and the sand came up warm against his cheek.

*Four heartbeats,* he thought, absurdly proud, as the cold spread up under his ribs to meet his throat. *I only needed the four.*

Her fingers were still locked around the hilt. He did not let go of them. It seemed impolite, somehow, to let go first.

**Decompression**

The inner door didn't fail so much as forget itself. One moment Ilse Warrender was reaching for the sample crate; the next, the air went out of the world with a sound like a held breath released, and she was going with it.

She had time — this was the cruelty of it — she had a great deal of time. Fifteen seconds of lucidity, the training manuals said, and the manuals were correct, and fifteen seconds is an unbearably generous allotment.

The first thing was her lungs emptying themselves without her permission. Not a scream; screaming requires atmosphere. The air simply left, dragged out of her chest through her open mouth, and she felt the tissue of her throat go cold and raw with the speed of its leaving. She had exhaled, thank God, out of instinct or luck, because the manuals said holding your breath would tear the alveoli like wet paper.

Then the boiling.

That is the word everyone uses, and it is nearly right. Her blood did not boil — the vessels held, the heart kept its stubborn pressure — but everything looser than blood began to turn to vapor inside her. The water in her tongue fizzed. She felt it distinctly: a sensation like carbonation on the surface of her mouth, the saliva going to gas beneath itself, an obscene tickling. The soft tissues under her skin swelled with it. Her hands puffed and stiffened, her forearms tightened inside their own casing, her face grew strange and heavy and unfamiliar, and she thought, with the last coherent thought she would ever have, *I am becoming something else.* Two times her volume. That was the number. Two times, and the skin holds, and you do not burst, you only bloat like bread proving in a warm kitchen.

Her eyes went last and went beautifully, which is the worst thing about it.

The moisture on them vaporized, and vaporization steals heat, and the heat came out of the surface of her eyes and left it behind as ice. She saw something like the inside of a snow globe, and then she saw grey, and then the frost closed over and she saw nothing at all, though her eyes remained open, and would remain open, glazed and gleaming, for a very long time.

She was unconscious by then. She had been unconscious for perhaps nine seconds already, which is a mercy the universe extends by accident rather than design. The heart went on a while longer, laboring in a body full of gas, and then it stopped.

And here is what the stories get wrong: she did not freeze. Not then. Vacuum is the finest insulator ever made; there is nothing to carry the warmth away, no wind, no cold air, no water to leech it out of her. She only radiated, slowly, patiently, the way a stone gives up the day's sun. Her core stayed warm for hours. # Forty-One Minutes

The Empathic Restitution Wing at Halvard occupies the lowest floor of the facility, below the laundry and the water reclamation plant, where the constant hum of machinery makes it hard for anyone to hear anything through the walls. The official reason is temperature stability. The chairs require it.

Inmate 8814 has been sitting in one of them for eleven years.

His name is Owen Mazek. He is fifty-three now, and looks older; the sessions age men the way radiation does, from the inside, indiscriminately. His hair went white in the third year. In the sixth he lost the ability to eat solid food in the two hours following a session, and now they give him a nutrient slurry and a plastic spoon, and a paper cup for when it comes back up.

The technician's name is Mirja Oduya. She has worked the Wing for four years, which makes her senior staff. Turnover is high. She has a rule she made for herself in her first month, which is that she always says the inmate's name before she starts, and never says the victim's.

"Owen," she says. "Session eleven forty-four. You know the sequence."

"I know the sequence."

"Say it back to me anyway."

He recites it in the flat voice they all develop. "Forty-one minutes. No interruption unless cardiac. I don't get to talk to her. I don't get to change anything. Coming out is worse than going in."

"That's right." She fits the crown over his skull, adjusts the temporal contacts, watches the impedance settle into green. "Anything you want to say first?"

He always says the same thing. He said it at his sentencing, and he says it now, and Mirja has stopped believing that he means it and started believing something worse, which is that he means it more each time and it has stopped mattering.

"I'm sorry."

"Okay," Mirja says, and starts the session.

---

The technology is not complicated, only expensive. Everyone born after 2061 carries a cortical lifelog: a lattice of filaments seeded in infancy, drinking the sensorium, spooling it into a bead of dense storage behind the mastoid bone. It was sold to the public as a medical device — early detection of dementia, of stroke, of the small silent bleeds that used to go unnoticed. It became, inevitably, a witness. Wills were settled with it. Marriages ended with it. And in 2079, in a case everyone has read about, a district court in Ohio ruled that a decedent's final recording could be entered into evidence not as testimony but as *experience*, and something in the architecture of punishment shifted and did not shift back.

The reasoning was elegant. Prison did not teach remorse; it taught grievance. Men entered with a story in which they were the protagonist and left with the story reinforced by twenty years of hardening. But you cannot narrate your way out of somebody else's nervous system. You cannot be the hero of a memory in which you are the thing coming through the door.

They called it Empathic Restitution. The families had to consent. The families almost always consented.

---

**19:42.** She is standing at the counter with her sleeves pushed up, cutting the woody ends off a bundle of asparagus, and she is thinking about a bus.

This is the part that nobody outside the Wing understands, and the part that Owen Mazek has come to understand better than his own life. The horror is not the violence. The violence is four seconds long. The horror is the asparagus and the bus.

The bus is the 14, which she has to catch at 6:50 tomorrow morning to get to the water district office in Rensfeld, because her car is making a noise. She is annoyed about the noise. She is planning to call her brother about it, because he knows about cars, and because it's been three weeks and she owes him a call. Under the annoyance is a good mood she isn't paying attention to. She has a glass of wine two inches from her left hand. There is a song playing that she doesn't like enough to have chosen, which means it's on shuffle, which means she is going to die in a room with music in it that she was indifferent to.

Her name — Mirja never says it, but Owen holds it like a stone in his mouth for all of the eleven years — is Nell Achterberg. She is thirty-four. She is a hydrologist. She is five foot four and her hands are cold, always, and she is thinking about a bus.

**19:44.** The knock.

He knows what he looked like on the other side of that door. He knows the whole thing from outside, from his own recording, which the prosecution also played: a heavy man in a wet jacket, pipe wrench in his coat pocket, four months behind on a debt he had bought from a man named Kessler for pennies on the dollar because he thought collecting was easy work. He knows how he stood there rolling his shoulders. He remembers being cold and bored.

From inside, the knock is nothing. It is a Tuesday-night knock. She wipes her hands on a dish towel, and there is a flicker of *who is that* which is not fear, which is the ordinary curiosity of a person whose life has never once been interrupted by anything worse than a broken car, and she goes to the door and opens it.

That is the crushing part, in the early years. She opens it. She opens it every time. She opens it fourteen hundred times and there is nothing he can do, no muscle to seize, no throat to shout with, because he is not in his body, he is in hers, and hers is walking toward the door with a dish towel in its hand.

**19:47.** The argument. Money she doesn't have. She is not frightened yet; she is *irritated*, which he could not have predicted and which humiliates him more than any sentence a judge could have handed down. She thinks he is a nuisance. She thinks he is a man who has come to the wrong house, a mistake in paperwork, and she is composing the email she will send tomorrow to have it corrected.

He watches her decide to close the door.

**19:48.** He was told, at intake, that the mind does not record pain accurately. This is true. There is a spike, a white obliteration with no shape to it, and then a gap of perhaps six seconds in which the recording carries only tone: a low sick swaying, like being far underwater.

What comes back is the floor.

**19:49.** She is on the kitchen floor and she does not know how she got there. This is the beginning of the forty-one minutes.

The first thing she thinks is that she has fallen. She has an entire theory — she slipped, the tiles are slick, she should have wiped up the water from the asparagus — and she is embarrassed, actually embarrassed, and she tries to get up and cannot, and the theory does not survive that. Something is wrong with the right side of everything. Her arm is there but it is a rumor.

The front door is open. She can feel the air from it on her cheek. He is gone; she doesn't know that yet, and for eight of the forty-one minutes she is lying very still because she believes he is standing behind her, in the hall, watching, deciding.

That is the first weight. Eight minutes of holding still to survive a man who has already left, driving north on the Bellamy road with the radio on, feeling nothing at all.

**19:57.** The phone. It is on the counter, one hundred and ten centimeters above her head, and she can see the edge of its case, and she works on the problem of it for eleven minutes with the patient competence of a woman who has spent her professional life on hydraulic models. She gets her good hand to the cabinet handle. She gets her hip to turn. Something in her head goes wrong when she lifts it — a rising roar, a sense of the room tipping like water in a bowl — and she has to stop and lie flat and wait for the roar to go out.

She thinks: *this is how people die.* It arrives calmly, as information. She rejects it. She is thirty-four and there is asparagus on the counter and she is going to be on the 14 bus at 6:50 tomorrow morning.

She tries again. She gets the towel down off the handle. She does not get the phone.

**20:09.** The bargaining. Not with God; she has no God. With the house. She thinks about the neighbor, Denise, who sometimes comes over on Tuesdays and does not come over this Tuesday. She thinks about her cat, who is in the bedroom, and who she can hear moving, and she is worried — this is minute twenty-three, this is a woman with a fractured skull and a subdural bleed and a cold tile floor — she is *worried* that if she dies here the cat will be alone in the house for days.

She thinks about her mother's face at a funeral. Not her own funeral: her father's, nine years ago, the way her mother's mouth had gone. She thinks: *she can't do that twice.* She thinks: *I have to get up because of my mother's mouth.*

**20:16.**

The following draws on documented accounts of botched electrocutions — the testimony of Willie Francis, who survived the chair in 1946, and witness reports from the executions of John Evans (1983), Jesse Tafero (1990), and Pedro Medina (1997).

---

The first thing is not pain. It is the absolute theft of the body.

At the instant the switch closes, some two thousand volts drive through the skull electrode, down the length of the spine, and out through the calf. Every voluntary muscle in the body contracts simultaneously and stays contracted — the jaw clamps down on the leather bit, the spine arches against the straps hard enough to crack the seat frame, the fingers curl into fists so tight the nails open the palms. The diaphragm locks. There is no breath, therefore no scream. The throat is a stopped pipe. Whatever the mind is doing in there, it has no instrument left to speak with.

Then the heat arrives, and it arrives from the inside.

Flesh is a poor conductor, and poor conductors turn current into heat. The dense tissue nearest the electrodes takes the worst of it: the scalp beneath the copper cap, the shaved patch on the calf beneath the leg band. The sensation is not the surface sting of a flame but something deeper and more wrong — a scorching pressure under the skin, as though a coal had been pushed beneath the bone. Willie Francis, who lived through it, said only that he felt his mouth fill with cold peanut butter, and that his head and left leg were burning, and that he jumped against the straps.

The failure, when it comes, is almost always mundane.

The headpiece is designed around a natural sponge soaked in brine, a wet interface to spread the current evenly across the scalp. If the sponge has dried, or if someone has fitted a synthetic one, the resistance at that contact point climbs catastrophically. Now the electrode is no longer delivering current through the skull; it is cooking a two-inch disc of scalp like meat on a griddle. The sponge itself ignites. Flame comes up around the edge of the cap in a ragged crown, six inches, eight, blue-white at the base and orange at the tip, and smoke pours out from under the leather mask in a thick column. The witness room fills with a smell that everyone who has described it describes the same way: pork.

The leg electrode fails in its own fashion. A loose buckle, a band strapped over stubble instead of bare skin, and the current arcs across the gap. Sparks fan out from beneath the strap in a bright spray. The skin blisters, splits, and blackens in a ring, and the fat beneath it renders and runs. Steam hisses from the wound where the water in the tissue flashes off faster than it can escape.

And still the body sits there rigid, hands white on the arms of the chair, absolutely silent, because it cannot do anything else.

Then the switch is pulled and the current stops.

This is the part that makes a botched electrocution what it is. The muscles let go all at once. The body slumps into the straps, the chest heaves, and there is a sound — a grunt, a long groan, air dragged in over a scalded throat. The head lifts. The chest continues to rise and fall. Blood runs from under the mask where the capillaries in the face have burst; the pupils, if anyone could see them, are wide. The prisoner is breathing, and if he is breathing, the question in the room becomes unbearable: what does he know?

Because the current was not enough to destroy the brain. It was only enough to paralyze, and to burn. And now the tissue that was cooked in those first seconds — nerve endings intact, everything intact — is reporting in. Third-degree burns on the head and leg. A cracked tooth. Torn tendons in the shoulders. Bowels emptied. And the electrodes are still fastened on, still touching, and the men behind the glass are conferring about the equipment, and the second jolt is coming.

Then it comes, and everything locks again.

It may take three cycles. It may take fourteen minutes. In the intervals the body breathes, and the smoke goes on curling up out of the mask toward the ceiling, and the witnesses look at their shoes.

Then the switch is pulled and the current stops.

This is the part that makes a botched electrocution what it is. The muscles let go all at once. The body slumps into the straps, the chest heaves, and there is a sound — a grunt, a long groan, air dragged in over a scalded throat. The head lifts. The chest continues to rise and fall. The prisoner is breathing, and if he is breathing, the question in the room becomes unbearable: what does he know?

Torn tendons in the shoulders. Bowels emptied. Then it comes, and everything locks again.

It may take three cycles. It may take fourteen minutes. In the intervals the body breathes, and the smoke goes on curling up out of the mask toward the ceiling, and the witnesses look at their shoes.

The floorboards were only inches from her cheek, and they told her everything.

She'd pressed her face there because it was the only place left to put it, and now the wood was a second skin, a drumhead reading out the room above her in tremors. Each footstep arrived first as a low swell in the boards, a compression she felt in her jaw before she heard it — and then, trailing half a beat behind, the sound itself: the creak, the small groan of nails working loose in their old holes.

Then the axe.

It came as a grain, a roughness. He wasn't lifting it. He was letting the head hang and drag, and the steel found every seam and joint and knot in the floor, and every one of them shuddered into her. She felt it climb her cheekbone into her back teeth. She felt it in the small bones of her ear like a wire being pulled slowly through them. Grit sifted down from the bedframe with each pass — dust, a curl of somebody's hair, flecks of paint — settling on her open eye, and she could not blink hard, could not move her hand to wipe it, because motion was noise and noise was the end.

The crying had started before she could catch it. It had started in her stomach, some animal thing that didn't ask her, and now it was in her throat, swelling, a fist trying to force its way out. She had her sleeve jammed into her mouth up to the second knuckle. Wool, wet through, tasting of salt and the copper smell of the house. She bit down until she felt her jaw creak and thought, absurdly, *he'll feel that too, he'll feel my teeth in the boards.*

Tears did not fall the way they should. Lying on her side, they ran sideways — down across the bridge of her nose, pooling in the hollow beside it, running warm into her ear where they cooled almost instantly. Her nose filled and she could not sniff. That was the worst of it, not the fear but the plain physical indignity of it: her sinuses swelling shut, her body demanding air through the only passage left while her mouth was stoppered with her own arm. She let her lips part around the wool. Drew a thread of air. Held it. The breath wanted to come out shaped like a word, like *please*, and she strangled it back down.

Her diaphragm was in revolt. It jumped, hitched, tried to sob without her permission, and each spasm knocked her ribs against the floor, and she was certain — absolutely certain — that he could feel her heartbeat coming up through his boot soles.

The dragging stopped.

The silence was not empty. It had weight and shape, the shape of a man standing still and listening. She could hear the wet click of her own throat swallowing. She could hear the blood in her head. Her whole body had become a thing that made sound, an unbearably loud machine, and she lay inside it begging it to be quiet.

A board settled. The axe head shifted — a single scrape, a quarter-inch, almost thoughtful — and the vibration went through her like a struck bell.

*Don't.* Her fingers closed on the tacked-down fabric of the bed's underside. *Don't don't don't.*

Somewhere behind her sternum the sob was still rising, patient as water finding a crack, and she understood with a terrible clarity that she could not win. That she would hold it for another ten seconds, or twenty, and then her body would betray her the way bodies always do, and she would make one small human sound.

She squeezed her eyes shut against the dust.

And the boards began, slowly, to speak again.

# The Fifth Sun

Ixtli had carried the water jar up the ninety-one steps every morning for three years, and never once had he been permitted past the threshold of the sanctuary. Today he stood inside it, and the smell of the place made his eyes water — copal smoke thick as wool, and beneath it something older, iron-sweet, soaked so deep into the plaster that no amount of lime-wash would ever lift it out.

Outside, the drums began.

They started slow, the great skin drum at the base of the pyramid, one beat for each breath a resting man takes. Then the shell trumpets found it, and then the voices — three hundred voices in the plaza below, the low unison chant that had no melody, only weight. *Tonatiuh, Tonatiuh, in mixtli, in xochitl.* Sun, sun, the cloud, the flower. The words came up the steps like water rising in a well.

The old priest, Tecpatl, did not look at him. "Hold the bowl at the level of my elbow. Not higher. Not lower. When I speak, you will not answer."

"Yes, Grandfather."

"He is not a goat." The old man's voice was flat, unhurried, as though correcting the placement of a mat. "You will not think of him as a goat. He has been the god for twenty days. He has eaten from the temple's plates and slept in the temple's rooms and the women have washed his feet. He is not a goat and this is not a slaughter, and if you vomit I will not forgive it."

The chanting swelled. Ixtli heard the sandals on the stone.

They brought him up between two attendants, though he did not need to be held. He was perhaps twenty, his body painted in chalk-white and blue, his hair bound with heron feathers, his face so calm it frightened Ixtli more than screaming would have. On each step he had broken a clay flute — Ixtli had heard them cracking, one by one, all the way up, the sound of a man discarding the instruments of his own music. His hands were empty now. He had nothing left to break.

He looked at Ixtli as he passed, and — this was the thing Ixtli would carry for the rest of his life — he smiled. A small, tired, ordinary smile. The kind a man gives a stranger at a well.

They laid him back over the sacrificial stone, the *techcatl*, a low block of basalt worn into a shallow curve by generations. It was cut so that when a man's spine bent across it his chest arched upward, offered, taut as a drumhead. Four attendants took his wrists and ankles. A fifth cradled his head. They did it gently. That was what no one had told Ixtli — how gentle it all was, how much it resembled the tending of the sick.

Tecpatl stepped to the head of the stone and raised his arms, and the chant below broke into a single sustained note, three hundred throats holding one open vowel, and the sound of it went into Ixtli's chest and sat there, buzzing in the hollow of his ribs.

The old priest took the knife from the cloth.

It was obsidian, and it was beautiful, and Ixtli understood suddenly why they used no other stone. Volcanic glass, black as the inside of a closed eye, flaked to an edge finer than any metal the smiths could hammer — an edge that ended, truly ended, in nothing at all. Its faces caught the brazier-light and threw it back in slow oily rainbows. The haft was wrapped in leather stained dark by hands. Ixtli had seen bronze blades and copper blades. They looked like tools. This looked like a decision.

"Ompa onquiza," Tecpatl said, and it was not to the crowd, and it was not to Ixtli. *There it goes out.*

The blade came down beneath the arch of the ribs, below the breastbone, a short transverse stroke, and the young man's body went rigid — not fighting, only the great involuntary bracing of flesh — and the note from the plaza climbed and climbed. Tecpatl set the knife on the stone. He did not fumble. His right hand went into the opening he had made, up under the sternum, along the diaphragm, with the unhesitating economy of a man reaching into a familiar dark cupboard for a familiar dark thing. Ixtli saw the muscles of his forearm turn.

There was a sound. Ixtli had no word for it then and never found one after.

And then it was out, and it was in the old man's fist, and it was still *going*. That was the horror and that was the whole point of it, Ixtli realized, all of it, the twenty days and the flutes and the ninety-one steps — that it should still be moving. It squeezed against the priest's fingers, blind and dutiful, three times, four, slower, a fist inside a fist. Blood ran down Tecpatl's wrist and dripped from his elbow into the bowl Ixtli held at exactly the level he had been told.

Tecpatl raised it toward the smoke-hole and the blue rectangle of sky.

"He climbs," the old priest said. "He climbs. He is the water and the drought is broken and the Sun eats and the Sun moves. Look at it, boy."

Ixtli looked. It was smaller than he had imagined. Everything was smaller than he had imagined.

Below them, the note broke apart into weeping and cheering, indistinguishable, one great animal noise of relief, and somewhere a woman was singing a lullaby at the top of her lungs.

The heart stopped moving.

Tecpatl laid it in the eagle vessel, wiped his hands on a cloth, and picked up the obsidian knife to clean it, because it was the most valuable thing in the room and would be needed again before the month was out.

"Now," he said. "The bowl. Steady. There are three more."

# The Terms

The knife lay on the table between them, and Vance had placed it there the way a host sets out a dish he's proud of.

"You're overthinking it," he said. "That's the trouble with men like you. You want a third door."

Behind him, through the doorway, Mira was singing. Six years old and tone-deaf and utterly unaware, arranging the buttons Vance's man had given her into a spiral on the floorboards. Something about a boat. She'd been singing it for weeks. Ilya had asked her, twice, to please sing something else, and now he would have given the rest of his life to hear the boat song for another hour.

"There is no third door," Vance said. "There's an eye, or there's her. And I want you to understand that I don't especially care which. That's the part you keep resisting. You keep looking for the answer that pleases me."

Ilya's hands were on his knees, and he could feel them there — a distant, dumb pressure, like the hands belonged to someone in the next room. All of him had gone remote. The despair wasn't sharp. He had expected sharpness, had braced for something like grief, and instead there was this: a flat grey weight settling through him from the crown of his head downward, filling him like sand poured into a sack. It pressed his organs down. It made his tongue heavy.

*This is what dying feels like,* he thought, *and I'm not even the one dying.*

Because there was no decision. That was the obscenity of it. Vance had framed it as a choice, had draped it in the language of agency — *you decide, it's yours, isn't that generous* — but Ilya had known the answer before the sentence finished. Any father would. That was the cruelty. Vance wasn't offering him a choice; he was offering him the *experience* of choosing, the theater of it, so that afterward Ilya would remember his own hand and not Vance's. So it would live in him as something he had done.

He understood, and understanding changed nothing, and that was where the despair actually lived — not in the loss ahead but in the perfect uselessness of his own mind. He could see the whole machine. He could not touch a single gear.

The boat song stopped. Started again from the beginning.

He reached for the knife.

His arm didn't want to go. There was a genuine resistance in it, a physical argument in the muscle, the way an arm refuses to press into cold water — and he had to push through that, had to *drive* the hand out over the tabletop while his shoulder locked and something in his chest tried to fold him in half. His breath came shallow and fast and useless, all at the top of his lungs, none of it reaching anywhere. Sweat had broken out along his hairline and in the small of his back; his shirt was suddenly cold against him.

The handle was bone or bone-colored and it was warmer than he expected. That was the detail that nearly broke him — the warmth. Someone had been holding it. Vance had been holding it, turning it in his hands while he talked, and now it carried a stranger's heat into Ilya's palm like an intimacy.

His fingers closed. They didn't feel like closing; they felt like watching a hand close on a screen. The weight of the thing was ridiculous, so much less than it should have been. Nothing this light should be able to do what it was about to do.

His eyes had begun to water — both of them, stupidly, in solidarity — and he thought, with a lurch of something almost like laughter, *how am I supposed to see well enough to*—

"Papa?"

He did not turn around. He would not have survived turning around.

"Keep singing, little bird," he said, and his voice came out steady, which was the last mercy he would ever be granted, and he was so grateful for it that a sob rose in his throat and he swallowed it whole.

The song resumed. Something about a boat, and a harbor, and coming home.

Ilya lifted the knife.
