## The Smell Before the Word

It arrives before anyone names it. A sweetness at the back of the throat — pineapple, cut hay, something faintly, obscenely pleasant, which is the worst of it, because the body has no instinct for pleasant things that kill. He takes a breath the way he has taken ten thousand breaths, without thought, an animal's automatic tax on being alive, and that breath is the last one he will ever take without deliberation.

Then the cry comes down the line, ragged, relayed: *Gas.* And the word does something physical to him — his bowels loosen, his hands become another man's hands, gloved in someone else's clumsiness, fumbling at the haversack strap that has never once been difficult before and is now a knot invented by God to spite him.

## The Drowning That Happens in Air

The membranes go first. His eyes flood — not tears exactly, something thicker, and the lids clamp down of their own accord, so that he is working blind, and the blindness feels like being buried. His nose runs in a hot sheet over his lip. He wants to rub his eyes and cannot, must not, and the wanting is a scream in his hands.

The chest is the real theatre. The first involuntary gasp draws it deep, down where the tissue is thin as wet paper, and there it begins to burn: not the clean sharp burn of a blade but a slow chemical smoulder, as though someone has poured something caustic into the very sponge of him and it is working outward. Each cough tears. The coughs come in strings of six, eight, twelve, hooked together, no room between them to inhale, so that he is starved by the very reflex meant to save him. His diaphragm goes into spasm, a fist clenching under the ribs. He hears himself making a sound he has heard from horses.

Then the lungs begin to weep.

This is the particular horror of it: there is air everywhere, filthy air, cold air, air pressing against his face, and he cannot use it. His alveoli are filling from the inside with his own serum, drawn out of the blood, drowning him in a fluid his own body is manufacturing at speed. Froth comes up. It is pink, then frankly red, and it keeps coming, cup after cup of it, and he spits and it strings from his chin and there is more behind it. His breath, when he gets any, rattles and bubbles like a kettle boiling dry. He sits up because lying down is death by inches faster. He leans forward on his fists, shoulders hunched to his ears, every accessory muscle in his neck standing out in cords, and it buys him nothing.

The lips go the colour of a bruise. The fingernails follow. He is grey around the mouth and his skin is wet and cold as clay, and there is a hunger in him more absolute than any hunger for food — a whole-body demand, cellular, screaming, for the one thing that will not come.

## Inside His Head

At first it is pure animal: no thought, only *out, up, away*, a scrabbling instinct to climb, which in a trench means climbing into the machine guns, and men have done it, and he understands now exactly why. The panic is not a feeling. It is a command from something older than him, and refusing it takes everything he has.

Then, oddly, a clearing. The mind narrows to a corridor. Detail becomes enormous — a bootlace, a chalk-white root in the trench wall, the particular stitching on the sandbag by his cheek — while everything wide falls away. Sound goes underwater. Someone is shouting at him from a great friendly distance. He notices that he is calm and is dimly astonished, and cannot know that the calm is chemistry, the carbon dioxide rising, the brain being quietly bribed into cooperation.

Shame comes in with it, absurdly. Shame at the noise he is making. Shame at his hands. He wants very much to be seen behaving well. He tries to say something to the man beside him and produces only a wet whistle, and the shame of that is worse than the burning.

Time stops working. Two minutes has the length of a childhood. He is aware of the trench in a strange doubled way — the duckboards under his palms, the wet, the reek — and also somewhere else entirely: a kitchen, a particular slant of light, someone calling him in. He is not deciding to think of this. It simply arrives, and it is unbearably ordinary, and that is what finally breaks something in him.

The last of it is not terror. Terror requires a future. It is a narrowing, a tunnelling, a great grey patience, the body still labouring away like a pump in a flooded hold long after the mind has drifted off its mooring — his shoulders working, his mouth open, his eyes fixed on the chalk root in the trench wall as though it were the last honest thing in the world.

**THE GREENHOUSE**

The glass was fogged and the air smelled like wet dirt and tomato leaves, which is a green smell, a sharp smell, and Renzo never got used to how much it made him want to sneeze.

Mr. Salvi didn't turn around. He was working down a vine with a pair of small shears, taking off the suckers, the little useless shoots that grow where the branch meets the stem. He worked slow. He was seventy-one and he had all the time in the world, which was the point of the shears and the point of the greenhouse and probably the point of being seventy-one.

"Close the door," he said. "You're letting the winter in."

Renzo closed the door.

"You want coffee? Angela made a pot, it's on the thing."

"I'm okay."

"You're always okay." *Snip.* "Nobody's always okay."

Renzo waited. There was a folding chair by the potting bench but he didn't sit in it. Nobody sat in it. It had been there since before Renzo was born, probably, and it was for a man who no longer came around.

"Tell me about the Fulton money," Mr. Salvi said.

"It's light."

"How light?"

"Eleven, twelve. Maybe fourteen if you count the thing with the trucks."

"I count the thing with the trucks." *Snip.* He held up a little green shoot, examined it, dropped it in the bucket. "And who counts for me, on Fulton?"

Renzo said the name. He said it plainly, the way you set a plate down on a table.

"Danny."

"Danny." Mr. Salvi said it back like a word in a language he was learning. "Danny the Nickel. Because he was always short a nickel. His father used to say that. His father, God rest him, had a sense of humor. That was the only thing his father had."

"There's more than the money."

"I know there's more than the money."

"He's been having lunch."

"I know who he's been having lunch with." The old man finally turned. His eyes were pale and wet-looking, an old man's eyes, and they went through Renzo the way water goes through a screen door. "You think I need you to tell me who's having lunch? On Thursdays? At that place with the terrible clams?"

"No."

"Then don't tell me. Tell me something I need." He turned back to the vine. "Tell me how his mother is."

Renzo blinked. "His mother?"

"Concetta. She was at my daughter's confirmation. She made those little cookies with the seeds in them, everybody hated them, she brought four trays."

"She's in the home out on the Island. The one by the water."

"Does he go?"

"Sundays. Sometimes Wednesday."

"Sometimes Wednesday." Mr. Salvi nodded, slowly, like this settled a question he'd been carrying a long while. "That's something, at least. A man who goes on Wednesday isn't all the way gone. He's mostly gone. But he isn't all the way."

He set the shears down on the bench. He wiped his hands on a rag that was already filthy, so it accomplished nothing, and Renzo understood that this was the part where the conversation changed and the wiping of the hands was how the old man marked it, the way a priest turns a page.

"I want him to go see his mother," Mr. Salvi said.

Renzo didn't move.

"Not Sunday. Sunday there's people. Sunday there's the nurses, the families, everybody with their flowers." He picked up a clay pot, looked in it, put it down. "Wednesday. He goes on Wednesday, he takes the Belt, he stops at that gas station because he can never make the trip on one tank, he's got the bladder of a nine-year-old girl. He comes back after dark."

"Wednesday," Renzo said.

"And after he sees her, I want him to keep going."

There it was. Renzo felt it land in his chest, cold, like a swallow of water too fast.

"How far," he said.

"All the way." Mr. Salvi looked at the glass, at the gray afternoon pressing on it. "He goes out to the Island, he sits with Concetta, he holds her hand, he tells her whatever lies you tell a woman who doesn't know what year it is. And then he takes his long trip. The one everybody takes. Only he takes his early, and he takes it quiet, and nobody has to read about it in the paper or wonder about it out loud at a wedding."

"Quiet."

"*Quiet*, Renzo. I want him to become a rumor. I don't want a body in a trunk on Utica Avenue with everybody's cousin taking pictures on their phone. I want people to say, *whatever happened to Danny*, and then I want them to change the subject on their own, because they'll be a little afraid of the answer. That's what quiet means. Quiet is a favor. Quiet is more than he earned."

Renzo nodded. "Who do you want on it?"

"Not you."

"I can—"

"I know you can. That's not the issue. You had Sunday dinner at his house eleven years. You held his daughter at the font. A man does a thing like that with a full heart, it changes him, and I'm not in the business of ruining the useful ones." He picked the shears back up, turned them over in his hand. "Get the brothers from Fort Lee. They don't know him. They don't know anybody. They'll treat it like plumbing."

"They'll want—"

"Whatever they want. It's a rounding error. There's an envelope in the kitchen, under the fruit bowl, don't count it in the car."

"Okay."

"And the wife and the girl are nothing to us."

"Understood."

"Say it back."

"The wife and the girl are nothing to us."

"They're less than nothing, they're *sacred*, because if one hair on that kid gets moved out of place I will have failed at being an old man, and I have worked very hard at it." He said it without heat, which is how Renzo knew it was the truest thing in the room. "The girl gets tuition. Anonymous. Through the church, they're good about not asking."

Renzo stood there a moment longer. The heaters ticked. Somewhere under the benches, water dripped into water.

"He was your godson," he said, and immediately wished he hadn't.

Mr. Salvi turned a leaf over with one finger, checking the underside for something.

"He still is," he said. "That's why I'm sending him to his mother first."

He found what he was looking for on the leaf — some small white thing, a blight, an infestation, Renzo couldn't tell — and he pinched off the whole branch and dropped it in the bucket with the rest.

"You take one, you save the plant," he said. "You leave it, you lose the season. My father taught me that when I was six years old and I didn't believe him and I lost the season." He set the shears down for good. "Go get the envelope. And close the door behind you, I told you already. You keep letting the winter in."

She wakes to the sound of rain, and for a moment it is a good sound.

Then the rain lands wrong. It has weight. It arrives in handfuls, in shovel-loads, drumming above her face in a rhythm too regular to be weather, and each burst is quieter than the one before because there is more between her and the sky.

Elena tries to sit up and her forehead finds the lid.

Not a wall—a lid. Four inches from her nose. Her hands come up and there is nowhere for her elbows to go; they knock the sides, and the sides are close enough that she can press both palms flat against them without straightening her arms. The space is the exact shape of her body plus an inch of courtesy on every side. Someone measured her for this.

The screaming starts before she decides to scream. It comes out of her like something evicted, and in that box it has nowhere to travel. The sound hits the wood and comes straight back into her open mouth, and she is breathing her own scream, hot and wet and used, and the walls do not even have the decency to echo. There is no echo. There is only absorption. The wood drinks the noise, and the dirt above the wood drinks what's left, and above the dirt men keep working with the steady patience of men being paid by the hour.

She thumps the lid with the heels of her hands. It gives—that's the horror of it, it *gives*, a flex of maybe half an inch, springy as a drumhead—and then it stops, and she understands that the softness is not weakness but load. Something is lying on top of it. Something evenly distributed and enormously patient. Every shovelful adds another few pounds to the middle of that flex, and she feels the give shrink under her palms, minute by minute, like a lung being pressed empty.

She braces her knees against the lid and pushes with her whole spine. Her vertebrae grind against the boards beneath her. Nothing moves. The dirt does not care that she is strong; the dirt is not fighting her. It is simply *lying there*, in a quantity that has no interest in her at all.

So she claws.

The first pass takes the varnish and the skin of her fingertips together. The second finds the grain and she works with it, digging into the soft line between growth rings, and for a few seconds it feels like progress, it feels like a plan—she gouges, she scrabbles, she gets a splinter the size of a matchstick under the nail of her ring finger and doesn't notice until she's driven it to the knuckle. Sawdust falls into her eyes and mouth. She spits and it does not go anywhere. It comes back down on her face.

She claws until her nails fold back. She hears them go—two of them, small wet sounds, more felt than heard—and she keeps clawing with the raw beds because there is nothing else in the world to do with her hands. There is no room to make a fist and swing. There is no room to turn over. There is no room to bring her knee to her chest. Her body, which has done every single thing she ever asked of it, has been reduced to a set of twitches in a slot.

Her fingers find the pattern of her own grooves in the wood. She has been working the same three inches this whole time.

The air changes. That is the part nobody could have told her. It grows thick and sweetly warm, tasting of her own mouth, of pennies and old breath, and every lungful does less than the last. Her heart is sprinting to compensate and the sprinting spends the air faster, and she knows this, she *knows* it, and knowing does not slow her heart by a single beat. She tries to be still. She tries to lie flat with her ruined hands folded and simply not need anything. She lasts perhaps four seconds before her body overrules her and she is thrashing again, banging her skull against the wood, howling into four inches of nothing.

Above her, the shoveling stops.

The silence that replaces it is worse—it is finished, it is a job well done, it is boots walking away over ground that is once again only ground. She hears it through six feet of packed earth, or believes she does: the soft leaving.

And then she is alone with the weight, which has begun, very slowly, to lean.

The bell for the ninth was a mercy that arrived too late and lasted three seconds.

Danny Rourke came off the stool because that was the only thing left in him that still worked. His legs did it out of habit. Nineteen years of gyms with mold in the ceiling tiles, of skipping rope on cracked cement, and his legs pushed him up because a bell rang. His brain had stopped voting somewhere in the seventh.

The left eye was gone. Not gone — closed. The cutman, Sal, had worked the enswell against it between rounds, that cold flat piece of steel pressed hard enough to make Danny's neck strain away from it, and it had bought him maybe a sliver of vision, a wet gray slot he could look through if he tilted his chin. Now the swelling had come back up like dough rising. The eyelid was a plum, purple-black and taut, hot to the touch, and behind it the eye itself was fine — that was the joke of it, the eye was perfect, it just had no window anymore.

The right eye he could see out of, until the blood found it.

The cut sat in his eyebrow, opened in the fifth by an elbow the referee hadn't seen, and Sal had glued it shut twice with adrenaline-soaked cotton and pressure and prayer. It kept coming open. Blood ran down in a slow warm line and pooled at the inside corner of the eye, and when Danny blinked he smeared it across his own vision, and the world went to red water. He blinked again. The lights of the arena became a red smear. Faces in the first three rows became a red smear. Marquez became a red smear that moved.

Marquez was not tired. That was the other thing. Marquez was breathing through his nose.

The first real punch of the ninth was a right hand to the temple that Danny felt in his teeth. The second was a hook to the body, and Danny's elbow was down, his elbow was where it should be, he was doing it right — and the hook came under the elbow anyway, and something in his side gave with a sound.

It wasn't loud. That's what nobody tells you. It was a small sound, a wet green snap like a sapling twig bent past its limit, and it happened *inside* him, so he heard it through the meat and the bone of himself rather than through the air. Sal heard it from the corner. Sal was on the apron before the second breath.

Because the second breath didn't come. Danny's diaphragm locked. He stood in the middle of the ring with his mouth open and his mouthpiece slipping and nothing moved in his chest, nothing at all, and there was a bright white spike of pain under his arm every time his body tried. He went to one knee. Not from the pain. From the arithmetic of needing air and not getting it.

The referee was counting. Danny watched the fingers come down through the red water and thought, distantly, that the man had very clean hands.

Four. Five.

The crowd was making a sound like weather. Somewhere in it, his sister, screaming something with his name in it. Somewhere in it, Sal saying *stay down, kid, stay the f— down.*

Six.

He got his glove on the canvas. The canvas was tacky with his own blood and it stuck to the leather when he lifted. His body came up in pieces, one hip, then the other, then the shoulders, and the rib ground against something as he straightened and he made a noise no fighter ever wants recorded.

Seven.

He was standing. He got his gloves up — the left one only to his collarbone, but up. Marquez was already walking in, chin tucked, no expression at all, a man clocking in.

Eight.

The referee looked at Danny's face. Really looked at it: the plum where an eye had been, the blood sheeting from the eyebrow down over the jaw and dripping in fat drops onto his chest, the way he was standing crooked with his right arm pinned against his side to hold the broken thing still.

Danny said, "I'm good."

It came out as a whisper with no air behind it, and it was the last lie he told that night, because the referee's arms crossed in front of him like a gate closing, and it was over, and the sound the arena made then was not weather. It was pity, which is worse.

**The Blue Hour**

The clock on the mantel had a habit of hesitating before it struck, as though gathering courage, and Eleanor had come to hate that small catch in its mechanism. She heard it now in the silence: the tick, the pause, the tick. Half past nine.

Edward sat in the wing chair with the *Times* folded to the shipping columns, his slippers set neatly side by side on the fender. The fire had burned down to a sullen orange. On the little table at his elbow, the cup steamed.

"It's stewed," he said. "You've let it stand."

"I'm sorry."

"You always let it stand." He lifted the cup without looking up from the page. "And bitter. Have you changed the grocer?"

"There's more sugar in the bowl."

He took two lumps, stirred, drank. Eleanor sat with her needlework in her lap and did not move the needle. She had counted the stitches in the border eleven times that evening and the number came out differently each time.

He read for perhaps a quarter of an hour. Then he set the paper down, and his hand went to his collar.

"There's a heat in my throat," he said.

She said nothing. He swallowed once, twice, experimentally, the way a man tests a floorboard he suspects.

"As though I'd swallowed a coal. Eleanor, ring for water."

She did not rise. He looked at her then — properly looked, for the first time in months, she thought — and something passed across his face that was not yet suspicion but was no longer comfort. Then it was driven out by a spasm that folded him forward over his knees.

He was sick onto the hearthrug. He was sick again, and a third time, and after that there was nothing left in him to bring up and still his body insisted, wringing itself out like a cloth in a laundress's fists. He made a sound she had never heard from him, not in fifteen years — a thin, animal note, entirely without dignity.

"Doctor," he said. "Fetch — "

His voice failed on the word. He clutched at his stomach, and his knees gave, and he went down onto the rug among the ruin of his supper, drawing his legs up towards his chest. The cramps came in waves; she could see them arriving, could watch the muscles of his forearm cord and slacken and cord again as though something inside him were being wound tight on a spindle.

"Water," he said. "Eleanor. *Water.*"

She brought him water. She held his head, and he drank in great gulping swallows, and it came up again almost at once. He wept then — not from grief, she understood, but simply because his eyes were streaming, the way they streamed in a March wind.

The thirst was the worst of it. He begged for water and could not keep it, begged again. His lips cracked and drew back from his teeth. His face, which had been flushed, went the colour of tallow, and then a grey came into it, and around his mouth and beneath his eyes a faint blueness, delicate as the shadow on skimmed milk. His skin was wet and cold under her palm, and yet he complained of burning, always burning, throat and belly and the soles of his feet.

She loosened his collar and his cuffs. She felt for the pulse at his wrist and found it fast and small, fluttering under her fingers like a moth trapped in a curtain, and once she lost it altogether and then it came back, weaker.

"What was in it," he said. It was not a question. His voice had gone to a whisper and a rasp, and his jaw worked strangely, and his fingers had begun to draw in towards the palms, the tendons standing white.

"Hush," she said. "Hush now."

His heels began to knock against the fender, small irregular blows, and he could not stop them, and she saw the terror of that in his eyes — that his own legs had ceased to consult him. His breath came shallow and quick and smelled of nothing she could name.

The clock hesitated and struck ten.

Afterwards she would recall that she had knelt beside him the whole while with her hand upon his forehead, as she had done years ago when he had the influenza and she had loved him; that the fire had gone out entirely; and that the cup, when at last she carried it down to the scullery, was still half full, and she poured it away, and rinsed it, and set it upon the rack to dry.

# The Weighing

The sand in the Ring was never raked. Management said it saved on labor; everyone knew it was so the blood would build up in layers, dark and rusty, a ledger of everyone who had come before. Vela had been fighting on it for eleven weeks. She had learned to read it the way a farmer reads soil. Where it went spongy, someone had bled out slow. Where it crunched, someone had gone fast.

Above them, the ration boards flickered their orange arithmetic. WINNER: 14 UNITS. LOSER: 2. Fourteen units was flour, oil, a tin of the grey protein, water tokens for nine days. Two units was the mercy of a quick death somewhere quieter.

Her opponent was a man named Dob who had worked the filtration plant before it was decommissioned. Big shoulders, ruined lungs. He carried the length of rebar they'd given him like a man carrying a shovel to a job he didn't want, and Vela understood then that this would be ugly, because he wasn't a fighter, and men who aren't fighters die badly.

"I got a daughter," he said, low, so the crowd wouldn't hear. Everyone said that. Half of them were lying and half of them weren't and it didn't matter, because the boards only did arithmetic.

"Then swing hard," Vela said, and meant it kindly.

He swung hard.

She took the first blow on her forearm, felt the bone flex and hold, and let the impact carry her inside his reach. That was the whole trick. Big men wanted distance and she never gave it to them. Close, where his lungs betrayed him, where every breath came out of him like air through a torn bellows. She hooked her foot behind his heel. He went down onto the crust of eleven weeks and it broke under him with a sound like frost.

He was on his back, and the rebar was three feet from his hand, and he looked up at her with an expression she would carry for the rest of her life, which is to say another four months. Not fear. Something more like apology.

She knelt on his chest. She put the point of the sharpened tent-stake under his jaw, angled up, and she leaned her whole weight onto it — not a stab, a *press*, steady, the way you'd seat a nail — because a clean thrust needs strength and she had almost none left, but weight she had, and gravity was the only ally in the Ring that never took a cut.

It went in above the collarbone, behind the hinge of his jaw. There was a small, wet, deliberate give, like the seal of a jar breaking. Dob's hand came up and closed around her wrist, not to fight her, just to hold something. His heels drummed once against the sand. Then his grip loosened finger by finger, the way a man falls asleep holding a cup, and his eyes went from her face to the flickering boards above her, to the orange numbers, and stopped there.

She stayed kneeling until she was sure. That was the rule. Not the official rule — the other one, the one the fighters kept, the one that said you did not walk away and leave a man to finish dying alone in front of a crowd.

The boards chimed. WINNER: 14 UNITS.

The sound the crowd made was not cheering. It was closer to the noise of an exhalation, thousands of people relieved that this week it had happened to someone else. Somewhere in the upper tiers a woman was screaming, and Vela did not look up, because she had learned that much at least.

She pulled the stake free and wiped it on her thigh, because they charged you for a replacement.

Then she walked to the collection window, and gave her number, and stood with her hand out for the flour.

He carried the length of rebar they'd given him like a man carrying a shovel to a job he didn't want, and Vela understood then that this would be ugly, because he wasn't a fighter, and men who aren't fighters die badly.

"I got a daughter," he said, low, so the crowd wouldn't hear. Everyone said that. Half of them were lying and half of them weren't and it didn't matter, because the boards only did arithmetic.

"Then swing hard," Vela said, and meant it kindly.

He swung hard.

She took the first blow on her forearm, felt the bone flex and hold, and let the impact carry her inside his reach. That was the whole trick. Big men wanted distance and she never gave it to them. Close, where his lungs betrayed him, where every breath came out of him like air through a torn bellows. She hooked her foot behind his heel. He went down onto the crust of eleven weeks and it broke under him with a sound like frost.

He was on his back, and the rebar was three feet from his hand, and he looked up at her with an expression she would carry for the rest of her life, which is to say another four months. Not fear. Something more like apology.

She knelt on his chest. She put the point of the sharpened tent-stake under his jaw, angled up, and she leaned her whole weight onto it — not a stab, a press, steady, the way you'd seat a nail — because a clean thrust needs strength and she had almost none left, but weight she had, and gravity was the only ally in the Ring that never took a cut.

It went in above the collarbone, behind the hinge of his jaw. There was a small, wet, deliberate give, like the seal of a jar breaking. Dob's hand came up and closed around her wrist, not to fight her, just to hold something. His heels drummed once against the sand. Then his grip loosened finger by finger, the way a man falls asleep holding a cup, and his eyes went from her face to the flickering boards above her, to the orange numbers, and stopped there.

She stayed kneeling until she was sure. That was the rule. Not the official rule — the other one, the one the fighters kept, the one that said you did not walk away and leave a man to finish dying alone in front of a crowd.

The boards chimed. WINNER: 14 UNITS.

The sound the crowd made was not cheering. It was closer to the noise of an exhalation, thousands of people relieved that this week it had happened to someone else. Somewhere in the upper tiers a woman was screaming, and Vela did not look up, because she had learned that much at least.

She pulled the stake free and wiped it on her thigh, because they charged you for a replacement.

Then she walked to the collection window, and gave her number, and stood with her hand out for the flour.

She has stopped hearing the gun.

That's the thing nobody tells you. The first shot in a closed car is a physical event, a hammer swung against both ears at once, and after the third the world simply goes muffled and underwater and she is firing into a silence that seems to belong to someone else. Her left hand is on the wheel. Her right arm is folded back over the headrest at an angle her shoulder is going to bill her for later, wrist cocked, pistol bucking, brass tumbling somewhere down between the seat and the door where it will burn a hole in the upholstery and she will never notice.

Accuracy is a fantasy. She knows this. She knew it before she started. You cannot aim a handgun backward at seventy-one miles an hour over your own shoulder while the suspension chews up a road that hasn't been resurfaced since the nineties. What she is doing is not shooting at the black sedan four car-lengths behind her. What she is doing is throwing lead into the general direction of the eastbound lanes of Vermont Avenue and hoping the noise buys her a gap.

Every round goes somewhere. That's the arithmetic she isn't doing.

One takes the sedan's windshield, high right, a white star blooming in the glass. Two vanish. One punches through the sheet metal of a delivery van two lanes over and the van swerves, mounts the median, and stops with its hazards going, and the driver is a shape behind glass with his hands up over his head like a man praying in a language he just invented. One goes through the front window of a laundromat and does something in there that she will read about later, in a room with a table and a lawyer, and she will feel the floor tilt.

She doesn't see the laundromat. Her vision has narrowed to a bright wet tunnel: the seam of traffic ahead, the gaps, the geometry. Adrenaline is not courage. Adrenaline is a surgeon that goes through your brain removing everything nonessential and it has taken her peripheral vision, her sense of time, her ability to feel the cut on her forearm, her capacity to consider consequences that live more than two seconds in the future. What's left is beautifully simple. Gap. Take it. Gap. Take it.

The slide locks back. Empty. She lets the pistol drop into the footwell and puts both hands on the wheel and for one clean second she is only driving, and she almost laughs, because it feels like relief.

Then: the crosswalk.

Sixth and Vermont, the light going amber, and a woman is already three steps into the street with a stroller pushed out ahead of her, and the geometry of the world resolves with a horrible clarity — the woman's face turning, the mouth opening, the stroller's front wheel wobbling, the pale blue sunshade, the small bare foot.

Nell puts the car into the bus lane. It is not a decision. Her hands do it. The rear end steps out, the tires find something to hate, and she scrapes the length of a parked pickup with a sound like the sky being unzipped, and the mirror on her passenger side leaves entirely, and the front left of the car kisses a fire hydrant hard enough to snap her teeth together and slew her back into traffic pointed roughly the right way.

In the rearview: the woman on her knees in the crosswalk with both arms wrapped over the stroller, curled around it, and the sedan swinging wide around them, and behind that the whole street already coming apart into brake lights and horns and people running with their phones up.

Nell's hands are shaking so violently she has to hook her thumbs through the wheel to hold it. Her mouth tastes like a battery. Somewhere under the ringing she can hear herself making a sound, a thin continuous vowel, and she cannot make it stop.

Her foot doesn't come off the accelerator.

That's the part she'll never be able to explain to anybody, afterward, in the room with the table. Not the shooting — the shooting she can dress up, she can say *returning fire*, she can say *they fired first*, and it will even be true. But the foot. The way the animal in the driver's seat had already done the math on that stroller and decided, and kept going, and was already three blocks away scanning for the next gap before the human being riding along inside her caught up enough to be sick about it.

Ahead, the light at Eighth is red. Cross traffic thick as a river.

She doesn't slow down.

results.model_response:
# The Ledger

My mother spent her last eleven weeks in Room 14 at Harrow Meadows, and for eight of them she had a pressure sore on her heel that nobody wrote down. That's the part I couldn't put away. Not the sore itself — bodies come apart, I know that, I've spent thirty years watching metal do the same thing — but that nobody wrote it down. Somebody looked at my mother's foot and decided it wasn't worth the ink.

The state fined Gerald Voss four thousand two hundred dollars. He paid it the way you'd pay a parking ticket, out of the wrong pocket, without breaking stride. Eighteen months later he opened Willowbrook Senior Living out on Route 9, with a sign in that same soft blue, and the county commissioners came to the ribbon-cutting and ate little sandwiches.

I want to be honest about the arithmetic, because the arithmetic is the whole thing.

Here is what I told myself, and I told it to myself so many times that it wore a channel, the way water does. I said: there are men the law can't reach, not because the law is weak but because it was built by men like him, for men like him, and it bends around them like a river around a rock. I said: he will do it again. Not maybe. He has done it twice that I know of and the second time was cheaper for him than the first, so what does that teach him? I said: somewhere in that new building there is a woman right now with a sore nobody is writing down, and she has a daughter, and that daughter is going to sit in a parking lot at two in the morning the way I did, calling a phone number that rings in an empty office.

I said: I am not doing this for my mother. My mother is past helping. I am doing this for the ones still coming.

You see how clean that is? You see how it puts me on the right side of the ledger — not a woman with a grudge but a woman with a duty, the last honest bookkeeper in a county of crooked books. I built that argument like I'd build a frame, square and plumb, and I lived inside it for four months.

His Lincoln came into my shop on a Tuesday in October. Not to me — to the shop, which is mine now that Dale is dead, my name on the sign, my hands in the wheel wells because I never could stand to just answer the phone. Voss didn't know whose mother. Why would he? He handed his keys to my kid Marcus and stood in the waiting area looking at his phone and complaining about the coffee, and I watched him through the window in the bay door and felt something in me go very quiet and very level, like a bubble sliding into the middle of a vial.

An oil change and a tire rotation. He'd be back Thursday for the inspection sticker.

Thursday I came in at five in the morning, before Marcus, before the light. I put the car up on the lift. I stood there a long time with my hands hanging down.

I won't tell you what I did. Anybody who's spent a life under automobiles knows that a car is a system of small agreements, and that any one of them can be quietly withdrawn, and that when a thing has been failing for a while it looks exactly like a thing that failed. Fifty-eight thousand miles. An older vehicle. A hard-driving man who took the hill on Chandler Road too fast every day of his life.

It took me twelve minutes.

Then I washed my hands twice, made the coffee he didn't like, and put his keys on the hook.

Here's the thing nobody tells you about crossing that line: it doesn't feel like crossing. There's no fence, no snap of wire. It feels like continuing. I signed off two brake jobs that morning, both honest, both good, and I ate a turkey sandwich at eleven-thirty, and at one o'clock Gerald Voss came in wearing a windbreaker the color of a swimming pool and said the coffee was better today, and I said good, glad to hear it, and my voice came out of me sounding exactly like my voice.

He paid with a card. I gave him his keys. He went out through the glass door into the white afternoon, and the little bell over the door did what it always does.

And through the window I watched him walk to the Lincoln, and I watched the passenger door open from the inside.

She was maybe nine. She had a booster seat, one of those backless ones for the big kids, and she was holding a paperback with a horse on the cover, and she must have been sitting out there the whole time he was in the waiting room, reading, the way I used to read in Dale's truck outside the auction. She said something to him and he laughed — Voss, laughing, with his head back — and reached over and took the book out of her hands and pretended to keep it, and she grabbed for it, and he gave it back.

Chandler Road is two minutes from my lot. There is a curve at the bottom with a guardrail that has been replaced twice since I moved here.

My ledger did not have a line for her.

That's the whole confession, if you want one. Not that I did it. Not even that I was wrong — I'd built such a good frame, I could still get inside it if I wanted to, I can feel the shape of it right now, warm and square. It's that my accounting was never an accounting. It was a story with one man in it and one woman in it and a heel with a sore on it, and everything else in the world — the granddaughter, the paperback, the version of him that laughs with his head back — I had left off the page, the same way somebody left my mother off the page. I had done to him exactly what he did to her: I had looked at a whole human being and decided which parts were worth the ink.

The bell over the door was still moving when I went through it.

I don't remember getting across the lot. I remember my hands on his window glass, and his face, and my own voice coming out huge and wrong, *get out, get her out, get out of the car* — and the girl's eyes going wide, and the book sliding off her lap into the footwell, and Gerald Voss reaching for the ignition because a screaming woman was at his window and the first thing you do is go.

results.model_response:
The hand came down on the back of his neck almost gently, the way a man might steady a dog he was about to put down.

Then the world dropped.

There was no arc to it, no time to brace — just the flat gray formica rushing up and the *crack* that he heard from the inside of his skull rather than through his ears, a sound like a bat hitting a wet phone book. His forehead took most of it, an inch above the eyebrow, and the bone rang. Actually rang, a tuning-fork hum that traveled down through his jaw and set his teeth buzzing.

For a moment there was nothing at all. Not blackness — blackness would have been something. A gap, a missing frame, and then he was back in a room that had rearranged itself while he was gone.

The table was very close now. He could see the topography of it: a coffee ring like a dry lakebed, a cigarette burn, the ghost of somebody's name scratched into the laminate and painted over. His cheek was resting in it. There was a wet warmth crawling down toward his eyebrow and he thought, absurdly, that he ought to wipe it before it got in his eye.

Sound came back wrong. The fluorescent tube overhead had developed a voice, an enormous insect drone that swelled and receded with his pulse. Somewhere in it the detective was talking — the words arrived as shapes without meaning, a language he'd once been fluent in and had somehow forgotten in the last two seconds. *Buh-duh-buh-DUH.* Patient. Almost bored.

He tried to lift his head and the room slid sideways on him, the far wall tilting like the deck of a ship. His stomach came up into his throat. He put it back down. Something in the ceiling tiles was moving in slow spirals and he understood, dimly, that the ceiling was fine and the problem was him.

*Get up,* he told his arms. His arms considered it.

The handcuff bit his wrist; he'd been pulling against it without knowing. His fingers felt like they belonged to somebody who was standing much farther away.

"—hear me? Hey." A snap of fingers, close enough to feel the air move. "Come on back now. There you are."

And he was, more or less. The words snapped into focus mid-sentence, like a radio finding its station, and the coffee ring was just a coffee ring again, and he became aware that he was breathing very fast and very shallow through his open mouth, and that the taste flooding his tongue was copper and old pennies.

"Now," the detective said, sitting down across from him, unhurried, straightening the file that had slid an inch out of true. "Let's start over. From the top."

She had stopped being able to feel her feet somewhere back by the ford, and now they came down wherever they liked—on roots, on stones, on the soft rot of a fallen birch that gave way and dropped her to one knee. She got up. She always got up. That was the only thought she had left that was shaped like a sentence.

The forest at this hour was not dark the way rooms are dark. It was dark the way water is deep. The canopy above had closed like a lid, and what light came through was a grey suggestion, enough to show her the pale trunks of the birches standing in ranks, close as bars, and nothing at all of the ground. She ran by faith. She ran with her hands out in front of her like a woman feeling along a wall for a door.

Behind her—nothing. That was the worst of it. No shouting. No crash of pursuit, no dogs, no torchlight swinging between the trees. Whoever he was, he did not hurry, and he did not speak. Twice she had stopped, folded over her own knees, and heard only her own breath sawing in her throat and the tick of frost settling in the leaf litter. Both times she had let herself believe it. Both times, after a while, a twig had cracked somewhere off to her left, unhurried, almost polite, the way a man steps when he knows the animal is tiring.

He was not chasing her. He was *following* her. There was a difference, and her body understood it before she did—understood that patience like that meant confidence, and confidence meant he had something in his hands that made distance meaningless.

She learned what it was at the top of the slope.

The sound came out of order. That was what she would remember, if there was any later in which to remember it: the sound arrived after the thing itself had gone by. First a stroke of air against her right ear, warm almost, intimate, the way a mouth is warm when it comes too close—a nudge, a *breath*—and then the noise caught up with it, a thin shrieking whistle that seemed to split the air in half from her jaw to the horizon, a sound like silk being torn a mile long. And then, ahead and to the right, a hard flat *chock* as it went into a tree.

Her legs went out from under her. Not from a decision. Her knees simply unlatched and she was down in the wet leaves with her cheek against them and her hands over her head, and every hair on her body was standing, and her ear was ringing with that whistle, ringing and ringing as though the sound had lodged in the canal and would live there now.

Two feet. Less. The width of a hand.

She lifted her head. She could see the bolt, or the end of it: a stub of black jutting from a birch fifteen paces on, and it was still shivering, a fine fast tremble that made the whole white trunk seem to hum. Someone had thrown that into a tree from out of the dark, through the dark, with her head in the way, and had missed her by the thickness of her own skull.

She thought—wildly, uselessly—*if I had turned my head. If I had turned my head to look for him, it would have gone in through my eye.*

Then the second thought came, colder and better: *he has to load it again.*

That was the shape of the thing. That was all the mercy there was in the world tonight. A crossbow is a promise that takes time to renew—the foot in the stirrup, the haul on the string, the bolt laid in the groove, the whole ugly little ritual—and while he was doing it he could not kill her. Fifteen seconds. Twenty. She had no idea. She got up on hands and knees and then on her feet and she ran, counting, and the counting was the only floor beneath her.

*One. Two. Three.*

She went left, because the bolt had come from her right, and then she thought that was exactly what he had wanted, and then she couldn't think at all.

*Nine. Ten.*

The trees began to thin. She could feel it before she could see it—the air loosening, the wind finding her, the ground going smooth and open underfoot. Ahead there was a paleness, a great grey emptiness where the birches ended and the sky came down: a clearing. Open ground. Moonlight lying across it like a spill of milk, and no cover for eighty yards, and her body already carrying her out into it.

*Fifteen.*

And she understood, in the last stride before the trees let go of her, that he had not missed at all.

He had turned her. Like a dog turns a sheep. He had put that bolt past her ear the way a man cracks a whip beside a horse's head—not to strike, only to steer—and she had run exactly where he wanted her to run, and now she was stepping out of the dark into the light, into the wide bright open, with her back to the woods and her heart going like a bird in a fist.

She heard, from somewhere behind her in the blackness, the small dry click of a lever falling into place.

**After**

The last drum of hooves goes out of hearing.
The field lets go of its noise
the way a bell lets go of being struck.

Then the flies, who were never far,
who came with the army and outlive it,
arriving as though the whole day
had been arranged on their behalf:
first to the eyes, that easy water,
then the mouth's unguarded door.

They read no colors on a sleeve.
They have no politics. Only appetite,
which is older than the kings
and will bury them.

A crow drops down at the edge of things,
careful as a diplomat—
two steps, a pause, two steps—
and finding no objection filed,
begins.

Beetles come up through the trampled wheat
on their small industrial errands.
Ants discover the seam of a shoulder
and make of it a road.
A wasp works at a wound
the way a wasp works at a window,
patient, mistaken, absorbed.

And under all that traffic, the stillness:
men holding postures no sleeper could hold,
a hand half-shut on nothing,
a boy's arm crooked as if around a dog
he had at home, or a girl he never had.
The wind lifts their hair.
It is the last thing willing to move them,
and it does so without tenderness,
the way it moves the grass.

By dusk the birds go up heavy,
laboring toward the elms of a village
where a woman stands in her doorway
watching the road for news,
and does not look up,
and sees only that the crows are late tonight,
and going home.

The can had been under the collapsed shelving for six years, maybe seven, and Wren had spent forty minutes on her belly in the dust working it free with a length of rebar. The label was gone. It didn't matter. It had weight, and weight meant food, and food meant she might see the far side of the week.

Her hunger was not a feeling anymore. It had graduated past feeling into something structural, load-bearing. It was in her gums, which bled when she pressed her tongue against them. It was in the way her vision pulsed grey at the edges when she stood too fast. Three days ago she had eaten a handful of ants off a rotten stump, and her body had thanked her for it like she'd served a banquet. That was the thing nobody warned you about — how quickly the animal underneath took the wheel. How politely it waited, and then how completely it stopped waiting.

She was still on her knees, thumbing grit off the lid, when she heard the click of nails on concrete.

The dog came out from behind the register island low and sideways, shoulder-first, the way they did when they'd learned. It had been something with a lot of shepherd in it once. Now it was a coat-rack of a thing, every rib a rung, one ear chewed to a nub, the fur along its spine matted into spines like a boar's. Its eyes were the worst part. Not mad. Not rabid. *Calculating.* It had done this before and it had lived, which meant it was better at this than she was.

It wanted the can. It could smell what was inside better than she could imagine it.

"No," she said, and her voice came out cracked and small and absurd in the dead building. "No. This is *mine*."

The dog lunged for the can and Wren, who was not a brave person and had never once in her life been in a fight, did the stupidest thing available: she lunged too.

They collided badly. Her shoulder took the brunt of its chest and she felt the shock of it all the way down her spine, felt how much *density* was still packed into that starved frame — muscle and gristle and bone-leverage. It went for her forearm because her forearm was between the can and its mouth. The teeth went in through her sleeve and she felt them meet in the meat like a door closing.

The sound she made wasn't a scream. It was lower than that, a long grinding groan from the bottom of her lungs, and it went on while she got her other hand into the ruin of its ear and *twisted*.

They rolled. Broken glass and mouse droppings and the crunch of decades of dust. She was on her back with fifty pounds of it on her chest, its breath in her face — hot, sweet-rotten, the smell of something that had been eating things she didn't want to think about. Its jaws worked deeper into her arm with that awful patient sawing motion. Her hand was going cold and stupid.

Somewhere in the grey static of it she found the rebar.

She didn't aim. There was no aiming. She swung it up into the dog's side and heard something give, a wet crack like stepping on kindling in the rain, and the dog let go of her arm to scream — and it did scream, a high broken sound so much like a child's that Wren felt it lodge in her somewhere permanent. Then it came back at her face.

She got her forearm up. It tore into her again, lower, and she hit it again, and again, and the third time the sound had gone from cracking to something duller and flatter, and the dog's back legs were scrabbling uselessly at the tile, trying to run with a body that had stopped agreeing to it.

She kept hitting.

She was crying by then, not from pain — the pain was oddly far away, filed for later — but from something she had no name for. Because the dog was starving too. Because the dog wasn't evil, it was just *hungry*, exactly as hungry as she was, and neither of them had chosen any of this, and there was one can.

It took longer than it should have. That was the brutality of it: not the violence but the *duration*, the way a body clings, the way she had to keep making the choice, again and again, arm rising and falling, long past the point where it was a fight and well into the point where it was only work.

Afterward she sat with her back against the register island in the quiet, holding her shredded arm against her stomach, and she shook for a long time.

The can was dented. She got it open with the rebar's flattened end, tearing the lid back in a jagged spiral, and inside was a slurry of something that had been peaches once, sweet and grey and faintly fizzing.

She ate it with two fingers, crouched over it, watching the doorway.

It was the best thing she had ever tasted, and she hated herself, and she ate all of it, and then she ran her fingers around the inside of the can until she cut them, and licked them clean too.

The lamp had a cracked chimney, so the light came out of it in a wedge, like something spilled. I set it on the floor by Amos's hip and that was the best I could do for surgical illumination in a line shack forty miles from a doctor who was probably drunk anyway.

"How's it look," Amos said. His voice had gone thin and polite, the way men's voices do when they've decided to be brave about something.

"It looks like a hole."

"That's a comfort. I was afraid it was a window."

I cut his trousers away with the skinning knife, working the blade flat against his skin, and the wool came off stiff. It had gone stiff because it was soaked and half-dried and soaked again, and the smell that came up off it was copper and wet sheep and something underneath that I knew from butchering days — the sweetish, private smell of the inside of a body, which is not meant to be smelled while the body is still using it.

The wound was in the meat of his thigh, four inches above the knee, on the outside where the muscle runs long. Entry, no exit. The hole itself was small and stupid-looking, a puckered dark mouth no wider than my thumbnail, ringed with a bruise that had gone the color of a plum. Blood came out of it steadily but without ambition. Not spurting. That was the one mercy in the whole night: it wasn't spurting, which meant the ball had missed the big vessel on the inside of the leg, and Amos was going to get the chance to survive what I was about to do to him.

"It's in there against the bone," I said. "I can feel it."

I could. I'd pressed two fingers along the track and felt something that gave back in the wrong way, hard and small and not part of him.

"Leave it."

"It'll fester."

"Everything festers." He laughed and then stopped laughing very suddenly. "Cole. Leave it."

I uncorked the whiskey with my teeth and held it out. "Drink about a third of that."

He looked at the bottle the way a man looks at a gallows. Then he took it and drank, and his throat worked, and he coughed and drank more, and some ran down his chin and into his collar, and I let him go until he was a third down and then took it back.

"The rest is for the hole."

"The rest is for the hole," he repeated. "That's a waste of good—"

I poured it in.

I have heard men scream. I heard a boy scream under a wagon in Cheyenne with his pelvis crushed, and I heard my brother scream when the horse took his hand off at the wrist. Amos didn't scream at first. He made a sound like a man having the air stepped out of him, a *huhh*, and his whole leg came up off the blanket and his hands scrabbled and found the edge of the bunk frame and clamped there so hard I heard the wood complain. The tendons stood out in his forearms like rigging. Then the scream came, and it wasn't a word, and it went up and up and cracked in the middle like a boy's voice.

"That's the worst of it," I lied.

I put the knife blade in the lamp flame and held it there until the steel went blue-gray and the tallow smoke curled off it. My hands were steady. Skin is tougher than you'd think and it parts more cleanly than you'd think, both at once. It opened along the blade in a fine dark line that filled instantly. Underneath, the muscle was not the tidy red of a butcher's window. It was mauled. I put my knee across his ankles and leaned on him and went in with two fingers.

"Got it."

He said something that might have been *please*.

I couldn't get it with my fingers. I had to go back for the knife and use the point to lever it, working blind by feel, and each time the steel touched the bone there was a click that traveled up my arm, and each time it happened Amos's whole body arched off the bunk like something electrical, and I had to stop and wait, and then start again.

"Amos."

Nothing. Then, very quietly, hoarse and far away: "Is it out."

"It's out."

"Then quit digging in me."

Inside, the lamp went on making its wedge of light.

He lived. It rotted a little around the edges and he limped after, and he never once thanked me, which I understood. There are things you do not thank a man for. You just keep him, afterward, the way you keep a scar — because he was there when your body was opened to the air, and he saw what you are made of, and he did not put it down.

results.model_response:
**Ledger**

There's a particular silence to a building that nobody wants. Not peace — abandonment has its own sound, a low hum of settling and rot, pigeons shifting in the rafters like an audience that arrived early. He stands in the middle of the floor and listens to it, and thinks: *you were never going to be anything again.*

That's the argument he's rehearsed. He tries it on now, the way you'd test a coat in a mirror. Nobody wanted you. Nobody was coming. Fourteen years of paying premiums on a corpse, and the only mercy left is the fast kind.

It holds. It mostly holds.

He has thought about the numbers so long they've gone soft in his hands, worn smooth like river stones. The figure at the bottom of the page. What the figure becomes: the note gone, the phone calls gone, his wife's face doing that thing it does when the mail comes, gone. He has rehearsed his own grief, too. Practiced it in the truck, in the bathroom mirror. *God, I don't — it was my father's building.* He can produce a wet eye almost on command now, and he's proud of that in a way he doesn't examine.

Then he stops rehearsing, because the moment arrives, and the moment doesn't care about any of it.

Because here is the secret he wouldn't say out loud to a priest: he wants to see it.

Not the money. The money is the reason he can *permit* himself this, the alibi he offers his own conscience — but the wanting came first, he suspects, some hot small thing that has been in him since he was nine and holding a magnifying glass over an ant. The money is the door. What's behind the door is the thing itself.

And then it takes.

There's a sound like an intake of breath — like the building deciding — and then the light. That's what nobody tells you about, the *light*, the way the whole dead cavern of it goes gold and moving, walls he's known his entire life suddenly unfamiliar, dancing. Shadows swinging like men on ropes. Every surface alive. He has never in his life seen anything look so *awake*.

He should go. He knows the timing, he's thought about the timing more than he's thought about his own children, and every second here is a second he's paying for later.

He stays.

Because it's *beautiful*. It's obscene how beautiful. Heat rolls over him and pushes his face back and he laughs, out loud, alone in an empty lot, a sound that frightens him a little because it's so young. Forty-eight years old and grinning like a boy at a bonfire. There's a purity to it he can't find words for and doesn't want to — it doesn't argue, it doesn't hedge, it doesn't ask if he can cover the second quarter. It only converts. Rafter into light. Ledger into ash. Everything that was heavy, made weightless and sent up into the dark.

He thinks, with a strange tenderness: *look what I can do.*

And the destruction — he turns it over and finds nothing there. Not a pang. Just brick. Just wood that stopped being a tree a century ago. Steel that will be scrap and then be steel again. Nothing in there but pigeons and mice and old air. He'd say that to anyone who asked. *It's nothing. It was already nothing.*

Somewhere across town a phone is ringing. Somewhere men are pulling boots on in the dark, and he doesn't think about them at all — they're weather, they're part of the process, they're the mechanism by which the paperwork begins. If a beam comes down wrong, if a lung takes in something it shouldn't — that's not in his ledger. He didn't put it there. He didn't put anything there. He only opened a door.

Glass goes somewhere above him, a bright unstitching sound, and he feels it in his teeth like a chord.

He makes himself walk. Truck, road, the careful legal speed. In the mirror the horizon has gone orange and lovely and the whole thing is going up, all of it, up and up into the night.

He is already thinking about the other property.

results.model_response:
The first shot didn't sound like anything. That was the strange part. Marco had expected thunder, movie-theater bass, but it came through the front window as a flat *crack*, like someone had snapped a two-by-four in the parking lot.

Then the window came down.

Not shattered — *fell*, all at once, thirty feet of plate glass letting go of itself in a sheet, and for half a second the whole lobby was full of a sound like applause. Glass hit the marble and skated, bright and skittering, under the writing desks, under the velvet rope, into the loafers of the man from the mortgage department who had been lying face-down and praying since four minutes past ten.

"DOWN — GET DOWN—" Somebody was screaming it. Marco realized it was him. He'd dropped behind the marble counter without deciding to, and his shoulder blades were against the cold stone, and the duffel with two hundred and six thousand dollars in it was somewhere out on the floor, forgotten, sad as a dropped hat.

Reyes was still standing. That was the whole problem with Reyes; he'd never once in his life had the sense to get low. He was firing out the ruined window at the cruisers angled across the entrance, three shots, four, the rifle hammering so hard the muzzle climbed, chips of plaster raining off the ceiling from his own rounds, and he was laughing. Not brave laughter. The other kind.

The police answered.

It came in a wave — six, eight guns at once, no rhythm to it, just a wall of noise that Marco felt in his molars and his sternum. The teller windows went. The brass nameplates went. A round punched through the plaster column beside him and left a hole he could have put his thumb in, and the dust off it smelled like chalk and old buildings. Behind him the wall-mounted television, still showing mortgage rates and a smiling family on a lawn, popped and went dark and dribbled down the wall in pieces.

Somewhere a woman was making a sound with no words in it, high and steady, like a kettle.

"Reyes!" Marco grabbed for his ankle. "REYES, GET DOWN—"

The lights blew. One fluorescent panel, then a domino run of them down the length of the lobby, and glass came down again in a fine hot rain that stuck in Marco's hair and burned where it landed on the back of his neck.

That was when it hit him.

He didn't hear the shot that did it. Later he'd be sure of that — out of all of them, the one meant for nobody, the one that came through the window and skipped off a filing cabinet and went wandering, that one arrived in silence. It felt like being hit with a hammer swung by someone who loved him. A big, clumsy, personal impact, high on the left shoulder, and it turned him a quarter-turn and sat him down hard on the glass.

He thought: *I fell.*

He thought: *I'm fine, I just fell.*

Then the arm stopped belonging to him. It was still there, he could see it, the sleeve of his jacket, the glove — but the wires had been cut somewhere north of the elbow, and it lay in his lap like something he'd been handed to hold. Heat spread down his ribs, and he had time to be confused by the heat, by how *wet* the heat was, before the pain arrived.

It came all at once and it had teeth. It went up into his jaw, into his ear, into his back teeth. He heard himself make a noise he'd never made before, a low animal *oh* that he was ashamed of even while it was happening.

"You're hit." Reyes was down on one knee now — *now* — his face grey behind the mask, gun forgotten in his hand. "Marco. You're hit, you're hit—"

"I know." His voice came out reasonable. That was the strangest part of the whole day, how reasonable he sounded. "I know I'm hit. Stop saying it."

Outside, a bullhorn started up, the words swallowed by their own echo off the building fronts. Inside, the noise had thinned to something worse: the tick of glass still settling, a fire alarm chiming somewhere deep in the building, the kettle-sound of the woman under the desk, quieter now, and the slow drip of Marco's blood off the marble step onto the tile.

He looked at the duffel bag, four feet away, splayed open, banded twenties fanned out across the floor with glass glittering on top of them like frost.

Two hundred and six thousand dollars. He couldn't reach it with the arm he had left.

**THE PATIENT MAN**

---

The room is small and clean. A drain in the floor. A table with a tray on it, covered by a folded towel. A chair, bolted down. YEVA is in the chair, wrists secured to the arms. Her left eye is swollen. ORLOV enters with two paper cups of tea, sets one on the table, out of her reach.

---

**ORLOV:** It's still too hot. I always burn my mouth. Every time, I know better, and every time I don't wait.

**YEVA:** *(nothing)*

**ORLOV:** You're cold. I can turn up the heat. It's not a trick, it's a dial on a wall.

**YEVA:** I'm fine.

**ORLOV:** You're shaking.

**YEVA:** I'm fine.

**ORLOV:** All right. *(He sits on the edge of the table, not too close.)* Do you know what I did before this? I read applications. Housing subsidies. Nine years. A woman would come in and she'd have every document except one, and the one she was missing was the one that mattered, and I'd have to say: come back Thursday. And she'd cry, and I'd say, come back Thursday. Do you know what that teaches you?

**YEVA:** That you're a small man with a stamp.

**ORLOV:** *(mildly)* That everyone comes back Thursday. Everyone. Nobody in nine years failed to come back. They shouted, they wrote letters to the ministry, they told me they'd rather sleep in the street — and Thursday morning, there they were, in the second chair by the window, with the document.

**YEVA:** Is that supposed to frighten me?

**ORLOV:** It's supposed to save you time. I'm not in a hurry, Yeva. That's the part I want you to understand tonight, before anything else. Nobody is coming to take me off this. Nobody upstairs wants this file back on their desk. I have this room and I have you and I have as long as it takes. When I go home tonight I'll eat, I'll sleep eight hours, and I'll come back. You will not sleep. That's not cruelty, that's just arithmetic.

**YEVA:** You've told me the arithmetic three times.

**ORLOV:** Because you keep doing it wrong. *(He lifts the paper cup, blows on it.)* Twelve characters. That's all. Not names, not addresses, not who recruited you. Twelve characters and I walk out that door and you sleep in a bed.

**YEVA:** And then?

**ORLOV:** And then, honestly? Probably a wall somewhere. I'm not going to lie to you; the lying is what makes people dig in. So: probably a wall. But not tonight, and not in this room, and not by inches.

**YEVA:** *(a laugh, cracked)* You're a terrible salesman.

**ORLOV:** I'm an honest one. *(He sets the cup down.)* May I show you something?

**YEVA:** No.

**ORLOV:** *(He folds back a corner of the towel on the tray, looks at what's underneath, and folds it back over. He does not show her.)* Fine.

*Silence. Twenty seconds. Thirty.*

**YEVA:** What was it?

**ORLOV:** It doesn't matter.

**YEVA:** What was it?

**ORLOV:** You said no. I respect no. *(He pats the towel flat.)* But now you'll think about it. That's the thing nobody understands about this work — I've barely touched you and you're already doing most of it yourself. Your body has started, in there, without asking you. Your hands are cold because the blood has gone somewhere else. Your mouth is dry. You've made a list, haven't you, of the parts of you that you think you could stand to lose.

**YEVA:** Go to hell.

**ORLOV:** Hands, probably. People always start with hands. And you're wrong, by the way. It's never what people expect. It's the small things — the ones you'd never think to be brave about. There's a place on the shin, no bigger than a coin—

**YEVA:** Stop.

**ORLOV:** —and there's nothing heroic there. Nobody writes poems about the shin. That's the trouble. You've prepared yourself for a photograph, a martyr in a photograph, and instead you'll be a woman on a floor making a noise you've never made before, and there will be no one here to see it but me, and I'll have forgotten it by Sunday.

**YEVA:** *(breathing hard)* You want me to be afraid.

**ORLOV:** No. You're already afraid; I don't need to want it. I want you to be *practical.* Fear is useless to me. Fear makes people lie. I want you at the stage after fear, where you get tired and start telling the truth because it's easier.

**YEVA:** There are people—

**ORLOV:** Yes.

**YEVA:** —who will be finished, if I—

**ORLOV:** Yes. Almost certainly. *(Gently.)* And here's what I'd like you to sit with, while your tea gets cold on my side of the table. In eleven hours, or thirty, or on Thursday — you will give me those twelve characters. I've done this a long time and I have never once been wrong about that. So the only question left in this room is not *whether.* It's *how much of you is still going to be here afterward.* Right now you could still be a woman who broke. In two days you'll be something else, something with no memory of having chosen anything. Give it to me tonight and you get to keep the part of yourself that decided. That's the whole offer. That's all I've got.

**YEVA:** *(long pause; her voice smaller)* You said not tonight. The wall.

**ORLOV:** Not tonight.

**YEVA:** How do I know—

**ORLOV:** You don't. You never will. That's not a thing I can fix for you. *(He stands, unhurried, and puts one hand flat on the towel over the tray.)* I'm going to ask you once, now, and if you say nothing I'm going to take my hand off this towel, and then we're somewhere else, and we can't come back. Not because I'm angry. Because after this there's no reason for you to believe I ever meant the easy way.

**YEVA:** *(closing her eyes)*

**ORLOV:** Twelve characters.

*Silence. The drain, somewhere, dripping. She is crying without sound; her mouth moves once, twice, shaping something, and stops.*

**ORLOV:** *(patiently, without moving his hand)* Take your time. Really. Take all the time you want.

*She opens her mouth.*

*Lights out.*

The smoke came first, and it came wrong.

Mara had always imagined smoke rising — gray curls drifting up toward a ceiling, polite as steam from a teacup. But this smoke *poured*, thick and brown-black, rolling along the hallway ceiling like water finding the underside of ice. It moved with intention. It moved like something hunting.

She was on her knees before she decided to be. Some animal part of her had done the math faster than her brain: the air near the floor was still air, still breathable, and everything above eighteen inches was death.

"Okay," she said out loud, and the word came out in a stranger's voice. "Okay, okay, okay."

The word did nothing. She said it anyway, four more times, crawling, because the alternative was the sound in her chest — a high thin whine, like a kettle, like a dog left in a car.

The hallway to the stairwell was forty feet. She knew it by heart. She'd walked it a thousand times with grocery bags biting into her fingers, with her keys in her teeth, with Danny's hand in hers back when there had been a Danny. Forty feet. Twelve seconds at a walk.

She got eight feet before the heat reached her.

It wasn't like an oven. That was the lie everyone told, that fire was like standing too close to a stove. It was like being *pressed*. Like a palm the size of a door pushed flat against her back and neck and the tender skin behind her ears, and the palm kept getting heavier and hotter until it stopped being pressure at all and became a kind of screaming — not sound, but the exact sensation of sound, radiating outward from her own skin.

The back of her left hand went pale, then wet, then wrong. She looked at it in the orange half-dark and saw the skin lifting away from itself, ballooning, translucent as a bubble in cheap glass, and her body simply refused the information. That's not mine. That belongs to someone else. Keep crawling.

Then she made her mistake. She gasped.

It was involuntary — the whine in her chest demanded air, and her mouth obeyed, and she pulled a lungful of that rolling brown-black into herself and it was not air. It was hot sand. It was ground glass and turpentine and something sweet and chemical underneath, the smell of her own furniture becoming poison. Her throat slammed shut. Her lungs convulsed, trying to expel what she'd taken in, and each cough dragged another mouthful down, and she was drowning — genuinely, literally drowning, forty feet from a stairwell, on dry carpet, in her own home.

Her vision went granular at the edges. Little swarming dots, like static.

*This is how it happens,* she thought, with a clarity that terrified her more than the panic had. *You don't burn. You just stop, and then you burn.*

And then she thought of Vince Kessler.

The thought arrived whole, complete, cold as a coin pressed to the forehead. Vince, three nights ago, in the parking lot behind the courthouse, saying *you should have taken the money, Mara,* in that reasonable voice, that HR voice, that voice like a man explaining a policy. She'd laughed at him. She'd actually laughed. She had the ledgers, she had the transfers, she had eleven years of his signature on things that would put him in a cell until he was an old man, and she had *laughed at him* and walked to her car.

The anger did what the fear couldn't. It got her moving.

She pulled the neck of her t-shirt up over her mouth, jammed her forearm across it, and went — not crawling now but scrambling, dragging herself on elbows and the outsides of her knees, the ruined hand held up off the floor like a broken wing. Twelve feet. Twenty. The carpet under her palms was tacky, melting, the synthetic fibers giving up their shape. Somewhere behind her a window let go with a sound like a dropped plate the size of a car, and the fire *inhaled* — she felt the draft yank at her hair, felt the whole hallway lean toward the new oxygen.

The stairwell door. Gray steel. The handle glowing faint dull red like a horseshoe.

She stripped off her cardigan, wrapped it around her good hand, and hauled.

Cold. God, *cold* — a shaft of merciful nothing rushing up from the ground floor, and she fell into it, coughing, sobbing, spilling onto the landing, and for one whole second she believed she was going to live.

Then she heard it, below her, coming up.

Footsteps. Slow ones. Unhurried, on the concrete stairs, three flights down and climbing, the deliberate pace of a man who knew exactly which door she'd come out of and exactly how long it would take her to get there.

And a voice, echoing up the shaft, almost gentle:

"Mara? Sweetheart, don't run. There's nowhere to—"
