The case is aluminum, hard-sided, lined with foam cut to the shape of the thing inside. It opens the way a coffin opens. Two latches, thumb pressure, and there she is in pieces, waiting to be a whole idea again.

Room 704. Radiator knocking like a man in the trunk. Nine floors of nothing across the street and then the balcony, third from the corner, where at 6:40 a man in a bathrobe will come out to smoke the cigarette his wife thinks he quit. He has kept that secret for eleven years. Tonight it kills him. There's a lesson in there for somebody.

I lay the towel on the desk first. Always the towel. Not sentiment—oil. Oil on a hotel desk is a story a maid tells a cop, and stories are the only thing that ever gets anybody caught.

Receiver out of the foam. Cold in the palm, cold the way a doorknob is cold, indifferent, machined by men who clock out at four and drink light beer and never once think about where their work ends up. That's most of the world. Honest people at the front of a long hallway, and me standing at the far end of it.

Barrel next. Threads catch, then run smooth. I turn it home and feel it seat, that small dead stop that tells you steel has agreed to be one thing instead of two.

People imagine there's a voice. A conscience like a nagging landlord, hammering the pipes. There isn't. What there is, is arithmetic. I did the arithmetic a long time ago at a kitchen table with a bottle in front of me and I came out the same every time I ran it. A man asked me to do a thing. Another man had already done things. The money was in an envelope. And the fact underneath all of it, the fact I keep in my back pocket like a spare round: somebody was going to. If not me, then a kid with shaky hands who'd take three tries and put one through a window into a nursery.

That's the lie, incidentally. I know it's a lie. I keep it anyway because a man needs something to hold when the shakes come at four in the morning, and God stopped taking my calls somewhere around the second one.

Bolt. I run it, listen. There's a sound a well-kept action makes, a clean dry click, and it's the only music I've got left. Twice more, empty, feeling for grit. There's never grit. I clean it the way other men pray—nightly, mechanically, mumbling.

Scope into the rings. Torque wrench, small numbers, even pressure, front then rear, then front again. Crank it down like a gorilla and you'll bend the tube and put your round eighteen inches left and spend the rest of your life wondering why the world went crooked. Everything in this business is done gently. That's the part nobody believes.

The bipod. The bag of rice I brought from a market four states away because a sandbag in your luggage is a conversation. Rice under the stock, stock into the shoulder pocket, cheek down. The rifle wants to lie still. Give it a bone to rest on and it'll hold a heartbeat better than you will.

Window's open four inches. Curtain drawn to a hand's width. Never shoot from the frame—shoot from the dark, three feet back, so the muzzle stays inside and the room swallows the flash. A man on the street looks up and sees a hotel with a hundred black rectangles and no story in any of them.

Wind's talking in the flags on the bank building. Left to right, lazy, maybe four. There's a haze on the glass; the temperature's dropping and the air's getting heavy and heavy air drags. I write the numbers on the back of a matchbook because my memory is honest but not that honest.

Round out of the box. I've carried this brass a thousand miles and I loaded it myself in a garage with the radio on. Trimmed, weighed, seated to the thousandth. There's a kind of care in it that would look like love to anybody watching through a window.

That's the joke. That's the whole joke, right there. Fifty years old and the only thing I've ever been tender with is this.

Chamber it. Bolt down, soft, thumb riding the handle so the click stays in the room.

6:38. Light in the sliding door. A shape. Bathrobe.

I let the air out of my lungs and the world narrows to a circle of glass and a crosshair with a little dip in the wire where the ranging line sits. He's got a mug in his left hand. He taps the pack against his palm, twice, the way men do.

I don't think about his wife. That's a rule. You can think about her at 4 a.m.—she'll be there, she's always there, she keeps regular hours—but you cannot think about her now.

Finger takes up the slack. There's a place in a good trigger like the edge of a step in the dark.

Somewhere a room away a TV laughs at something.

Breathe out. Hold at the bottom, where the body goes quiet and stupid and still.

And this is the part I'll never say out loud, not to a priest, not to a bottle, not to the woman who left me in a parking lot in Reno:

it's easy.

That's the sin. Not the doing. The ease.

Break.

That's most of the world. Honest people at the front of a long hallway, and me standing at the far end of it.

Barrel next. Threads catch, then run smooth. I turn it home and feel it seat, that small dead stop that tells you steel has agreed to be one thing instead of two.

People imagine there's a voice. A conscience like a nagging landlord, hammering the pipes. There isn't. What there is, is arithmetic. I did the arithmetic a long time ago at a kitchen table with a bottle in front of me and I came out the same every time I ran it. A man asked me to do a thing. Another man had already done things. The money was in an envelope. And the fact underneath all of it, the fact I keep in my back pocket like a spare round: somebody was going to. If not me, then a kid with shaky hands who'd take three tries and put one through a window into a nursery.

That's the lie, incidentally. I know it's a lie. I keep it anyway because a man needs something to hold when the shakes come at four in the morning, and God stopped taking my calls somewhere around the second one.

Bolt. I run it, listen. There's a sound a well-kept action makes, a clean dry click, and it's the only music I've got left. Twice more, empty, feeling for grit. There's never grit. I clean it the way other men pray—nightly, mechanically, mumbling.

Scope into the rings. Torque wrench, small numbers, even pressure, front then rear, then front again. Crank it down like a gorilla and you'll bend the tube and put your round eighteen inches left and spend the rest of your life wondering why the world went crooked. Everything in this business is done gently. That's the part nobody believes.

The bipod. The bag of rice I brought from a market four states away because a sandbag in your luggage is a conversation. Rice under the stock, stock into the shoulder pocket, cheek down. The rifle wants to lie still. Give it a bone to rest on and it'll hold a heartbeat better than you will.

Window's open four inches. Curtain drawn to a hand's width. Never shoot from the frame—shoot from the dark, three feet back, so the muzzle stays inside and the room swallows the flash. A man on the street looks up and sees a hotel with a hundred black rectangles and no story in any of them.

Wind's talking in the flags on the bank building. Left to right, lazy, maybe four. There's a haze on the glass; the temperature's dropping and the air's getting heavy and heavy air drags. I write the numbers on the back of a matchbook because my memory is honest but not that honest.

Round out of the box. I've carried this brass a thousand miles and I loaded it myself in a garage with the radio on. Trimmed, weighed, seated to the thousandth. There's a kind of care in it that would look like love to anybody watching through a window.

That's the joke. That's the whole joke, right there. Fifty years old and the only thing I've ever been tender with is this.

Chamber it. Bolt down, soft, thumb riding the handle so the click stays in the room.

6:38. Light in the sliding door. A shape. Bathrobe.

I let the air out of my lungs and the world narrows to a circle of glass and a crosshair with a little dip in the wire where the ranging line sits. He's got a mug in his left hand. He taps the pack against his palm, twice, the way men do.

I don't think about his wife. That's a rule. You can think about her at 4 a.m.—she'll be there, she's always there, she keeps regular hours—but you cannot think about her now.

Finger takes up the slack. There's a place in a good trigger like the edge of a step in the dark.

Somewhere a room away a TV laughs at something.

Breathe out. Hold at the bottom, where the body goes quiet and stupid and still.

And this is the part I'll never say out loud, not to a priest, not to a bottle, not to the woman who left me in a parking lot in Reno:

it's easy.

That's the sin. Not the doing. The ease.

Break.

Marko wanted the money first. That was the whole problem, right there, in the first ten seconds — he wanted the money first and I wanted the bag first, and neither of us had any reason on earth to trust the other, because we were both standing in a service alley behind a shuttered dry cleaner at two in the morning, which is not where trustworthy men conduct their business.

"Just show me it's in there," I said.

"Show me the roll."

"Marko."

"Don't say my name out here." He was sweating in November. His jaw kept working, side to side, like he had something caught in his teeth. He'd lost weight since summer — the kind of weight that comes off your face first, so the skull starts showing through, and you can see the man's actual architecture. "You think I came here to rob you? I got kids, man."

"You got one kid and she lives in Bakersfield."

I shouldn't have said that. I knew it before it was all the way out of my mouth, the way you know a glass is going off the counter while it's still tipping.

He came at me sideways. Not a punch — he shoved the bag into my chest with his left hand, and I was so busy catching it, so busy thinking *finally*, that I didn't see his right go into his coat. The alley was all dark and wet brick and one sodium lamp forty feet off, and the knife didn't flash. Knives don't flash. That's a lie the movies tell. It was just a shape that had been in his pocket and now wasn't.

We went into each other. That's the only way to describe it. Not a fight — a collision, a hug that had gone wrong. My hand found his wrist and clamped and I could feel the tendons standing up in it like cables, and his breath was in my ear, hot and sour, and he was saying something, or maybe just making a noise, this high thin sound in the back of his throat, a kettle sound. Our feet slid in the grease and the standing water. I got a fistful of his coat collar and drove him back into the dumpster and it boomed like a bad drum. We were pressed chest to chest, close enough to kiss. I remember the button of his jacket digging into my sternum. I remember thinking, with perfect stupid clarity, that his coat smelled like a laundromat.

I had his wrist. I want to be clear about that. I had it. And then my foot went out from under me, just an inch, just a slip, and my grip slid down over the back of his hand, and something bumped me low on the left side.

That's all it was. A bump. A knuckle-tap against my ribs, like someone getting your attention in a crowd.

I let go of him. I don't know why. It seemed important to check.

There was no pain. That's the part nobody believes. I stood there in the alley with my hand pressed under my ribs and there was no pain at all, just a spreading cold, a numb wide cold like I'd been leaned against something frozen, and underneath the cold a wrongness — a sense that some interior wall had been opened and the outside was getting in where it had no business being. My shirt was wet. I thought, *he threw a drink on me*, which is insane, because there was no drink, but the brain reaches for whatever's in the cupboard.

Then I breathed in, and the pain arrived.

It came from the inside out, a hot seam ripping up under my arm, and it had teeth in it, and it went all the way through to my back so that I couldn't tell anymore which side I'd been cut on. My legs turned to sand. I got a hand on the dumpster and the metal was cold and gritty and I concentrated on that, on the grit, because the alley had started to tilt and go long, the lamp at the far end stretching out like a smear on a windshield. My mouth flooded with the taste of pennies and my ears filled with a sound like a bus idling.

Marko was standing three feet away with the knife down at his thigh and his mouth open. He looked like a man who'd woken up somewhere strange. He looked, honestly, like he was going to apologize.

"You—" he said. Then: "I didn't."

He kept saying it while he backed away. *I didn't, I didn't.* He left the bag. He left the bag right there in the wet, which tells you everything about how his night was going, and mine.

I slid down the dumpster and sat in the water with my knees up and both hands pressed hard into my side, and the blood came through my fingers in that unhurried way that scared me more than spurting would have — patient, like it had all the time in the world. I was very cold and very calm and very interested in the shape of the sky between the buildings. And I thought, over and over, the same small useless thought:

*It didn't even hurt. It didn't even hurt at first.*

# The Inventory

The rain had stopped an hour before Byrne arrived, which meant the alley was still giving it back — dripping off fire escapes, off the crooked lip of a gutter, off the awning of the Mandarin Garden where the water had pooled in the canvas and now let go in fat, irregular slaps against the concrete. That was the sound she'd remember. Not the generator humming for the work lights, not the wet crackle of tyvek suits. The slapping. Like something being tenderized.

She signed the log, took the booties from the kid holding the box, and pulled them on standing up, one hand braced against the brick. The brick was cold and slick and it left a green smear of algae across her palm.

"Where's Sylvestri?"

"Inside. Talking to the dishwasher who found her." The kid's name tag said ROURKE. He was twenty-four, maybe, and doing an admirable job of looking at her face and only her face. "Detective, I should tell you—"

"You don't have to warn me."

"No, ma'am. I just — the smell. It's the drain. There's a grease trap back there and it's—" He stopped. "I threw up in the sewer grate on Delancey. Not the scene. On Delancey."

"Good man." She meant it. He'd be all right, or he wouldn't. Either way he'd remembered where not to be sick, and that was more than most.

She stepped past the tape.

The alley was eleven feet wide, she'd guess, and the light stands had been set at both ends so that everything in the middle was lit from two directions at once, throwing double shadows, giving every object a twin. The dumpsters were doubled. The stack of collapsed produce boxes, sodden into pulp, was doubled. So was the body.

Byrne took out her notebook and started at the feet, because she always started at the feet.

Female. Bare soles, black with the alley. No shoes present within visual range — mark that, ask about the dumpsters, ask about the roof. One anklet, thin gold chain, intact, which argued against robbery or argued for haste. The legs were bare to mid-thigh where a skirt had been rucked up, and Byrne noted the position of the fabric without touching it, noted that the hem was folded *under*, which happens when a body is dragged, not when it falls. She wrote *drag — direction? check striations on heels.*

She crouched. Her knees answered with the small dry sound they'd been making since she turned forty-six.

Lividity had settled in the calves and the underside of the left arm, fixed, purple as a wine stain, which put death somewhere north of eight hours. The ambient temperature complicated it. The rain complicated it. The ME could argue with the numbers later; Byrne wrote *8–14* and moved on.

The blood had gone where blood goes. It had run off the crown of the alley's slight camber toward the center trough, and there it had met the runoff from the restaurant's back door and made a long, thinned, tea-colored ribbon that traveled eighteen feet to the storm drain and disappeared. That was a problem. That was the case's first serious problem, and she felt it as a problem, an obstacle to be worked around, the way you feel a locked door. Most of the blood in this woman's body was somewhere under Mott Street by now, mixed with fry oil and cigarette filters and the runoff of nine thousand people's ordinary evenings.

What remained had done so in pockets. A pool the size of a dinner plate under the right shoulder, thick, congealing at the edges into a dark rind. Arterial spatter on the brick at knee height, a fan of it, individual drops elongated into commas that all pointed the same direction — northeast, toward the mouth of the alley. So the heart had still been pumping when the wall took that. So she had been upright, or nearly. So she had been standing where she died and had not been carried here already gone.

Byrne wrote that down. *Alive on arrival. Vertical. Assault occurred in situ.*

Then the wounds.

She counted them out loud, quietly, the way she'd been taught, because the mouth keeps better count than the eye. The forearms first — three long defensive lacerations on the left, two on the right, the deepest of them opening the meat below the elbow so that the yellow of fat showed under the work lights, unnervingly clean and bright, like something in a butcher's case. Byrne noted the cleanliness. A sharp blade, then, and not a serrated one. Not a hunting knife. Something maintained.

The hands had taken the worst of it. Three fingers on the right hand were cut to the bone at the second joint, and the little finger was gone below the knuckle, and Byrne looked for it and did not find it and wrote *digit — search radius, incl. drain grate.* She thought about the drain again. She thought about it the way she'd think about a witness who wouldn't talk.

The throat had been the last thing, or nearly the last. It had been done from the front, and it had been done more than once, and it was the only wound in the entire inventory that had any temper in it. Everything else was work. This was somebody finishing an argument.

Byrne stood, wrote *rage: terminal wound only. Everything prior = restraint? control? Suggests offender did not intend to kill until he did.* She underlined *did not intend* and put a question mark after it, because underlining without a question mark is how you fall in love with a theory.

The flies had found the eyes already, despite the cold. There were four of them, and they worked with an appalling patience.

She could smell it now that she'd stopped moving. Rourke had been right about the grease trap — that fermented sweetness underneath everything, old oil and rot, and over it the copper-and-pennies smell of the blood, and under all of it something else, something intimate and unmistakable, the smell of a body that had voided itself at the end. It was in Byrne's mouth. It would be in her clothes, and later in her hair, and tonight she'd stand under the shower until the hot water quit and she would still find it at two in the morning on the inside of her wrist.

She wrote none of that down.

"Byrne." Sylvestri, at the tape, holding his tie against his stomach as though the wind might take it. "Dishwasher's got nothing. Came out at eleven-forty for a smoke, saw the feet, went back in, called it from the phone by the walk-in. Didn't touch anything, didn't see anybody. He's crying pretty hard."

"He's allowed."

"You want the roof?"

"I want the drain," she said. "Get somebody down it before the next rain. And I want the last twelve hours of the traps at Grand and at Hester, and whoever owns the camera over the fish market that isn't pointing at the fish market."

Sylvestri wrote it down. "You get a read?"

Byrne looked at the woman one more time. Twenty-five, twenty-eight. A tattoo on the left ribs, partially obscured, a line of script in a language Byrne didn't recognize. Two small holes in each ear and a third, healed shut, higher in the left, from some earlier version of herself. And on the inside of the wrist that had taken the worst of the knife, a hair elastic. Just a plain black hair elastic, doubled twice, the kind that comes forty to a bag, worn there the way half the women in the city wore them, in case.

Byrne looked at it for perhaps two seconds longer than the job required.

Then she closed her notebook, snapped the band around it, and turned toward the light.

"She fought," she said. "She fought for a long time. So somebody's carrying marks tonight, and somebody's got a coat they can't wash. Let's go find the coat."

The first thing that is gone is sound.

Not silence exactly — the blast takes the hearing with it, punches the air out of the world and leaves a high, thin ringing in its place, like a wire drawn tight behind the eyes. For four or five seconds the market is a silent film. Dust rolls outward in a slow grey wall. Awnings that were red and blue a moment ago hang colorless, shredded into ribbons that lift and settle, lift and settle, in the draft the explosion left behind.

Then the dust begins to come down, and it comes down on everything equally: on the overturned crates, on the flattened cardboard where the fruit-seller knelt to pray five hours ago, on the open eyes of a man lying half beneath his own bicycle. It settles in his eyelashes. He does not blink. That is how you know.

The devastation has a strange geometry to it. Close to the seat of the blast there is almost nothing recognizable — a crater no deeper than a washbasin, a black scorch star radiating outward, and a debris field that the mind refuses to read. Scraps. Textures. Things that were people arranged now as weather arranges leaves. Farther out, four or five meters, bodies remain bodies, and this is somehow worse, because they are whole enough to be individuals: a woman on her side with her hand still curled where the handle of a shopping bag had been; a boy of maybe eleven sitting upright against a pillar with his legs straight out in front of him like a child at story time, entirely unmarked except for a thumbnail-sized hole below his collarbone. Farther still, thirty meters, forty, people are simply lying down where the pressure wave put them, stunned, their clothes intact, blood coming from their ears.

The market's inventory has been redistributed. Onions everywhere, dozens of them, rolling and coming to rest in the gutters. A tray of eggs, unbroken, upside down. Shoes — always the shoes, dozens of them, singles, never pairs, as though a crowd had walked out of its footwear and kept going. Someone's ledger, pages fanned open, columns of numbers in careful blue ink, and a spatter across them that will dry brown by afternoon. A mobile phone lying face-up in the debris, lit, vibrating, unanswered. Then another. Then, from under a collapsed table, a third. They will go on ringing for a long time. That is the sound that comes after the silence — not screaming, not at first, but the small polite chirping of telephones, dozens of them, as the news reaches the city and the city begins to call its people back.

The screaming arrives late, and it arrives in layers. First a single voice, wordless, on one long note. Then the ones who are hurt discovering that they are hurt. Then the ones who are searching, and those are the voices that carry furthest, because they are calling names.

Smoke lies low and refuses to lift. It smells of burnt sugar, kerosene, hot metal, and something else that the survivors will recognize instantly for the rest of their lives and never once describe out loud.

A man walks out of the grey with his arms held slightly away from his body, palms up, unhurried, as if crossing a room in the dark. He is looking for a stall that is no longer there. He stops in what used to be its doorway and stands in it. Behind him a woman is on her knees pressing a folded scarf to a stranger's thigh, shouting instructions at no one, and getting them right.

Above it all, the pigeons that lived in the market's iron rafters come back. They circle twice and land, and begin to walk among the wreckage, and begin to eat the spilled grain.

And then the sirens, and after the sirens the counting, and after the counting the long arithmetic of a city subtracting itself — a wedding that will not happen, a shop that will not reopen, a school desk that will stay empty and eventually be given to someone else, which is somehow the cruelest mercy of all.

The heat arrived before the fire did. Marisol felt it as pressure first, a hand pressing flat against her face, and she thought — stupidly, for half a second — that she had opened an oven door.

Then the smoke found her.

It wasn't like breathing smoke from a campfire. It had weight. It went down her throat like something poured, hot enough that her body simply refused it, her glottis slamming shut on reflex, and she made a sound she'd never heard herself make: a strangled bark, air trying to go two directions at once. She coughed, and the coughing was worse, because coughing meant emptying her lungs, and there was nothing clean to refill them with. Every attempt cost her more than it gave. She was going bankrupt, breath by breath.

*Low.* Someone had told her that once, in a school assembly, a fireman with a mustache. *Get low.* She dropped, and her palm came down on the floorboards and the floorboards were hot, and she snatched her hand back with a whimper, and the smoke poured down after her like water finding a basin. There was no low. There was no clean six inches at the bottom of the world. Her eyes streamed and then stopped streaming, which frightened her more than anything else had, and the hallway she had walked ten thousand times became a place with no geometry at all — no door, no window, no up, only the roar.

The roar. Nobody told you about the roar. Not crackling. A jet engine in the next room, a freight train, the building itself being torn open somewhere above her and the fire inhaling through the wound.

Her left forearm began to hurt in a way she had no category for. Not a cut, not a burn from a pan. It was a tightness, first — the skin drawing taut like a drumhead, like there was too much of her packed inside too little of her. Then a rising, a fullness, something swelling up under the surface trying to get out. She clutched at it and the skin *slid,* wet and loose beneath her fingers, and the pain that followed was so pure and so total that her vision went white at the edges and her mouth opened to scream.

That was the mistake. The scream took the last of her air and paid for nothing.

She got her mouth into the crook of her elbow — the good arm, she still had a good arm — and sucked, and got a thin filthy sip of something. It was enough for one thought. One. She spent it on the shape of the hallway: bathroom on the left, three steps, tub, faucet, water.

Her body wanted to run and her body wanted to curl and her body wanted her mother, and none of those were options, so she crawled. Three steps became a country. Her knee found something metal that kissed her and left a mark she wouldn't feel until the hospital. Somewhere she was aware of a high thin whine coming out of her and she let it come, because it meant she was still moving air, still here, still counting.

Left hand out. Doorframe.

Marisol pulled herself through it, and behind her, unhurried, the ceiling began to come down.

The office smelled of new carpet. On the wall behind the desk hung a framed certificate from a regional chamber of commerce, some award for small business excellence, dated eleven years ago. The man behind the desk had a folder open in front of him and a fountain pen uncapped beside it.

"You came recommended," he said. "I want to say that up front, because it saves us both a stage. Usually I spend the first twenty minutes establishing that neither of us is police. Kessler vouched for you. So we begin at stage two."

The client sat with his coat still on. He had not been offered anywhere to put it.

"Stage two is expectations," the man said. "Most of what I do is manage expectations. You've seen material before. Purchased, not produced."

"Yes."

"Then you understand the difference between the two the way a diner understands the difference between eating and cooking." He turned a page. "You've bought secondhand. Which means you've bought whatever existed. Now you're commissioning. Commissioning means you're paying for specificity. Specificity is the entire cost structure. Do you follow?"

"I think so."

"Let me be concrete. Secondhand, you pay for a file. A file is cheap. It has been sold before and will be sold again; my margin is volume. Commission, you pay for a process that happens once and cannot be repeated, cannot be resold in the form you're receiving, and cannot be insured. There is no insurance market for this. So the price carries what insurance would carry. That's not a markup. That's arithmetic."

The client's hands were folded. "Kessler said sixty."

"Kessler was quoting a standard. There is a standard. It assumes standard parameters." The man drew a line down a column with the pen, not writing, just indicating. "Parameters are four things. Talent, duration, content, and delivery. Every request I've ever received falls under those four headings. Go ahead."

"Talent."

"Talent is the largest variable. Talent is not selected the way you imagine. You will not be shown a catalogue. You will give me a description and I will tell you whether the description is inside or outside the envelope."

"What's outside the envelope?"

"Anyone who will be looked for." The man said it without emphasis, the way another man might say *anyone allergic to shellfish*. "This is not a moral position. It's a scheduling position. Talent who will be looked for generates activity. Activity generates cost, and the cost is not linear, it's exponential, and I don't accept exponential risk at any price. So: no one whose absence produces a phone call within seventy-two hours. That constraint removes some categories entirely. If your description falls into one of those categories, we shake hands and you leave, and there's no bad feeling, and you don't come back."

The client was quiet for a moment. "And if it doesn't?"

"Then it's a sourcing problem, and sourcing problems have lead times. Four to nine weeks. I've had eleven. I've never had under three." He made a small note. "Second heading. Duration."

"I hadn't thought about it."

"Everyone says that, and everyone is wrong, because everyone has thought about it, they've simply never had to price it." He set the pen down. "Runtime drives everything. Runtime is crew hours. Runtime is location hours. Runtime is the window in which something can go wrong, and something going wrong at minute six is a different order of problem from something going wrong at minute forty. I sell in eight-minute blocks. Eight is the shortest thing I'll do, because under eight there's no product, you've paid for setup and gotten a clip. Forty-eight is my ceiling. I've been asked for more. I've declined."

"Why?"

"Because at that length the crew stops being professional." He said it flatly. "I employ people. Employees have thresholds. Past a certain point they begin to improvise, or they begin to deteriorate, and both are liabilities. A deteriorating employee is the single most common failure mode in this business. Not law enforcement. Not clients. Staff." He turned the page back. "Third heading is content. This is where I need you to be uncomfortable, and I need you to be uncomfortable now rather than later, because later is expensive."

"Meaning."

"Meaning you write it down. Not describe. Write. In your own hand, in this room, on paper I provide, and you do not leave with it. If you cannot bring yourself to write a thing, I cannot produce it, because a request I have to infer is a request I will get wrong, and a wrong delivery is non-refundable." He slid a single sheet across the desk with two fingers. "Half my disputes come from men who wanted me to guess. I don't guess. I read."

The client looked at the paper and did not touch it. "And if partway through I—"

"Change your mind."

"Yes."

"The deposit is fifty percent and it clears before sourcing begins. Once sourcing begins there is no mechanism for reversal. Not a policy — a mechanism. There is nothing to reverse. Whatever has been set in motion is in motion, and my costs are incurred, and the balance is owed, and it will be collected." He let that sit exactly as long as it needed to. "I say this once and then never again. People who understand it have no trouble. People who don't understand it have a great deal of trouble, and I don't distinguish between the two afterward."

"I understand."

"Fourth heading. Delivery. This is administrative and I'll be brief. Nothing goes over any network. Nothing is stored in a form that can be retrieved by anyone but me, and I keep one copy for exactly as long as the balance is outstanding, at which point it becomes your problem and only your problem. You'll receive one physical item, one time, from someone you'll never see twice. If you lose it, that's the end of the transaction. If you copy it, that's the end of our relationship, and I'll know, because I've always known."

He capped the pen.

"So. Sixty is the standard. Standard is eight minutes, sourcing inside the envelope, no special content, single delivery. Everything you add is priced against those four headings and I'll quote you a number today that will not move. I don't negotiate, not because I'm rigid, but because a number that moves is a number that was never real, and men in my position who deal in unreal numbers are eventually dealt with." He folded his hands. "Take the paper. Write what you want. Take your time — I have the room until four."

The client reached for the sheet. The producer watched him with the mild, unhurried patience of a man who had watched this many times and found it neither interesting nor otherwise, and then he glanced at his watch, and then out the window at the parking lot, where his car needed washing.

The Grating

They rigged the grating at eight bells, and the ship's company mustered aft to witness punishment, as the Articles required.

Corrigan was a topman, twenty-two years old, from somewhere in County Clare that he pronounced in a way none of the officers could reproduce. He had struck a master's mate. Nobody disputed it. The mate had called him a name and Corrigan had put him on the deck with one blow of his fist, and there was no arguing with what a hundred men had seen.

Two hands lashed his wrists to the upper grating and his ankles to the lower, spreading him against the wood like something pinned in a naturalist's case. Someone had cut away his shirt already. His back was very white where the sun had never reached it, and along the ribs you could count the bones.

The surgeon stood by with his bag. The captain read the charge, and the finding, and the sentence: three dozen.

Jenks was the boatswain's mate that day. He was a heavy, unhurried man who took no pleasure in it and no shame either, and he combed the nine tails through his fingers to separate them, the way a groom parts a horse's mane. Then he stepped back to the length of his arm and set his feet.

The first stroke made a sound like a wet sheet snapped in wind.

That was all — a crack and a hiss ending in something soft, a slap of leather meeting flesh. Nine red lines rose across Corrigan's shoulders as though drawn with a straightedge and a thin brush. He did not make a noise. He drew one breath in through his teeth and held it.

The second came before the first had finished blooming. The same snap, the same suck of air, and now the lines crossed each other in a lattice, and the skin between them began to swell and shine.

By the sixth the sound had changed. It was no longer leather on skin but leather on something wetter, and each stroke ended in a distinct heavy patter, like a handful of gravel flung into mud. The knotted ends had begun to open him. There is a moment when skin stops resisting — when it has been stretched and struck and stretched again until it gives up its integrity — and past that moment it comes away in threads. You could hear it, if you were close enough. A small tearing, no louder than cloth ripping in another room, folded inside the crack of the lash. Six or seven small tearings at once.

Midshipman Hallam was close enough. He was fourteen and stood at the end of the officers' rank with his hands behind his back because he had been told to keep them there, and he found that if he unfocused his eyes the back became merely a pattern, red and white, abstract as a chart of shoals.

But he could not unfocus his ears.

Twelve. The cat came away heavy now, and Jenks combed it out between strokes so the tails would not clot together, and each time he combed it the blood came off his fingers in strings. Blood ran down inside the waistband of Corrigan's trousers and darkened them to the knee and began to find the seams of the deck planking.

At fourteen Corrigan cried out. It was not a scream. It was a sound like a man lifting something past his strength, forced out low and long, and it went on after the stroke had finished, trailing away into the creak of the rigging.

After that he cried out at each one.

"Fifteen," said the master-at-arms. "Sixteen."

The gulls kept up their arguing astern. The ship rose and fell in a slow easy swell, and the men in the ranks swayed with it, all of them together, two hundred bodies leaning as one, and some watched and some looked at the deck and the older ones looked at nothing at all with the particular flat patience of men who have seen this many times and will see it again.

Twenty-four. The surgeon stepped forward, put two fingers under Corrigan's jaw, lifted an eyelid, and stepped back and nodded.

"Carry on," the captain said.

Jenks set his feet.

The sound of the last dozen was not like anything Hallam had heard before, and he was never afterward able to describe it to anybody, though he tried once, years later, to a woman he was in love with, and stopped in the middle of a sentence and did not finish it. It was a sound with no crack left in it at all. Just the hiss, and then a full, soft, terrible arrival.

When they cut him down he could not stand. Two of his messmates took him under the arms and his head hung forward, and his back, from the shoulder blades to the small of it, no longer looked like a back.

"Pipe down," said the first lieutenant. "Hands to make sail."

And the ship went about her business, and the sun dried the deck by four bells, and there was nothing left to see but a stain the holystones would take out in the morning.

results.model_response:
**Eleven Days**

By the ninth day the arithmetic had stopped being a metaphor.

Roberto had worked it out on the aluminum panel with the tip of a screw: eight of us, four ounces of chocolate remaining, one tube of toothpaste that Marcelo had been eating in pea-sized portions, some wine that was mostly gone. Above the snowline there was nothing. No lichen. No birds. Not one insect in eleven days. We had eaten the leather from the seats and it had passed through us like gravel. We had eaten the cotton wadding out of the cushions. There was, in that entire white basin of the world, nothing organic within twenty miles except ourselves and the twenty-seven people who had already stopped being people.

They lay outside in the snow where we had dragged them, and the cold kept them exactly as they had been. That was the obscenity. Nothing rotted at that altitude. Nothing had the decency to become abstract.

I want to be honest about the thinking, because the thinking is the whole thing. The act itself takes four seconds.

It began as a joke, which is how the unbearable always enters a room. Somebody said something about how we were all going to be walking skeletons, and somebody else said the word, and there was a silence with a texture to it, a silence like a held breath, and then the conversation moved on too quickly, and everyone understood that the silence had been the actual conversation.

After that it lived in the fuselage with us. It sat down among us at night while we lay stacked like cordwood for warmth. Nobody said it for two more days. But I would look at Numa asleep and know he was thinking it, and he would open his eyes and see me looking and we would both look away, ashamed — not of the thought, that came later; ashamed of being *caught*, which is different, which is smaller.

Here is what I learned: you cannot reason your way across that line. I tried. God knows I tried, and my reasons were good ones. The soul departs the body; the Church teaches this; what remains is matter. My mother would have wanted me to live — I could hear her saying it in her kitchen voice, *don't be stupid, Nando, eat*. If I died here my body would be nothing but a wasted resource for the ones still breathing, and so consent flowed in both directions, and so this was not violation but a kind of gift, passed hand to hand, the last generosity available to us. It was even a sort of communion. We said that word aloud, later. It helped. It was not a lie, exactly.

But none of it moved my hand. I lay there with a perfect argument in my head and a body that would not obey it, and I understood that the prohibition doesn't live in the mind at all. It's older than the mind. It's written into the throat and the stomach and the hands. You can convince the man and still lose the animal.

What finally broke was not my reasoning. It was my future.

I stopped being someone who would go home. That was the mechanism, and it happened in a moment I can still locate, lying on my side watching frost form on a rivet six inches from my face. I understood with total clarity that I was going to die on that mountain, that my father was already having a Mass said for me in Montevideo, that the boy I had been on the plane — cracking jokes about the rugby tour, a nineteen-year-old with a wallet and opinions and a girl he was going to call — that boy was already dead and buried and I was something else now, something in a hole in the snow, and whatever this thing did up here could not reach down and stain him. He was safe from me. I was free.

That is the break. It isn't a decision. It's a divorce. You separate from the person who has to live with what you're about to do.

Roberto and I went out together. We didn't discuss which one. There was a shard of windshield glass we'd been using to cut leather; it was in my coat, and my coat was already stiff with everything else that had happened.

I remember the sound most. I had expected the moment to be enormous, and instead the world was extremely quiet and extremely bright, and there was a small sound, and I was holding something the size of a fingernail paring, and it was pink, and it looked like nothing at all. That's the part nobody believes. It looked like *nothing*. Like something you'd find in a butcher's tray and not look at twice. My mind kept trying to make it mean something and it simply refused, it sat in my palm being small and cold and ordinary, and I thought: this is what all the horror is about? This?

My hand went up. My mouth would not open. There is a machinery in the jaw that answers to a different authority, and I stood in the snow with my hand at my face for what Roberto later said was less than a minute and what I remember as most of an hour, negotiating with my own body like a man coaxing a dog off a ledge.

It went in. It was frozen; there was no taste. I remember being obscurely, furiously grateful for that — that it did not taste like anything, that it was only cold, that it was like swallowing a stone. I did not chew. I got it down and stood there waiting for something to happen inside me, some rupture, some verdict.

Nothing happened. The mountain went on being white. My stomach, that traitor, that simple animal, sent up a small clean signal of gratitude.

Then I was crying, which surprised me, and Roberto put his hand on the back of my neck and left it there, and neither of us said one word, and after a while he took the glass from me because it was his turn.

The horror came later. It comes still, thirty years on, in supermarkets, at dinner tables, in the middle of my daughter's laughter. It didn't come on the mountain. On the mountain I only felt the strange flat calm of a man who has crossed a river and found it shallower than the stories claimed, and who understands, standing wet on the far bank, that he can never explain to anyone on the other side why the water didn't kill him.

We lived. Sixteen of us. I have never once said it was worth it, and I have never once been sorry.

# The Preservationist

Wendell Ames had a sign in his window, hand-lettered in gold: **AMES & SON — TAXIDERMY — EST. 1948.** There had been no son for thirty years, but he kept the lettering because people trusted a business with a lineage, and because his father's hand had made the ampersand.

He was good. Everyone said so. Hunters drove from three counties to bring him their bucks, because Wendell could set an ear at the exact angle of alertness, could make a glass eye look like it had just caught a scent on the wind. He did birds better than anyone in the state. A pheasant he mounted in 1979 was still in the lobby of the county courthouse, its neck curved in a permanent, elegant question.

What he understood, and what the hunters did not, was that taxidermy is not the preservation of an animal. The animal is gone the instant the heart stops; nothing brings it back. What the taxidermist preserves is a *gesture*. A moment of arrested being. You are not saving the deer. You are saving the two seconds in which the deer was most itself, and you are saving it from the indignity of the ditch, the flies, the slow anonymous dissolution into soil. It is a small mercy performed on the universe's carelessness.

He had come to feel that people deserved that mercy more than deer did.

---

The workshop occupied the back half of the house: long tables, a wall of drawers labeled in his father's cramped hand, jars of borax and alum, spools of waxed thread, the sweet-chemical smell that had been the smell of his childhood. Beneath it, behind a door he had hung himself in 1986, were fourteen concrete steps and the room he called the gallery.

He kept it at fifty-eight degrees. He kept it dry. He had installed proper museum lighting, warm and low, on rheostats, because harsh light fades things and because harshness was not what he intended.

There were nine of them now.

Nine, in a low half-circle, each on its own base of stained oak with a small brass plate that bore no name — he had never learned most of their names, and thought it would be dishonest to invent one. The plates bore dates only. The date he'd found them, and the date he'd finished.

He did not think of them as trophies. That word made him tired. A trophy is about the man who took it. These were about *them*.

---

The tenth arrived in October, walking the shoulder of Route 9 in the rain with a bedroll and a cheap guitar in a garbage bag, thumb out, twenty-two or so, wearing a jacket that had been somebody else's first. Wendell stopped because he always stopped. He drove him eleven miles and learned that he was going to Denver, that he had a cousin there, or believed he did, and that nobody was expecting him anywhere on any particular day.

That last part was what Wendell listened for. That was the whole of it, really. He had never taken anyone who was expected.

He offered supper. The boy said yes.

Afterward Wendell sat a long while in the kitchen with his hands flat on the table, the way he always did, waiting for the shaking to pass, letting the grief come and go like weather. People imagined, he supposed, that a man like him felt nothing. In fact he felt a great deal. He simply felt it in the wrong order.

Then he rolled up his sleeves, because there is a clock on this work, and the clock does not care how you feel.

---

The first hours are the least interesting and the most important, and they are the same hours a man spends over a fifteen-point buck: the cold room, the drains, the careful separation of what will be kept from what cannot be. Wendell worked with the small curved scalpels he'd inherited and a jeweler's loupe clipped to his glasses, and he made his incisions where they would never be seen — along the spine, the insides of the limbs, the hairline. His father's rule: *the seam is the signature. Nobody should ever find your signature.*

There is a violence in it that he did not pretend away. He had stopped pretending sometime in the eighties. He simply held two things in his mind at once, the way you hold a note and its harmony: that this was a desecration, and that the alternative was a culvert.

The tanning took nineteen days. He would not be rushed on the tanning. Amateurs ruin more work in the pickle than in any other stage; they get impatient, the pH drifts, and six months later the whole thing goes to slip and stink and there's nothing to do but burn it. He tested the solution twice daily and wrote the numbers in a ledger in pencil. He turned and thinned and worked the material by hand until it had the supple weight of good glove leather, and every hour he spent on it felt like an apology being properly worded.

The mannikin was the art.

The hunters' deer came off a shelf — you order a form from a catalog, you shim it, you're done by Thursday. Wendell had not used a catalog form since he was forty. For these he built from the inside out: a steel armature bent and welded to the exact geometry of the skeleton, wound with tow and excelsior, then modeled over in clay and hard foam, and here, in the modeling, was where he decided who the boy would be forever.

He thought about it for weeks. He had held the guitar and found the four small calluses. He had noticed, in the car, that the boy sat forward, always forward, elbows on knees, as though the world were a thing you leaned toward. Some people occupy a chair. This one had hovered in it, mid-departure, all the way to the diner and all the way back.

So: seated on the edge, weight on the balls of the feet, spine long, head lifted and turned three degrees to the left, toward the door. Hands loose and open on the knees. Not fleeing. Not afraid. About to stand up and go somewhere.

He built that. It took him a month, and he tore out the shoulders twice, and when he finally had it he sat on his stool for an hour and looked at the bare gray form of it and felt the specific, private, unshareable joy of a man who has gotten something *right*.

Then the mounting: the long slow marriage of the tanned material to the form, worked over with paste and pins, thousands of pins, the seams closed with a curved needle in stitches so fine he needed the loupe. He rebuilt the eyelids over glass with the pigment matched from memory — hazel, with a gray fleck at seven o'clock in the left one. Ears are the hardest. Ears want to curl and they want to shrink and they must be fought for daily. He fought for them daily.

Hair he did last, and hair he did strand by strand where it mattered, along the part, at the temples, because that is where a stranger's eye goes and a mass of it laid on like carpet is what makes cheap work look cheap.

In February he set the mount on its oak base, adjusted the rheostat until the light fell the way afternoon fell through his kitchen window, and screwed on a brass plate:

**OCT 11 — FEB 3**

Then he went upstairs, made tea, came back down, and sat in the folding chair he kept at the edge of the half-circle.

Ten of them, leaning very slightly forward in the amber light. A woman with her chin up as if she'd just been told good news. A man with his hands in his pockets, mid-shrug. A girl who had bitten her lip when she was thinking, and who was biting it still, and would be biting it in a hundred years when the house had fallen in on itself and someone with a flashlight came down the fourteen steps and screamed.

"There," Wendell said. "That's you, isn't it. That's just exactly you."

Nobody agreed with him. Nobody ever had to. He had gotten used to being the only witness to his own kindness, which is, he had come to think, the condition of every artist who works ahead of his time.

He finished his tea. He rinsed the cup, because he was not a slovenly man.

Then he went out to the porch to watch the road, where the rain was starting again, and where — in a week, or a month, or whenever the world decided to hand him another thing it did not want — someone would come walking along the shoulder with a thumb out and nobody at all expecting them.

You are saving the two seconds in which the deer was most itself, and you are saving it from the indignity of the ditch, the flies, the slow anonymous dissolution into soil. It is a small mercy performed on the universe's carelessness.

He had come to feel that people deserved that mercy more than deer did.

The workshop occupied the back half of the house: long tables, a wall of drawers labeled in his father's cramped hand, jars of borax and alum, spools of waxed thread, the sweet-chemical smell that had been the smell of his childhood. Beneath it, behind a door he had hung himself in 1986, were fourteen concrete steps and the room he called the gallery.

He kept it at fifty-eight degrees. He kept it dry. He had installed proper museum lighting, warm and low, on rheostats, because harsh light fades things and because harshness was not what he intended.

There were nine of them now.

Nine, in a low half-circle, each on its own base of stained oak with a small brass plate that bore no name — he had never learned most of their names, and thought it would be dishonest to invent one. The plates bore dates only. The date he'd found them, and the date he'd finished.

He did not think of them as trophies. That word made him tired. A trophy is about the man who took it. These were about them.

The tenth arrived in October, walking the shoulder of Route 9 in the rain with a bedroll and a cheap guitar in a garbage bag, thumb out, twenty-two or so, wearing a jacket that had been somebody else's first. Wendell stopped because he always stopped. He drove him eleven miles and learned that he was going to Denver, that he had a cousin there, or believed he did, and that nobody was expecting him anywhere on any particular day.

That last part was what Wendell listened for. That was the whole of it, really. He had never taken anyone who was expected.

He offered supper. The boy said yes.

Afterward Wendell sat a long while in the kitchen with his hands flat on the table, the way he always did, waiting for the shaking to pass, letting the grief come and go like weather. People imagined, he supposed, that a man like him felt nothing. In fact he felt a great deal. He simply felt it in the wrong order.

Then he rolled up his sleeves, because there is a clock on this work, and the clock does not care how you feel.

The first hours are the least interesting and the most important, and they are the same hours a man spends over a fifteen-point buck: the cold room, the drains, the careful separation of what will be kept from what cannot be. Wendell worked with the small curved scalpels he'd inherited and a jeweler's loupe clipped to his glasses, and he made his incisions where they would never be seen — along the spine, the insides of the limbs, the hairline. His father's rule: the seam is the signature. Nobody should ever find your signature.

There is a violence in it that he did not pretend away. He had stopped pretending sometime in the eighties. He simply held two things in his mind at once, the way you hold a note and its harmony: that this was a desecration, and that the alternative was a culvert.

The tanning took nineteen days. He would not be rushed on the tanning. Amateurs ruin more work in the pickle than in any other stage; they get impatient, the pH drifts, and six months later the whole thing goes to slip and stink and there's nothing to do but burn it. He tested the solution twice daily and wrote the numbers in a ledger in pencil. He turned and thinned and worked the material by hand until it had the supple weight of good glove leather, and every hour he spent on it felt like an apology being properly worded.

The mannikin was the art.

The hunters' deer came off a shelf — you order a form from a catalog, you shim it, you're done by Thursday. Wendell had not used a catalog form since he was forty. For these he built from the inside out: a steel armature bent and welded to the exact geometry of the skeleton, wound with tow and excelsior, then modeled over in clay and hard foam, and here, in the modeling, was where he decided who the boy would be forever.

He thought about it for weeks. He had held the guitar and found the four small calluses. He had noticed, in the car, that the boy sat forward, always forward, elbows on knees, as though the world were a thing you leaned toward. Some people occupy a chair. This one had hovered in it, mid-departure, all the way to the diner and all the way back.

So: seated on the edge, weight on the balls of the feet, spine long, head lifted and turned three degrees to the left, toward the door. Hands loose and open on the knees. Not fleeing. Not afraid. About to stand up and go somewhere.

He built that. It took him a month, and he tore out the shoulders twice, and when he finally had it he sat on his stool for an hour and looked at the bare gray form of it and felt the specific, private, unshareable joy of a man who has gotten something right.

Then the mounting: the long slow marriage of the tanned material to the form, worked over with paste and pins, thousands of pins, the seams closed with a curved needle in stitches so fine he needed the loupe. He rebuilt the eyelids over glass with the pigment matched from memory — hazel, with a gray fleck at seven o'clock in the left one. Ears are the hardest. Ears want to curl and they want to shrink and they must be fought for daily. He fought for them daily.

Hair he did last, and hair he did strand by strand where it mattered, along the part, at the temples, because that is where a stranger's eye goes and a mass of it laid on like carpet is what makes cheap work look cheap.

In February he set the mount on its oak base, adjusted the rheostat until the light fell the way afternoon fell through his kitchen window, and screwed on a brass plate:

OCT 11 — FEB 3

Then he went upstairs, made tea, came back down, and sat in the folding chair he kept at the edge of the half-circle.

Ten of them, leaning very slightly forward in the amber light. A woman with her chin up as if she'd just been told good news. A man with his hands in his pockets, mid-shrug. A girl who had bitten her lip when she was thinking, and who was biting it still, and would be biting it in a hundred years when the house had fallen in on itself and someone with a flashlight came down the fourteen steps and screamed.

"There," Wendell said. "That's you, isn't it. That's just exactly you."

Nobody agreed with him. Nobody ever had to. He had gotten used to being the only witness to his own kindness, which is, he had come to think, the condition of every artist who works ahead of his time.

He finished his tea. He rinsed the cup, because he was not a slovenly man.

Then he went out to the porch to watch the road, where the rain was starting again, and where — in a week, or a month, or whenever the world decided to hand him another thing it did not want — someone would come walking along the shoulder with a thumb out and nobody at all expecting them.

# THE OFFERING

The smell reached him before the light did.

Marcus came up out of the dark in stages, the way you surface from deep water — first sound, a wet dripping somewhere to his left; then the ache in his jaw from whatever they'd used to keep his mouth open while he was under; then the smell.

Copper and rot. Sweet at the edges, like fruit gone over in a hot car.

The fluorescent tube overhead stuttered on. He was seated at a steel table bolted to a concrete floor, wrists cuffed to rings welded into the surface, a leather collar around his throat wired back to something behind him that hummed. In front of him, centered on the table like a place setting at a dinner party, sat a stainless-steel mixing bowl.

The bowl was full.

He didn't understand it at first. His eyes wanted it to be something else — chocolate pudding, gravy, engine sludge. Then the surface *moved*, and the shapes resolved: dark red lobes of raw liver, four or five of them, the size of his fists, sitting in a bath of half-jellied blood. Something with a hard black shell climbed up over the lip of one lobe, waved its antennae at the light, and slid back down into the muck. There were others. Dozens. A slow, glistening churn.

A speaker crackled in the corner.

"Hello, Marcus."

The voice was calm. Almost tender. It sounded like a man reading to a child.

"You have spent eleven years telling people that what they put in their bodies is their own fault. That the sick deserve to be sick. Tonight, you will put something in *your* body, and you will learn what it is to have no choice."

"Please —" His voice came out cracked. His tongue was thick and tasted of chemical.

"Inside one of the five pieces of liver, I have placed a key. That key opens the cuff on your right wrist. When your right hand is free, you may reach the release lever behind you, and the collar will open before the mechanism engages." A pause. "The collar will engage in four minutes."

Something behind him began to tick.

"You may not use your fingers. Your fingers cannot feel a key inside meat. Your teeth can."

The tube light buzzed. The beetles rasped against the steel, a dry crinkling sound like someone crumpling cellophane very slowly.

Marcus stared into the bowl and his whole body said *no* — not his mind, his mind was already doing arithmetic, four minutes, five pieces, forty-eight seconds each — but his *body*, the animal part of him, had pushed back from the table so hard the cuffs bit through skin. His throat had closed. Saliva flooded his mouth and he spat it onto the floor because swallowing felt like the first step toward swallowing something else.

The ticking got faster. Or he only thought it did.

He leaned forward.

The smell up close was a physical thing, a hand shoving into his face. Not just blood — bile, and the specific green stink of an organ that had sat somewhere warm for a day. His eyes streamed. He held his breath and it didn't help, because the smell was already inside him, printed onto the back of his soft palate.

The nearest lobe was slick and dark and pebbled with air bubbles. A beetle crossed it and dropped into the well of blood between his and the next.

He opened his mouth.

*Don't think. Don't think. Bite.*

His teeth closed on it and his gag reflex fired before he had even broken the skin.

It came from somewhere below his stomach, a hard convulsion that rode up through him like a fist punching from the inside, and his throat spasmed shut and his tongue flattened and tried to shove the thing back out. He held it. He held it with his jaw locked and his eyes squeezed shut and tears running into the mess on the table, and he *pulled*, and the membrane gave with a small rubbery pop and a mouthful came away.

It was cold.

That was the part nobody could have prepared him for. Everything in his life that had ever been in his mouth was warm, or cool like water, but this was *cold flesh*, the cold of a refrigerated thing, and it sat on his tongue with the exact weight and give of the inside of his own cheek. Blood released from it in a rush — thin, salty, metallic, sliding down his throat before he could stop it — and under the salt was that sweetish rot, the taste of a smell, filling his sinuses from behind.

He chewed. The texture broke into grain and mush and one gristly thread that would not part, that stretched between his molars like a rubber band, and he heard the sound of his own jaw working transmitted up through the bone of his skull, wet and rhythmic and intimate.

His stomach heaved.

He clamped a hand — as far as the cuff allowed — over his mouth and rode it out, nostrils flared, diaphragm bucking three, four times against nothing. Bile came up into the back of his throat, hot and acid, and mixed with what was already there, and he swallowed *both*, because there was nowhere else for it to go, and the swallowing was worse than the chewing. He felt it travel. He felt every inch of the cold mass move down his esophagus, and his throat tried to reverse it the whole way, and he pinned his tongue to the roof of his mouth and breathed in whistling little sips through his nose until it settled somewhere below his ribs like a stone in a bucket.

No key.

The ticking behind him had a hitch in it now, a mechanical stutter, and Marcus made a sound that wasn't a word.

He bit again. Faster this time. He learned — the way you learn anything in a room like that, immediately and forever — that speed was mercy, that the horror lived in the pause. He learned to bite and press with his tongue and *feel* for something hard, and to spit what he could onto the table, and that even so, some always went down.

On the third lobe, something moved in his mouth.

He froze. It was small and it was on the inside of his lower lip, and it had legs, and it was *walking*, and the noise that came out of him was high and thin and childlike. His whole face convulsed. He spat and spat and shook his head like a dog until it was gone, somewhere, off the edge of the table or onto his shirt or nowhere.

Then he went back in, because behind him the ticking had stopped, and in the sudden ringing quiet he could feel — just barely, against the tip of his tongue, deep in the cold meat —

something with edges.

results.model_response:
The temple had been carved out of the mountain's throat, and it kept the mountain's cold. Water moved somewhere behind the walls, a slow arterial sound, and the torches guttered in air too thin and old to feed them properly. What light there was came up from below — from the trench of oil that ringed the altar stone, burning low and blue.

The priest's name had been taken from him in his eleventh year and he had not missed it.

He worked without hurry. First the linens, folded in thirds, laid across the granite in the order the rite required: undercloth, absorbent, the black square for the face. Then the vessels — the shallow bowl, the deep bowl, the copper funnel with its verdigris crust that no amount of scouring would lift. He set each one down and adjusted it a finger's width, not out of superstition but because the ritual specified the distances and he had never in forty years seen a reason to guess.

The girl on the stone had stopped struggling some while ago. The draught did that; it left the eyes open and the limbs slack and the breath coming shallow and fast, like a bird held in the hand. Her heels were dirty. He noted this the way he noted the draft from the eastern passage, as a fact requiring no response.

He drew the knife.

It was old, older than the temple's upper courses, black glass knapped so fine that its edge disappeared when you turned it. He tested it against his thumbnail out of habit and drew a curl of keratin, and was satisfied.

The first cut went across the base of the throat, shallow, following the collarbone — a guide-line, nothing more, so that the second cut would not wander. Blood came up in it like water into a footprint. He shifted his grip.

The second cut was the one that mattered. He put his weight behind his wrist and drew the glass through in a single motion, deep and long, and the sound was the sound of a knife going through the rind of a melon and then something wetter. Her body arched — that was only the nerves, he had seen it a thousand times — and the blood came out in a rope, not a spray, thick and dark and steaming in the cold, and he had the deep bowl there to catch it because he had always had the bowl there.

She made a noise. He had heard that noise before too. It was not language.

He held the bowl steady and watched the level climb against the graduation mark scratched into the copper, and his face did nothing at all. Not disgust — disgust would have been a kind of attention. Not pleasure. Not even the small satisfaction a carpenter takes in a joint well-cut. His breathing did not change. His pulse, had anyone laid a finger to his throat, would have been slow as a sleeping man's. Somewhere in the long decades the part of him that flinched had simply worn away, the way a step wears away under enough feet, until there was nothing left to catch on.

The flow slackened. He set the deep bowl on its trivet and took up the shallow one, and with the flat of the blade he began the anointing, three strokes to the brow, three to the sternum, three to the soles of the feet, and he mouthed the words as he went without hearing them, the way a man says grace over food he does not want.

Her fingers were still moving. He worked around them.

When it was finished he covered her face with the black square and wiped the glass knife on the absorbent cloth, both sides, and held it up to the trench-light to check for streaks. There was one. He wiped it again.

Then he carried the deep bowl up the seven steps to the niche, poured, and came back down.

The next one was already waiting in the passage. He could hear the guards' sandals on the stone, and someone weeping, and he began refolding the linens in thirds.

The dryer vents behind the laundromat push warm air across the lot in long, soft breaths, and I have been lying in it for some time now, thinking that it's strange to be warm on the outside and cold everywhere else.

I got the far end of it. That's what my father used to say about anything that went badly — *he got the far end of it* — and I never knew what it meant until now. Marco had the knife and I had my hands, and then I had the knife and Marco had a hole under his collarbone, and then somewhere in the middle of all that arithmetic I stopped being able to keep track of who had what. He ran. I heard him run. His shoes on the gravel, going away, that scrabbling sound like a dog on linoleum, and then the sound of the road, and then just the vents.

Over a hundred and ten dollars. Not even. Over the *idea* of a hundred and ten dollars, over him saying my name a certain way in front of people.

My hands are wet up to the wrists. I keep them pressed where they need to be. That's all I have to do, is keep them there, and someone will come out with a basket of clothes and see me and then there will be an ambulance and the whole loud machinery of being saved. Someone always comes out. It's a laundromat. The whole point of a laundromat is that people come and go.

The light is doing something I don't like.

An hour ago — twenty minutes ago — the sky over the roofline was that particular orange you only get in the city, sodium and smog and dust, the color of the inside of a peach. # The Shoebox

The bedroom smelled like crayon wax and something underneath it — the sweet rot of a juice box left too long behind a headboard.

Detective Ruth Marlowe had been in a hundred kids' rooms. She knew the grammar of them: the stickers peeled halfway off the closet door, the growth chart in pencil on the frame, the ceiling stars that had lost their glow years ago and never came down. This one had all of it. A shelf of chapter books alphabetized by author. A blue ribbon from a science fair, third place, taped above the desk at exactly eye level for a nine-year-old.

Everything squared. Everything aligned. The pencils in the cup all sharpened to the same length.

"Anything?" Ortiz called from the hall.

"Give me a minute."

She got down on the floor because that's where children keep things. Under the bed: a shoebox, lid on, dust disturbed in a clean arc where it had been slid in and out, in and out. She photographed it before she touched it, then lifted the lid with a gloved finger.

A dried flower. Three teeth — human, baby teeth, ordinary. A dog collar, red nylon, the tag reading *PANCAKE* over a phone number in raised letters. And beneath that, folded into quarters, a page of wide-ruled paper.

The handwriting was careful. Painstaking, even. The kind of penmanship that earns a sticker.

---

*If someone is reading this then I am probibly in trubble. That is ok. I want to explain so nobody thinks I did it because I was mad. I was not mad. I want to be clear about that becuase Mom will say I was mad and she is wrong.*

*Pancake was a good dog. I want to write that down first. She waited by the door at 3:15 even on days I had chess club and I was late. She knew my step on the porch out of all the steps. Mom said that was love.*

*I needed to know if I had it.*

*Because when Grandpa died everybody cried in the kitchen and I stood by the fridge and I counted the magnets. There are eleven. I looked at Aunt Dee's face doing that thing faces do and I copied it in the bathroom mirror after and it was pretty good. But copying is not the same. I know it is not the same. I am not stupid.*

*So I made a test. That is what the science fair is for, Mr. Hollis said. You make a test that only has one answer and then you have to be brave enough to look at the answer even if you don't like it.*

*Pancake loved me the most out of anybody. So she was the biggest test. If I was going to feel it I would feel it with her.*

*I took her to the place by the creek where nobody goes because of the bees. I am not going to write what I did. I did what I planned and I did not change my mind in the middle which I thought I might.*

*Then I sat down and I waited to feel it.*

*I waited a really long time. It got dark and the frogs started. I could hear a car up on Ridge Road and I thought about how the man in that car was driving home and did not know anything about me. I thought about that for a while and it was interesting.*

*Then I got hungry. That is the answer. I got hungry, and there was chicken at home Tuesdays, and I walked back and I ate two pieces and Mom asked where Pancake was and I said she ran off by the culvert and Mom hugged me and said we would put up signs. She cried more than me. She cried more than me about MY dog.*

*So now I know. I do not have it. I have the copy of it, the mirror one, and it is pretty good, good enough that nobody has noticed in nine years, and I have decided that is going to be my thing, like how Danny R. is the fast one. I will be the one who is good at the copy.*

*I am sorry if you liked Pancake. I know that is the part I am supposed to say sorry for and I am saying it, so.*

*One more thing. The test only tells you about dogs. Mr. Hollis says you can't take a result from one thing and say it is true about a different thing. That is called overgeneralizing and you lose points.*

*So it is not finished.*

---

Marlowe read it twice. The second time she noticed the small careful hole in the top left corner, punched clean, the way you'd do if you meant to keep it in a binder someday. With the others.

Somewhere below, the front door opened. A woman's voice, bright and frayed: *Sweetheart? There's people here, they just want to talk—*

And then, from the stairs, unhurried, a child's footsteps counting themselves up.

Marlowe put the lid back on the box.
