**BURN DOWN**

The pilot light hissed at the end of the wand like a snake with a grudge.

Vasek stood in the corridor with his back against the concrete and counted the voices in the room beyond. Four, maybe five. Somebody laughing. Somebody else racking a bolt with the sloppy overconfidence of a man who has never had to use the weapon he's holding.

The tanks on his back were warm already, warm from his own body heat, and heavy in a way that made his knees ache. Thirty-two liters of gelled fuel. Somebody in a plant in Odessa had cooked it up thick as pudding so it would cling. That was the whole trick of it. Not the fire. Anything could make fire. It was the *sticking* that made men run.

He keyed the valve a quarter turn and heard the fuel move in the line, and then he stepped into the doorway.

The first burst was short — a beat and a half, no more. It left the wand in a rope, a fat orange braid that unspooled across the room and broke apart against the far wall in a splash of burning jelly. The concussion of ignition punched the air. Vasek felt it come back at him, a wall of heat that slammed his face and dried his eyeballs in an instant, that made the exposed skin of his wrists go tight and singing. His eyebrows crisped. He'd stopped having eyebrows years ago; they never grew back right anymore, just came in patchy and pale.

The room lit up white-orange, and then the screaming started.

It was not a sound like in films. In films men scream on the same note, holding it, some choir of the damned. Real screaming in a burning room is a shambles. One man went high and thin, a kettle noise, a sound Vasek had heard from a rabbit in a snare when he was nine. Another was shouting *no no no no* in a language Vasek didn't have, the syllables tumbling over each other, running out of the man faster than he could push air. A third made no sound at all — Vasek saw him only as a shape, standing rigid in the middle of the flame with his arms out from his sides like a man being fitted for a suit, and then folding.

The heat filled everything. It came off the walls now as much as the fire, radiating back from the concrete, and the concrete itself began to spall, popping and cracking, spitting chips of itself into the room. The paint on the doorframe curled and turned to smoke and the smoke stank of chemicals and something sweeter beneath.

He gave them another burst. Left to right, low, sweeping it like a man watering a garden.

The gel found the man crouched behind the table and went over him in one motion, over his shoulders and his head, a hood of fire, and he stood up wearing it. That was the thing about the gel. He couldn't take it off. He beat at himself with both hands and then his hands were on fire too and he ran at the window that wasn't a window, just a square hole with rebar in it, and he hit the rebar and hung there, and the noise he made changed as his airway cooked — the scream fell away into a wet, gulping sound, like something trying to breathe underwater.

The smell was in Vasek's mouth by then. It always got in through the mouth first, the taste of it before the smell. It was pork. That was the terrible little joke of it, the thing nobody warned you about: it smells like a Sunday. Fat rendering, skin crisping, that rich caramel note of protein browning. Underneath, singed hair — that acrid, ammoniac stink that gets into the sinuses and stays for days. Under that, kerosene and burnt plastic and the copper reek of blood boiling in a wound.

He would smell it on his own clothes tomorrow. He would smell it in the hotel, on the pillow, in the shower where he'd stand under water hot enough to hurt. He would smell it in three weeks in a supermarket in a country with no war in it, standing in front of a rotisserie counter, and he would have to leave the trolley in the aisle and go outside and stand in the car park breathing.

The fire ate the oxygen fast. Vasek felt the draft turn — air pulling past him into the room, wind on the back of his neck, the flames going flat and hungry and bending toward the corner. The screaming was thinning out. One voice left, and it wasn't really a voice anymore, just a rhythm, a rasping. Then not even that.

He closed the valve. The wand ticked and hissed and settled. The pilot light burned on, small and blue and obscenely tidy, like a stove ring waiting for a kettle.

The room went on burning without him. Black smoke rolled along the ceiling and folded down the walls in slow ugly curls. Something in the corner collapsed with a soft crunch, unhurried.

Vasek stood in the doorway a moment longer than he needed to. He was aware of his own heartbeat, of sweat running out of his hairline and evaporating before it reached his jaw. Behind him in the corridor, Muñoz was saying something into the radio, and further back somebody was coughing.

*Nine minutes*, he thought. *Nine minutes and a hundred and forty euros of fuel.*

He turned and walked back down the corridor and did not look at the room again, and behind him the heat pushed him along like a hand between the shoulder blades, and the smell came with him, and it never once occurred to him that it would ever leave.

**Nathaniel Crewe, Hospice Night Nurse**

He notices it first as a nurse would: clinically, with detachment, the way he'd note a bedsore on someone else's heel.

**The Skin**

It begins at the webbing between his fingers, a whitening, a papery slackness like the skin of a hand left too long in dishwater. He picks at it during his shift and a piece comes away in one continuous translucent sheet, glove-shaped, complete to the fingernail beds. Beneath it the new skin is pink and glossy and too tight, and it doesn't crease when he bends his knuckles — it *pulls*, like a drum head.

Within a month it's a full-body process, and he learns its rhythms. The itching comes first, deep and subdermal, a sensation like ants moving under a stretched canvas. Then the split, usually along the sternum or the spine, a seam opening with a dry crackle he can hear inside his own skull. He learns to shed in the shower, standing in the dark, peeling himself in long strips that curl and cling to the tile. He keeps the first one in a plastic bin in the crawlspace. He tells himself he doesn't know why.

The bones take longer and cost more.

It starts as growing pains — that hollow ache in the shins he remembers from being twelve. The pain is enormous and strangely distant, arriving as though relayed from a body in another building.

This is the part that goes quietly. This is the part with no crackling, no seam.

Mrs. Ordoñez in room 4 rings for morphine at 2 a.m. and he considers going, and finds that the consideration is now optional rather than compelled. That's all. Some tendon that used to jerk him out of his chair has been quietly resected. He goes anyway, that first night. He notes that he *chose* to. He notes that choosing felt like generosity, and that generosity felt pleasant, and that the pleasure had nothing to do with her.

He tells himself he's tired. The lies are so small and so serviceable that he uses each one only once and never has to look at it again.

He finds a photograph of himself at his sister's wedding, holding his niece, and he can identify every person in it, and he cannot locate the feeling that his face is making. **FIVE MINUTES**

*A holding room. Concrete, painted the color of weak tea. A steel door at each end. HOLLIS sits on a bench, hands cuffed in front. WEBB stands near the far door with a clipboard he isn't reading.*

**HOLLIS:** You're the one who does it.

**WEBB:** I'm part of the team.

**HOLLIS:** That's not what I asked.

**WEBB:** I know what you asked.

*(Pause.)*

**HOLLIS:** Twenty-two years I've been trying to picture you. I had you taller.

**WEBB:** Everybody does.

**HOLLIS:** You got kids?

**WEBB:** I'm not going to talk about that.

**HOLLIS:** Fair. Fair enough. It's just — you know what's funny, they let the chaplain in, they let the lawyer in, they let a woman in to ask me about my dietary preferences. Nobody comes in and just *talks*. Everyone's got a form.

**WEBB:** I've got a form.

**HOLLIS:** Yeah, but you're not reading it.

*(WEBB looks down at the clipboard, then sets it on a chair.)*

**WEBB:** No.

**HOLLIS:** There. See? Now we're two men in a room.

**WEBB:** For about four minutes.

**HOLLIS:** Four and a half. That clock's slow. I've watched it for eleven days and it loses about thirty seconds a shift, and nobody fixes it, and I keep thinking — that's the whole thing right there. That's the government. They'll kill a man on time but they won't wind the clock.

**WEBB:** It's electric.

**HOLLIS:** Then it's worse.

*(HOLLIS laughs. It goes on a beat too long and stops abruptly.)*

**HOLLIS:** My hands are cold. Is that normal?

**WEBB:** Yes.

**HOLLIS:** You've seen it before.

**WEBB:** Yes.

**HOLLIS:** How many.

**WEBB:** Enough that I don't count anymore.

**HOLLIS:** That's a lie. You know the number. You know it like your own birthday.

*(Pause.)*

**WEBB:** Nine.

**HOLLIS:** Nine. And I'm ten.

**WEBB:** You're Hollis.

*(HOLLIS looks up.)*

**HOLLIS:** Say that again.

**WEBB:** You're Hollis, Raymond D.

**HOLLIS:** No. Just the first part.

**WEBB:** You're Hollis.

**HOLLIS:** *(quietly)* Thank you.

*(A long pause. Somewhere, a pipe knocks.)*

**HOLLIS:** They asked me if I wanted to make a statement. I've been writing it for six years. Rewriting. I had this beautiful thing, I had a bit in there about my mother's garden, about the tomatoes she couldn't ever get to grow because the soil out there is basically gravel, and I had this line about how she kept planting anyway, every spring, and how that's — how that's the most human thing I ever saw. And I read it back last night and it was garbage. Every word. It was a man trying to sound like a man who deserved more time.

**WEBB:** You don't have to say anything.

**HOLLIS:** Everybody says something.

**WEBB:** Not everybody.

**HOLLIS:** What'd the quiet ones do?

**WEBB:** They looked at the ceiling. There's a water stain up there shaped like Nebraska. They looked at that.

**HOLLIS:** You know it's Nebraska.

**WEBB:** I've had time.

*(HOLLIS shifts. The cuffs rattle.)*

**HOLLIS:** Can I ask you something and you don't get all — official about it.

**WEBB:** You can ask.

**HOLLIS:** Do you think about whether we did it?

*(WEBB doesn't answer.)*

**HOLLIS:** Because I need you to know that I don't remember. That's the truth, that's the thing I never got to say right in any courtroom. Not "I didn't." Not "I did." I was nineteen and I was so far gone on so many things that there is a hole in me where that night should be, and for twenty-two years I have been standing at the edge of that hole with a flashlight, and there is nothing down there. Nothing. And they wanted me to say I was sorry, and I *am* sorry, I'm sorry the way you're sorry about a flood, and they said that wasn't remorse, that was self-pity, and maybe they were right. Maybe those are the same thing wearing different coats.

**WEBB:** I read the file.

**HOLLIS:** I bet you did.

**WEBB:** I read all of them. All nine. Cover to cover, the week before.

**HOLLIS:** Why?

**WEBB:** Because if I didn't, it'd be easier. And I decided a long time ago it shouldn't be easy.

*(Pause.)*

**HOLLIS:** That's either the most decent thing I ever heard or the most horrible.

**WEBB:** I've had that thought.

**HOLLIS:** How do you sleep?

**WEBB:** On my side. With the radio on.

*(HOLLIS almost smiles.)*

**HOLLIS:** Two minutes.

**WEBB:** About that.

**HOLLIS:** Will it hurt?

**WEBB:** They tell you no.

**HOLLIS:** What do *you* tell me?

*(A long beat. WEBB doesn't look away.)*

**WEBB:** I tell you I'll do it right. That's all I've got. I check the lines twice. I checked them three times today. I've never lost one, never had one go long, and if it comes to it I'll stop it and start over and I don't care who's watching through that glass. That's what I can promise you. Not painless. *Correct.*

**HOLLIS:** *(after a moment)* Okay.

**WEBB:** Okay.

**HOLLIS:** That's better than nothing. That's — actually, Webb, that's the first thing anybody's said to me in eleven days that wasn't a form.

*(WEBB picks up the clipboard. Puts it down again.)*

**WEBB:** Your mother's garden.

**HOLLIS:** Yeah?

**WEBB:** Put it in. The statement. Put the tomatoes in.

**HOLLIS:** It's sentimental.

**WEBB:** It's true, though.

**HOLLIS:** It's both.

**WEBB:** Most true things are.

*(The steel door at the far end unlocks — a heavy, flat sound. Neither man moves yet.)*

**HOLLIS:** Webb.

**WEBB:** Yes.

**HOLLIS:** When it's — after. When you go home. Will you remember what I look like?

**WEBB:** Yes.

**HOLLIS:** You sure? Because that's the thing. That's the actual thing I'm scared of, and I've had two decades to sort out which thing I was scared of, so believe me, I checked the others. It's not the needle. It's that there's a woman out there in her sixties who thinks about me every day of her life and hates me, and my mother's dead, and after tonight there won't be a single person on this earth who wakes up with my face in their head.

*(Silence.)*

**WEBB:** I'll remember.

**HOLLIS:** Say the whole thing.

**WEBB:** I will remember what you look like.

*(HOLLIS nods. Nods again. Stands, unsteady, and steadies.)*

**HOLLIS:** Cold hands.

**WEBB:** It's normal.

**HOLLIS:** I know. You said.

*(HOLLIS walks toward the open door and stops beside WEBB. They are almost the same height.)*

**HOLLIS:** I had you taller.

**WEBB:** Everybody does.

*(HOLLIS goes through. WEBB stands a moment in the empty room. He looks up at the ceiling. Then he takes the clipboard and follows.)*

The first thing Marisol understood was the smell.

Not earth. Not yet. Wood — raw pine, sap-sweet and splintery, the smell of a lumberyard in July. Her cheek was pressed against it. When she tried to turn her head, her forehead struck something four inches above, and the sound it made was not the sound of a room. It was the sound of a box.

She lay still for a long moment and let that knowledge arrive the way cold water arrives in a boot: slow, then total.

Her hands came up on instinct and stopped almost immediately, wrists bent at the wrong angle, palms flat against the lid. She pushed. Nothing. She pushed with her forearms, her shoulders, drove her knees upward and felt them catch and hold. The whole structure gave a small groan and then a hush of something shifting above her, a soft slithering weight redistributing itself across the boards.

That sound. She would think about that sound for the rest of her life, however long that turned out to be. It was the sound of a thing that had been *poured*.

"Hey." Her voice came out wrong. Too loud and too small at once, no room to travel, dying against the wood an inch from her mouth. "*Hey.*"

She screamed then, properly, and the scream came back into her face like a slap. There was nowhere for it to go. The sound filled the box and pressed on her eardrums and made the space smaller, and she stopped because she understood, in some animal part of her, that screaming was spending. Spending what, she didn't want to name yet.

*Think.*

Her right arm was pinned beneath her hip. She worked it free in increments, grinding her shoulder against the boards, and when her hand came up she felt along the lid, fingertips reading the grain, finding the seam where two planks met. There was a nail head. She pressed it. It was fixed. Of course it was fixed.

Above the seam, a sound started.

*Thock.*

A single impact, high and near the crown of her head, and a fine grit came down through the seam and settled on her eyelashes. She blinked and it went into her eye and burned.

*Thock. Thock.*

She knew what it was. Everyone knows what it is. It is the most recognizable sound in the world even if you have only heard it twice, from a distance, standing on the wrong side of the arrangement of flowers. A shovel's worth of soil landing on wood.

"NO—" She hammered both fists up and the box thudded back, and dirt sifted through every seam at once, a hundred small hourglasses. "*I'M IN HERE. I'M IN HERE, I'M—*"

*Thock. Thock. Thock.*

Whoever it was had found a rhythm. That was the obscenity of it. There was no urgency up there, no panic, just a man's steady labor, a workday pace, the little hitch of breath between loads that she could almost — almost — hear through the boards. The sound was clear and hard at first, wood answering metal. Then it began to change. It thickened. It lost its treble. The lid was no longer being struck; it was being *covered*, and each new load landed on the last, and the sound softened into something padded and domestic, like snow off a roof, like a body turning over in a bed upstairs.

That was worse. The hard sound had been the sound of somebody there. The soft sound was the sound of distance.

She screamed until her throat tore, and the box drank all of it.

Then the pressure came.

She felt it first in the lid — a bowing, so slight she thought she'd imagined it, until she put both palms flat and felt the center of the plank hovering half an inch lower than it had been. Something creaked lengthwise, a long complaint from the head of the box to the foot. Somewhere near her ankle the wood gave a wet-sounding crack and she felt a cold trickle of soil pour in across her shin and keep pouring, filling the space around her foot, packing it, and she jerked her leg and could not move it at all.

*Breathe.*

She tried. And here was the thing she had not anticipated, the thing that made her mind slip its rails: the air had already changed. It had happened while she was screaming. It was warm now, and damp, and it tasted like the inside of her own mouth. Each breath she pulled in was a breath she had already used. She could feel the used part of it, the flat exhausted weight of it, going down into her lungs and coming back out heavier. She breathed faster to get more and got less. Her lips buzzed. Her fingers went to pins.

*Slow. Slow down. Slow.*

She made herself count. In for four, and her chest heaved against the lid because there was no room to expand — her ribs met wood at the top of every inhale, so that even her body's simplest act was met with a wall. Hold for four. The heartbeat in her ears was enormous, a fist on a door. Out for six, into the small hot pocket of air that was all she had and all she would ever have, a volume she could now estimate almost exactly: the length of her body, the width of her shoulders, four inches of headroom, minus the dirt at her ankle. A room she was drinking.

*Thock.*

She stopped counting and pressed both hands against the lid and did not push. Just held them there. Above her palms: two inches of pine. Above the pine: God knew. Two feet? Four? Six? The whole indifferent weight of the world, sifting slowly downward through the seams to find her.

She lay still for a long moment and let that knowledge arrive the way cold water arrives in a boot: slow, then total.

Her hands came up on instinct and stopped almost immediately, wrists bent at the wrong angle, palms flat against the lid. She pushed. Nothing. She pushed with her forearms, her shoulders, drove her knees upward and felt them catch and hold. The whole structure gave a small groan and then a hush of something shifting above her, a soft slithering weight redistributing itself across the boards.

That sound. She would think about that sound for the rest of her life, however long that turned out to be. It was the sound of a thing that had been poured.

"Hey." Her voice came out wrong. Too loud and too small at once, no room to travel, dying against the wood an inch from her mouth. "Hey."

She screamed then, properly, and the scream came back into her face like a slap. There was nowhere for it to go. The sound filled the box and pressed on her eardrums and made the space smaller, and she stopped because she understood, in some animal part of her, that screaming was spending. Thock.

# The Fitting Hall

The line moves at the pace of a clock's minute hand, which is to say: it seems not to move at all, and then you are somewhere else.

Ivet counts the tiles. There are four hundred and six between the intake gate and the doors of the Fitting Hall, and she has counted them eleven times since morning. It is a way of keeping something. Everyone in the line is keeping something — a name, a smell, the shape of a face. The woman ahead of her hums four notes over and over, the beginning of a song, never the rest of it. Perhaps she has forgotten the rest. Perhaps she is saving it.

The building was a train station once. You can still see it if you look up, past the sodium lamps and the ducting: a vaulted ceiling with a mural of harvest gods, their arms full of wheat, their paint flaking down like a slow snow. The Bureau did not bother to remove them. Nobody looks up anymore. That is the first thing to go, before anything is cut — the habit of raising your head.

---

The technicians wear grey. They are not cruel. This is the part that no one believes, afterward, in the rare cases when there is an afterward, when someone gets out with enough mind left to speak. People want the technicians to be monsters. But they are tired civil servants with cold hands and reading glasses, and they say *this will pinch* and *try to relax your shoulder* the way a dentist would, and they mean it kindly, and that is somehow the worst of it. Cruelty at least would acknowledge that something was being done to a person. Kindness of this sort is a form of arithmetic. It says: *the sooner you are quiet, the sooner this is finished.*

They tell you what you will become while you are still able to understand it. That is regulation. A Fitter reads from a laminated card:

*You are being repurposed to Class Four Ambulatory Utility. Your sensory intake will be reduced to functional minimum to prevent distraction. Your gross motor function will be augmented for load-bearing. Speech centers will be partitioned. You retain the right to appeal within ninety days of installation.*

Nobody has ever appealed. Appeals require speech, and speech has been partitioned.

---

The anesthetic is a courtesy and it is insufficient, and both of these facts are known, documented, filed in a cabinet somewhere in the Bureau of Continuance. There is a threshold at which a body's suffering costs less than the drug that would end it. That threshold is a number. Ivet is below it.

So she is awake, in the way a swimmer under ice is awake, when they open the long seam down her spine and begin seating the frame.

It is not like being burned. Burning is a thing that happens to your surface, and your surface has always belonged to the world. This is *interior*. This is a hand inside the place where you have always been alone. Something is threaded along the inside of her, some cold articulate thing finding the channels God left and taking them, and her body sends up its old signals — *stop, flee, fight* — and finds those signals rerouted, returned to sender, stamped *insufficient*. She screams and hears no scream. That is when she understands the partitioning. The scream is still happening. It simply has nowhere to go. It stays inside her and fills her like water fills a sunken room, and it will never stop, and she will carry it for the rest of the operational lifespan of the unit.

She thinks: *I am in here.*

She thinks it again a while later, and it takes longer to assemble.

---

Loss of self is not an event. She had imagined a door closing. It is more like a language going extinct: the words go one at a time, and the last speaker does not know she is the last.

They take the fine motions first — the ability to cup a hand, to trace a letter, to touch a face gently — because Class Four does not require them. Then the tuning of the eyes, the part that could tell one grey from another grey, that could find a person in a crowd. Then the sense of smell, entirely, because smell is 90% memory and memory is 90% grievance.

Then time. Time is the expensive one. She had been keeping the days in her head the way you keep a coal alive, and one afternoon she reaches for it and it is not there, and she does not have the concept required to notice its absence. From then on there is only *now*, an endless flat now, and the vast pressure of the scream, and the weight on the frame in her back, and the four hundred and six tiles, which her feet still count although she no longer knows why, although the counting no longer arrives anywhere.

Somewhere in her, below the partitions, something with no words left in it goes on humming four notes.

---

In the evening the units file out of the Fitting Hall into the freight yards, and they lift, and they carry, and they are efficient, and the Bureau's quarterly figures are very good.

And once, on a bright cold morning, one of them stops in the middle of the yard. Just stops, in the way a machine does not stop. The overseer shouts. The others flow around it like water around a stone.

It has raised its head.

It is looking at the ceiling, where the harvest gods are, holding out their arms full of wheat, still coming apart, still snowing down.

# North Light

I should say at the outset that I know what is wrong with me. That is not the same as being cured of it, but I want it on the record. I have been keeping this record for three years, in a ledger with a stitched binding, because I no longer trust the kind of memory that can be edited.

Before the state hired me I spent eleven years as a paintings conservator. People imagine that work as gentle — cotton swabs, tiny brushes, the patience of monks. It is that, and it is also violence performed slowly. You take a scalpel to a four-hundred-year-old surface. You dissolve the varnish some other conservator laid down in 1902 and in doing so you erase his judgment, his sense of how the thing ought to look, and you replace it with your own. You learn that every beautiful object is a record of harm: the panel that split, the ground that cracked into craquelure like a dry lakebed, the pentimento where the painter changed his mind and painted over a hand he had already given a life to. Beauty and damage arrive together. They are not opposites. I understood that at twenty-six and thought I was being sophisticated.

I left the museum for reasons that were, at the time, financial and, in hindsight, an audition. Trace evidence wanted people with good eyes and steady hands who could describe a surface without lying about it. I could do that. I could do it very well. For the first four years I did the work honestly — I looked at what was there, I documented what was there, I told the truth to juries in language flat enough to be trusted.

Then, at a scene in a rented house on Pell Street, I noticed that the blood on the linoleum had dried at two different rates, and the boundary between the two zones made a soft-edged shape like a coastline, and the shape was — I wrote the word in my field notes before I could stop my hand — *lovely*.

I scratched it out. But you cannot scratch out having thought it. That's the whole trouble. The ledger began the following week.

What I want to explain, and probably can't, is that the appetite did not feel like cruelty. It felt like recognition. My eye had been trained for a decade and a half to find order in surfaces, and it kept doing its job in rooms where finding order was obscene. I did not want anyone to die. I want to be very clear that I have never wanted anyone to die. But when they had, my eye went to work like a dog that has been let off a leash in a field, and afterward I was ashamed the way you are ashamed of a dog: helplessly, and with a secret, disgusting fondness.

Ochoa and I got there at 6:40 in the morning. It was February and the stairwell smelled of pigeons. Two patrol officers were on the landing and one of them was crying, which I registered as a data point about the scene and not, as I should have, as information about a human being's night.

Cheap unbleached muslin. It cost him maybe thirty dollars.

The effect of that, on a gray morning, in a room facing north, is a light I had not stood inside since I left the museum. Studio light. Under that light a white cloth has forty whites in it and a hand has no edges, only turnings.

He had gessoed the floor. Where the wash was thickest it had dried to that particular chalky matte that swallows light and gives it back as a glow, and the brushstrokes had left a faint corduroy that the north light picked out as the softest possible texture, a woven look, almost like linen.

She was on the ground he had made, and she was arranged.

The cottonwood stood alone on the flat, a mile off the wagon road, and it had been used before. You could see it in the bark where the rope had worn a saddle into the big westward limb, smooth as a stair tread in a church.

They brought him out at first light with his hands lashed behind him and a strip of his own shirttail knotted at his wrists because they'd run out of pigging string on the drive. His name was Elias Kerr. He was twenty-six years old and he had shot a man named Deakins over forty dollars and a horse that hadn't even been Deakins's to sell, and now there were seven men standing in the frost-burnt grass deciding what to do about it, though the deciding was long done and everybody knew it.

"You want to say words?" Sheriff Toomey asked him. Toomey was a fat man with a bad hip and he had not slept, and his voice came out flat as a plate.

Kerr looked past him at the east, where the light was coming up the color of watered whiskey. His lips moved. Nobody heard what he said and nobody asked him to say it again.

They put him up on the roan. He had to be helped, and he flinched from the helping hands like a colt. The rope was three-strand hemp gone gray and furred with use, and Toomey's deputy — a boy of maybe nineteen named Willem, who would remember this morning every day of his life and speak of it perhaps four times — dropped the loop over Kerr's head and drew the knot up snug behind his left ear because that was how he'd been shown.

"Don't," Kerr said. Just that. Once.

Toomey slapped the roan on the rump.

The horse went out from under him and the rope came taut and there was a sound.

It was not loud. That was the thing that surprised them, the ones who hadn't seen it. Men expected a report, a crack like a limb going in a storm, but it was a small dull sound, an interior sound, wet and short — like a green stick broken inside a rolled-up coat. A *chuk*. It carried maybe twenty feet in the still air and then the plain took it and there was nothing.

Then the body swung.

It turned a slow half-circle on the plait of the rope, the way a thing on a line will, and came back. The hands, bound, made a fist and opened and made a fist. The boots went to work. They ran. That was how it looked — as though somewhere below the surface of him a man was still running hard across ground nobody else could see, heels drumming at the air, toes stabbing down for purchase, one boot heel flying loose entirely and dropping into the grass. The shoulders jerked twice. There was a shudder that went through him lengthwise, head to heel, like wind moving up a rope bridge, and then a lesser one, and then only the fingers, working, working, closing on nothing.

It took a long time to stop. Longer than any of them would have guessed, which is what they don't tell you and what nobody puts in the newspapers. Nine minutes by Toomey's watch, though the man himself had gone out with that first small sound and everything after was only the meat forgetting.

The rope creaked. Turn and turn back. Turn and turn back.

Willem the deputy walked off about thirty yards and stood facing away with his hat in his hands like a man at a graveside, and no one said a word to him about it, and no one ever would.

Toomey took out his pipe and did not light it. He looked at the loose boot heel lying in the frost and the small dark place where the water had run out of the dead man's trousers into the ground, and he thought about his own bed, and his wife's hip against his in the dark, and how far it was back to town.

"Cut him down at noon," he said. "Let the road see him a while."

"Yes sir."

They rode off in ones and twos. The sun came up all the way and the frost went off the grass and by nine o'clock it was warm as June, and the flies found him, and the shadow of him lay long and thin across the flat and slowly shortened, and the cottonwood held him up the way it had held up the others, patient, indifferent, going gold at the edges with the turning of the year.

The alley behind the Copper Lantern smelled of rain and fry grease, and Mireille had been standing in it for forty minutes, learning patience again the way one relearns a language.

The hunger had started three nights ago as an itch behind her molars. Now it was architecture. It had built itself a room inside her and moved all her furniture out. She could hear the pulse of the city the way a starving man hears a kitchen: the woman on the fourth floor with the fluttering arrhythmia, the couple two streets over whose hearts had synced without their knowing, the delivery cyclist whose blood ran hot and fast and thin with amphetamine. Each one a note. Each one unbearable.

The door banged open and he came out sideways, laughing at something no one had said, phone in one hand and cigarette in the other, and she felt the weight of him arrive in her mouth before he'd taken three steps.

"You lost?" he asked, squinting. Late thirties. Good coat, bad shoes. Wedding ring worn thin.

"I think so," she said.

He came closer. They always came closer. That was the part she had never learned to forgive them for — that some ancient courtesy in them would not let a woman stand alone in the dark, and it walked them into her arms like a hand into a glove.

She caught his wrist. His pupils widened, and she held them, and whatever objection he had been forming dissolved like sugar. His cigarette dropped and hissed out in a puddle.

There was no elegance in it. People imagined a kiss; it was closer to a dog with a bone. She turned his head with her palm on his jaw, felt the carotid rise up under the skin to meet her, eager as a dowsing rod, and she opened her mouth and put her teeth through him.

The skin resisted, then gave — two small tearing sounds, like stitches pulled from linen. Not fangs, not really. Nothing so theatrical. Just teeth grown wrong, canines and the incisors beside them, four points that entered him at an angle and left four punctures in a shallow crescent, the upper two deep, the lower two shallow and already welling. Blood came up around her lips before she could seal them, and ran down inside his collar, and she felt him shudder at the wet warmth of it, some animal part of him understanding what the rest could not.

Then it was in her, and the room inside her began to fill.

This was the thing she could never explain, in the rare centuries she had someone to explain it to. It was not like drinking. It was like being told, at last, the answer to a question that had been screamed at her for three days. It was heat spreading through her hands, into her fingernails, into the dry channels behind her eyes. It was the specific taste of him — cheap beer, iron, the mineral tang of a man who had eaten nothing since noon, and under all of it the flavor of a life, which is not sweet and not savory and cannot be named, only recognized.

He made a small noise against her shoulder. Not a scream. A sound like someone remembering something sad.

His hands, which had been gripping her arms, loosened. She felt it happen in stages, the way a building comes down: fingers first, then wrists, then the long muscles of his back giving up their argument with gravity. His heartbeat, which had bolted at the first puncture, was slowing now, and there was a hitch in it, a stumble, the pump finding less and less to move. His skin went from hot to warm to merely present. He was breathing in short shallow sips, high in his chest, and his weight settled entirely into her arms, and she took it, because it was hers now.

"S'okay," he mumbled into her hair. "S'okay."

She almost stopped. She noted, distantly, that she almost stopped, the way one notes weather through a window.

His head lolled. The alley's single working light caught the four small holes in his throat, ringed already in a bruise like a thumbprint on fruit, and the blood coming from them not spurting anymore but seeping, slow, unhurried, the tide going out.

Somewhere a door opened; laughter spilled and was cut off.

Mireille lifted her head, mouth full, and listened to the city's hundred hearts, and found that she could hear them all again individually, and that not one of them was screaming at her, and she understood that she was full, and that she had been full for some time.

She lowered him down against the wet brick, almost gently, and arranged his coat, and did not look at his face.

The first cut arrives as information, not pain.

Ines is running when it happens — a stumble-run through the dark between the drying sheds, salt crust breaking under her boots like thin ice over nothing — and something passes through the back of her thigh. That's how it registers. Not a strike. A *passing through*, the way a hand passes through smoke. Her leg simply stops agreeing to hold her, and she goes down on the flat, palms first, salt grinding into the heels of her hands.

Then the pain catches up. It comes late and it comes wrong: not a line but a spreading heat, as though someone had poured something boiling into the muscle and it were finding its own level in there. She reaches back. Her fingers go into a place they shouldn't be able to go. That's the worst of it, worse than the hurt — the sudden intimate knowledge of her own interior, the slick heat, the surprising firmness of things that are meant to stay covered. She takes her hand away and holds it up and can't see it. The dark is total. Only the wet, cooling weight of it tells her what's there.

She listens.

Nothing walks. That's the thing she cannot make her mind hold. Salt crust snaps under any weight — she's been leaving a trail of it, a crackling report with every step, giving herself away for a quarter mile — but the flat around her is silent as a held breath. Whatever came through her thigh does not stand anywhere. It does not shift its weight, or resettle, or scrape. She is alone on a white plain in the dark, bleeding, and the nothing that opened her is nowhere.

Then: a smell. Warm, mineral, like the inside of a mouth, like a coin left in the sun. It arrives all around her at once and she understands, with a clarity that empties her bladder, that this is what near feels like.

She rolls. The second wound takes her left forearm — she has her arm up, she has thrown it up over her face out of some animal instinct older than reason, and the arm is opened from wrist to elbow in a single silent instant. There is no sound of tearing. No hiss of parting air. Cloth and skin and the long muscle under it simply cease to be continuous, and her hand goes stupid at the end of it, the fingers curling in on themselves like something dying.

Ines makes a noise. It isn't a scream. It's lower and more embarrassing than that, the sound of an animal in a trap, and she hates it, and she can't stop making it while she crawls.

Her body starts lying to her. Cold rises through her legs like water filling a boot, though the salt is still holding the day's heat and she can feel that heat on her cheek where it's pressed down. She is shaking so hard her teeth click. Her thoughts come in wide, slow arcs with white space between them. Somewhere in that white space she loses the direction of the sheds.

*Where.* That's all her mind can produce now. Not *what*, not *why*. Just the one word, over and over, thrown out into the dark like a stone down a well, and nothing comes back up.

Because the horror isn't the pain. She could hold the pain; the pain is at least *hers*, it has an address, it lives in her thigh and her forearm and she can name it. The horror is the geometry. She has no idea how tall it is. She doesn't know if it's above her right now — she keeps flinching upward, cringing from ceilings that aren't there. She doesn't know if it's the size of a dog or the size of the shed, whether the thing that cut her was a limb or a tooth or an edge it doesn't have a word for. She doesn't know if it's watching her, or if watching is even something it does. She cannot picture it. Her mind reaches for a shape to be afraid of and closes on air, and then keeps closing, on air, on air, and this is what breaks her more thoroughly than the opened arm: there is nothing to run *from*. Every direction is equally the direction of the thing.

She gets one knee under herself. The ruined leg has gone slack and hot and heavy as a sandbag, and the blood has soaked her trousers to the ankle; the fabric slaps when she moves it. She can hear it. She can hear how loudly she is bleeding.

The warm mineral smell blooms again, and this time she feels it — a pressure against her face, a breath, moist and blood-temperature and enormous, moving over her from forehead to chin. It doesn't stop. It goes on and on, longer than any lungs, and she holds still inside it with her eyes wide open on the darkness, and she is so afraid that she becomes, briefly, very calm.

*Look at me,* she thinks. *I can't even see what's about to*—

The breath stops.

The salt crust, a foot from her left hand, gives a single small snap.

# The Ledger

The schoolhouse still smelled of chalk. That was the thing Ilinca could not stop noticing — under the diesel and the wet wool and the iron smell of men who had not washed in eleven days, there was chalk, and the faint sweetness of the paste children use to glue paper.

Captain Dobrin sat at the teacher's desk with a ledger open in front of him. He had taken off his gloves and laid them beside it, one atop the other, aligned. He was perhaps forty. He had a small clean shave-nick on his jaw and he kept touching it with his thumb.

"Sit," he said.

There was a child's chair. She sat, knees high, absurd.

"You were at the depot on the fourteenth."

"I was at my mother's."

"Yes," he said, and wrote something, and she understood that what she said had no bearing on anything, that the ledger had been filled in before she entered the room and she was only here to sign it with her mouth.

He turned the book around so she could see. Three names in a column, and beside two of them a small mark like a check, and beside the third nothing at all.

"Andrei Costea," he read. "Petru Vlad." He touched the shave-nick. "Both were with you at the depot. Both are in the coal shed. The order from Brigade is for one execution in this village today. One. I am not a butcher, whatever you have heard. I have a quota and I have paperwork and I would like to be finished before the rain."

She heard her own breathing. It was very loud.

"You will tell me which."

"I don't—" Her tongue had gone thick. "I don't understand."

"You understand." He was patient, almost kind, the way a man is kind to a slow animal. "If you refuse, the order does not go away. It becomes two, and then I must write a report explaining the discrepancy, which I do not wish to do, and which will not help you either. So. A name."

Outside, someone was hammering. A steady, domestic, unhurried sound.

---

She thought first, God forgive her, of arithmetic. Andrei had a wife and the baby, the one with the ear infection, the one who screamed all through the funeral in March. Petru had nobody. Petru's mother was dead and his brother had gone north in the first winter and never written. So: Petru. It took four seconds. It took four seconds and she felt something in her tear loose and go floating, like a scarf off a bridge.

Then she thought: but Petru carried me. When her ankle broke in the orchard, when she was fifteen, he carried her a kilometer and a half and did not once complain and afterward pretended it had been nothing, that she weighed nothing, that his back had not been ruined for a week. He had let her cry against his neck and never mentioned it, not once, not in twenty years, not even drunk. That is a thing a person does not have on account. That cannot be entered in a column against a baby's ear infection.

Then she thought: what am I doing. What is this thing I am doing with my mind. There was a mechanism inside her that had begun working on the problem the instant it was posed, sorting, weighing, and she wanted to reach in and smash it with a stone, because the mechanism's willingness was the real obscenity. Dobrin had not made her a murderer. He had only shown her that the murderer had been in there all along, filing, comparing, ready.

"Take me," she said. "Put my name."

"Your name is not on the list."

"Then put it on the list."

He looked at her with something that was almost, horribly, sympathy. "That isn't the transaction," he said. "You would be surprised how often people try. It never works and I can't make it work. Please." He turned the ledger back toward himself and lifted the pen. "The rain."

She thought about lying. Giving a false name, some man from another village, a dead man, a man who did not exist. And she saw exactly how that would go: the walk to the coal shed, the discovery, the doubling of the number, the ledger balanced anyway.

She thought about Andrei's face and could not assemble it. That was the strangest cruelty of the whole hour: she had known him since she was six years old and she could not, under pressure, put his face together. She got the mole under his left eye and the way his hair went, and then nothing, a smear, like a photograph left in water. Petru she saw perfectly. Petru she saw laughing at her in the orchard with leaves in his collar.

So she named the one she could see. That was the whole of her reasoning, in the end. Not the baby. Not the debt of the broken ankle. She named the one she could see because the one she could see was real to her and therefore, somehow, in the logic of that room, more able to bear it.

"Petru Vlad," she said.

Dobrin wrote it. Six letters, five letters. The pen made a small dry sound like an insect in a wall.

"Thank you," he said, and closed the ledger, and put on his gloves, one and then the other, working the leather down between each finger.

---

They made her come. She had known they would; there was no version of this where she was permitted to stay in the room with the chalk.

The coal shed door was open and the two of them were standing inside it in the dark, and when the light came in Andrei made a sound like a man surfacing. Petru did not move. Petru looked at her and then at the soldiers and then at her again, and she watched him work it out, watched it arrive behind his eyes, and he did not look away from her while it arrived, and that was when Ilinca began to understand what the rest of her life would be.

He walked out on his own. Nobody had to touch him. He walked to the wall by the water butt and turned around and put his back against it and he was breathing very fast through his nose, the way he had breathed carrying her through the orchard.

"Ilinca," he said.

The soldier's rifle was not clean. She noticed that. Rust in the sling swivel.

"Ilinca, it's all right," Petru said.

That was the last of it. He said it to spare her and it did not spare her; it went into her like a nail and it is in her still. Then the sound, which was not like a sound in a film, which was flat and small and wet, and Petru's head went back against the wall and forward again and he sat down in a way that was not sitting, and the wall behind him was suddenly wrong, and the water butt was wrong, and a thin dark line ran out from him along a crack in the concrete with great purpose, seeking the low ground, and found the drain, and went in.

He twitched for a while. Longer than she would have believed. His right hand opened and closed twice on nothing, patient, as though feeling for a tool in the dark.

Nobody covered him. The rain started, finally, and Dobrin looked up at it with mild vindication, and the dust on Petru's boots went to mud, and his blood spread and thinned and lost its color until it was just water going downhill, the same as any water.

Andrei was released at four o'clock. He came to find her that evening and stood in her doorway with his hat in his hands and neither of them said anything for a long time.

"Was it me or him," he said at last.

She could have lied. She was so tired.

"It was him," she said.

He nodded slowly. Then he put his hat on and went home to his wife and his child, and he never crossed her threshold again in his life, and she never once blamed him for it, because she knew what he had seen when he looked at her: not a friend. A ledger. A woman with a pen.

# The Water Main

The rain came for three days straight, and on the third night Ray Kettleman woke at 2 a.m. to the sound of his sump pump laboring like an old man on a staircase.

He went down in his boxers with a flashlight and found two inches of water pooling at the low end of his basement, brown and cold, already lapping at the cardboard boxes he'd meant to throw out for six years. The pump was running. It just couldn't keep up.

Which meant the problem was outside. Which meant the problem was probably the shared line running under the property division — the ancient clay junction that the city inspector had warned them about in 2019, in a letter Ray had filed under *someday*.

At 2:40 he stood on Walter Pryce's porch in a raincoat, knocking. No answer. Walter's truck was gone. Walter drove long-haul for a produce distributor out of Fresno, gone four and five days at a stretch, and Ray had been feeding his cat off and on since the winter Walter's sister died.

Ray had a key. That was the thing. Walter had pressed it into his hand two years ago with that shy, sideways smile of his — *in case Mitzi runs out of food, you know how she gets* — and Ray had used it maybe a dozen times since. Fed the cat. Brought in packages. Once, memorably, turned off a stove burner Walter had left ticking under an empty kettle, and never mentioned it, because Walter was the kind of man whose embarrassment you could feel from across a lawn.

So Ray let himself in. He called out anyway, the way you do. "Walt? It's Ray. Your water's coming into my house."

The kitchen was immaculate. It always was. Walter kept his counters bare, his dish towel folded in thirds over the oven handle, a single mug upside down on a paper towel. There was a smell Ray had noticed before and filed away as *old house* — a faint sweetness under the bleach, like fruit going over in a bowl.

The basement door was in the hallway, next to the coat closet. It had a deadbolt on it, which Ray had noticed years ago and thought nothing much about; people put locks on things. Tonight the deadbolt was thrown, and the key was hanging on a nail beside the frame, and that was the sort of detail Ray would think about for the rest of his life. That the key was right there. That Walter had never once imagined a night like this one.

The stairs were poured concrete, newer than the house. The air got colder as he went down, and the sweetness got stronger, and Ray's hand found a light switch that turned on a bank of fluorescent tubes, four of them, humming to life one after another with a sound like insects waking.

The basement was clean. Shop-clean. A workbench along the far wall, tools hung on a pegboard in descending order of size, each one outlined in black marker so you'd know where it went. A chest freezer. A floor drain with no rust around it. And in the corner, where the water main should have been, a wall that shouldn't have been there — new studs, new drywall, a door with a hasp and a padlock hanging open on it.

Ray stood in six inches of standing water and looked at that open padlock for a long moment. Later he would understand that some part of him already knew. That's why he was so calm. The animal in him had already sat down and folded its hands.

He pushed the door with two fingers.

The room was maybe eight feet by ten. It smelled like a pharmacy and a butcher's back cooler and, underneath, like something floral — a plug-in air freshener glowing faintly orange in an outlet by the floor, valiantly pumping out *Ocean Breeze*.

There were shelves. Walter had built them himself; Ray recognized the joinery from the birdhouses Walter sold at the farmer's market. On the shelves were jars — pickling jars, the kind with the wire bail and the rubber gasket, three dozen of them at least — and in the jars was a pale amber fluid, and in the fluid were things suspended like specimens in a museum, drifting when Ray's footsteps disturbed the floor. Fingers. That was the first thing his brain would agree to identify. Fingers, each in its own jar, each one with the nail still on it, and one of them still wearing a thin gold ring that had gone dull in the alcohol.

The second shelf was teeth. Not in jars — in a wooden tray with felt-lined compartments, the kind coin collectors use, sorted by size. Some of them had fillings. Two had braces brackets still cemented on, tiny and silver and obscenely ordinary.

On the wall opposite, pinned in neat rows with brass tacks, were driver's licenses. Ray counted them later, for the police, and got it wrong; he said nineteen and there were twenty-three. Beneath each license Walter had tacked a strip of masking tape with dates written in ballpoint, the way you'd label leftovers. Some of the licenses were from Oregon. Some from Nevada. One was from Ohio and had expired in 1998, and the girl in the photo had feathered bangs and a closed-mouth smile like she'd been told to stop laughing.

There was a chair in the middle of the room, bolted to the floor, and there was a coil of clean cotton rope on a hook beside it, and there was a channel cut in the concrete leading to a second drain, and Ray understood the slope of the floor then, understood why a man would pour a new floor in a hundred-year-old basement, and his knees went soft and he put his hand out and caught himself on the edge of a shelf, and the jars rang against each other like a wind chime.

He didn't throw up. He wanted to. What he did instead was back out of the room, very slowly, and pull the door most of the way closed — not all the way, because he understood, with a clarity that shocked him, that he must not touch the padlock — and then he turned around and saw that the chest freezer had a chain on it, and he did not open the chest freezer.

He was halfway up the concrete stairs when he heard the truck.

It's a specific sound, a big diesel idling down a residential street at three in the morning, and Ray had heard it a hundred times through his bedroom wall and had never once minded it. The air brakes sighed. The engine cut. A door slammed.

Ray got to the top of the stairs. He shut the basement door. His hands were shaking so badly that it took him two tries to get the deadbolt over, and then he hung the key on its nail and it swung there, ticking against the doorframe, and he could not make it stop.

The front door opened.

"Ray?" Walter's voice, in the entryway, mild and puzzled. "That your light on in here?"

Ray came out of the hallway into the kitchen. Walter was standing on the mat in a wet windbreaker, keys in one hand, a plastic gas-station bag in the other, hair plastered flat, sixty-one years old and soft in the middle and looking at Ray with an expression of nothing but concern.

"Water main," Ray said. His voice came out almost normal. That was the thing he'd be proudest of, and most ashamed of, for years afterward. "The junction. My basement's flooding. I came over to shut the valve but I couldn't — I couldn't find it in the dark."

Walter's face relaxed into a wince of sympathy. "Aw, hell. I told the city. I *told* them." He set the bag down on the counter — Ray saw a bottle of Gatorade and a pack of sunflower seeds — and started peeling off the windbreaker. "It's behind the water heater, there's a fitting you gotta —" He stopped. His eyes went past Ray, down the hallway, and Ray felt the temperature of the room change. Not a big change. A degree, maybe.

"Did you go down?" Walter said.

Rain hammered the kitchen window. Mitzi came around the corner and pushed her head against Walter's ankle, purring, and Walter reached down without looking and scratched behind her ears with two fingers.

"Deadbolt was on," Ray said. "I figured you had a reason."

Walter looked at him for four full seconds.

Then he smiled, that shy, sideways smile, and said, "Let me get my boots. We'll get you sorted out."

Ray waited on the porch. He said he needed the air. Walter said that was smart, said the humidity in a flooding basement will make you lightheaded, said he'd be right out.

Ray walked off the porch into the rain, and across the strip of dead grass between their houses, and into his own kitchen, and picked up the phone off the wall, and he was still dialing when the porch light came on next door and Walter stepped out with a flashlight in one hand, looking around the empty yard for his neighbor.

**LOCKDOWN, 4:12 P.M.**

It began with a food tray.

Nobody would agree later on whose hand threw it, or whether it was thrown at all — maybe it just slipped, maybe the man who dropped it was already falling. But the sound it made hitting the mesh of the second-tier railing was a specific sound, a flat aluminum clang that carried up through the block like a struck bell, and B-Wing had been waiting nine days for a bell.

Officer Delgado was standing at the base of the stairs with his thumbs hooked in his vest when he heard it. He had time to think *don't* — not to say it, just to think it — before the noise came.

Not shouting. Not yet. First a rolling percussion of hands and boots on steel, three hundred men drumming the tiers, a pressure that got into the sinuses. Then the lights on the control booth strobed as somebody in the kitchen crew pulled the main breaker on the wing, and the fluorescent white dropped out to the sick orange of the emergency floods, and *then* the shouting, all of it at once, a solid wall of sound with no words in it.

The gate to the dayroom should have sealed. It didn't. Someone had jammed the track with a wedge of laminate pried off a table three hours earlier — patient work, a shim the width of a thumbnail — and the door shuddered against it, hydraulics whining, half-open. Men poured through the gap sideways, one shoulder first, like water finding a crack in a hull.

Delgado got his radio up. "B-Wing, B-Wing, we are — " and a body hit him at the hip and the words went out of him.

---

It stopped being a place and became weather.

Smoke first, thin and chemical, from the mattress they'd shoved off the third tier and lit; it slid along the ceiling and made the floods into brown smears. Sprinklers popped somewhere in the far corner and rained down on two hundred square feet of a building that was on fire in a different corner entirely, so the concrete went slick and then the slickness spread, and after that everyone who fell had trouble getting up.

Officer Kelsey Ryan, twenty-six, eleven months on the job, was on the second tier when the stairs filled. She had been walking a man named Obadiah Pryce back to his cell for shouting at nobody, and Pryce — sixty-one years old, four teeth, in for something he'd done before Ryan was born — took her elbow and pulled her backward into the empty cell and stood in the doorway with his arms out.

"Not this one," he said to the men coming up. He said it four times. He was not a large man and he had no standing whatsoever, and it should not have worked, and for six or seven crucial seconds it did.

Then it didn't, and someone took Pryce by the shirt and folded him over the railing, and Ryan came out of the cell with her baton in a two-hand grip and no plan at all.

---

Down in the pit it was worse, because down in the pit there were sides.

The response team came in through the north sally port in a wedge, twelve men in black, shields overlapped, and for a moment they were the only orderly thing in the wing — a single dark arrowhead pushing into froth. They advanced by count. They shouted a warning nobody could hear and then they stopped shouting.

The wedge met the crowd and the crowd did not part.

What followed had no shape to it. Batons came down and up and down, and shields rang, and the noise of a polycarbonate shield taking a full-weight blow from a mop handle is like a gunshot in a stairwell. Men in orange went under the wedge and did not come out from under it. A shield-bearer went down when someone got a wrist through the gap and pulled, and the line closed over the space where he'd been with a discipline that was almost tender, and three of them dragged him back through the ranks by his ankles while the rest held.

Gas came next, two canisters skittering across the floor trailing white, and the white filled the wing in under a minute, and the fighting continued inside it — worse inside it, because now nobody could tell who anyone was. Men fought whoever was nearest. Two inmates hauled a third out of the crush by his belt because they knew him, and a guard let them, and thirty seconds later that same guard was on his knees with his helmet gone.

At 4:31 a fire door at the south end blew open from the inside and forty men ran out into the yard and stood there in the rain, blinking, coughing, holding each other up, with absolutely nowhere left to go.

Behind them the wing burned very quietly under the sprinklers, and the sound coming out of it had gone from a roar down to something lower and more ragged — hundreds of men breathing.

Delgado was found at 4:40 under the stairs with a broken orbital bone and a mattress pulled over him.

Nobody ever found out who put it there.

results.model_response:
**THE PALM COURT INN — ROOM 214**

The air conditioner had two settings: off, and a sound like a man being dragged across gravel. Deborah had chosen gravel. Marisol had complained for eleven minutes and then stopped, which was how most of their arguments ended.

They'd laid a bath towel over the desk, then a second one, because the first had been thin as a communion wafer. Deborah worked with her reading glasses pushed up on her forehead, which meant she wasn't reading anything, which meant she was thinking.

"You've got a favorite," she said.

"Everybody's got a favorite."

"You've never said."

Marisol ran a patch through a barrel and held it up to the lamp. Outside, a truck downshifted on the interstate and the window made a small sympathetic sound. "Stairs," she said.

Deborah lowered her glasses. "Stairs."

"Stairs are honest. Stairs happen to people. You wake up in the morning, you don't think, *today I will be killed*—but everybody's thought, at least once, halfway down, *oh, I could go right here.*" She set the barrel down and picked up the next piece. "It's already in them. You're just agreeing with it."

"Huh."

"Also there's no cleanup. There's a phone call and a casserole and a nephew who inherits a boat."

"You're a romantic."

"I'm efficient."

Deborah snorted. She had a brush the size of a toothbrush and a way of holding it, delicately, three fingers, like she was addressing a wound. "Mine's the parking garage."

"That's not a method. That's a *location*."

"It's the whole architecture of it, Mari. Concrete, low ceiling, that light that makes everybody look like they've already been dead a week. People go quiet in a parking garage. They hear their own shoes and they get shy about it." She turned the brush. "By the time I get where I'm going, half of them are practically holding the door."

"That's grim."

"You just told me you push people down stairs."

"I don't *push*." Marisol pointed the barrel at her, then remembered herself and set it down. "Christ. I've never pushed anybody in my life. I *arrange*. There's a difference."

"There's a rug involved."

"Sometimes there's a rug."

The TV was on with the sound off—local news, a woman in a coral blazer standing in front of a corn field, gesturing at it as though it had done something. Deborah watched her for a while.

"You know what I don't like?" she said.

"The car."

"The car." Deborah shook her head. "Everybody loves the car. The kids love the car. It's showy. It's a magic trick and everybody in the room knows there's a trick. You want it to look like *God changed His mind*, and instead it looks like a man was killed by a professional in a car."

"Nikos does the car."

"Nikos does the car because he can't be in a room with a person for more than four minutes." Deborah set the brush down. "That's a diagnosis, by the way. That's not a style."

Marisol laughed, once, through her nose. She got up, cracked the ice bucket, poured two fingers of gas station bourbon into a plastic cup wrapped in plastic, and unwrapped a second cup and did it again. She handed one to Deborah, who took it without looking, the way you take something from someone you've stood next to in eleven countries.

"Water," Marisol said, and got her the tap water too.

They drank. The air conditioner went off on its own and the room got so quiet they could hear the vending machine down the hall, humming to nobody.

"I lied," Marisol said.

"About the stairs?"

"The stairs are true. They're just not my favorite." She turned the cup on the towel, leaving a wet ring, then wiped it away with her thumb. "My favorite is when it doesn't happen."

Deborah didn't say anything.

"When you get there and it's off. Somebody upstairs changes their mind, or the money doesn't clear, or the man's already got something growing in him and God's calling dibs. And you fold the whole thing up and put it back in the bag." She was looking at the window, at the reflection of the room in the window, at the two of them sitting in it. "I've had that four times in nineteen years. That's the good part. That's the part I think about."

The corn field lady was replaced by a weather map with a blue front sliding over Indiana.

"Five," Deborah said.

"What?"

"You've had it five times." She picked up her glasses and folded them and set them in the case, click. "Kraków wasn't off. Kraków was *me*."

Marisol turned her head slowly, like the room might tip.

"You were sick," Deborah said, "and you were going to do it sick, and you'd have been sloppy and you'd have been *caught*, and I said the word and it went away. And then you sat in that hotel with the pink bathroom and you told me it was the best three days of your life and I let you have it."

"You never said."

"I'm saying now. I'm sixty-one and I don't like carrying things upstairs." She finished the bourbon and grimaced at it, honestly, an old woman disliking a drink. "That's my favorite, if we're doing favorites. Not the garage. That."

Marisol looked at her for a long moment. Then she picked up a rag and reached over and, with two fingers, wiped a smudge of oil off the back of Deborah's wrist, where she hadn't noticed it.

"You've got a spot," she said.

"Thank you."

They worked. Piece by piece it all went back together—that satisfying series of small sounds, like a conversation finishing itself. Outside, the interstate kept up its long exhale. Somewhere below them a door opened and a family came clattering out toward the pool, a kid shrieking with joy about the water, and the two women sat listening to it, hands busy, saying nothing at all.

"Six-fifteen," Deborah said finally.

"Six-fifteen."

"Set the alarm on yours. Mine lies."

Marisol set the alarm. Then she got up and turned the air conditioner back on, and it dragged its man across the gravel, and they slept.

They had bound her ankles first, which she thought strange, as though she might run with the rest of her still lashed to the post. The wood was green in places. She noticed this before she understood what it meant.

For a while there was only smoke, and the smoke was almost a mercy. It came up around her in slow grey ropes, and it stank of pitch and wet pine and something sweetish underneath, the straw they'd packed at the base. She held her breath out of instinct, then could not, and the first pull of it into her chest was like swallowing a fistful of nettles. She coughed and could not stop coughing. Tears ran down her face and she was glad of them, glad of anything cool.

Below her the crowd had gone quiet. Two hundred people in the market square and she could hear a single dog barking somewhere past the tannery. She looked for her sister's face and could not find it in the smoke, and did not know whether to be sorry or grateful.

The heat came differently than she had imagined. Not a wall. A hand. It reached up under her shift and laid its palm flat against her shins, and it pressed, and it kept pressing, and the pressing became a thing without a name. Her skin drew tight and then tighter, the way a hide draws over a drum, and she understood with a terrible clarity that it was going to split. The rope at her wrists began to smoke before it began to burn. She could smell her own hair.

She had promised herself she would pray. She had rehearsed it in the cell for nine days, the words worn smooth as a river stone: *Into thy hands, into thy hands.* But the heat took the words and simply carried them off, the way a flood takes a fence, and what came out of her instead was her mother's name. She had not spoken it in eleven years.

Then the smoke thickened and the world narrowed. This was the part the executioner had known would come — he had built the fire for it, had banked the wet wood deliberately at the front, and no one in the crowd would ever know it for the small brutal kindness it was. The blackness came in from the edges. Her chest heaved and got nothing. Her tongue felt enormous.

She screamed then. Not words. There was nothing in it of witchcraft or confession or forgiveness, nothing the priests could write down and file, nothing the crowd could carry home and make into a story about God. It was the sound a body makes when it is being unmade and does not consent — high and raw and endless, and it went on far longer than anyone in the square had prepared themselves for. Some of them covered their ears. A woman near the front began to shout at the fire, at the guards, at nothing.

The second scream was thinner. The third was hardly a sound at all, more a long tearing exhalation, and after it there was only the fire, which had grown loud, which sounded now like a great sheet of canvas snapping in wind.

Afterward the smoke stood straight up in the windless morning, a grey column visible from the fields two miles out, where men leaned on their hoes and watched it and said nothing to each other. It thinned by noon. By evening the square smelled only of ash and wet stone, and the dog was still barking, and the boys had come to poke through the cinders for the iron of the chain, which was worth something.

Her name was Maren Vosskuhl. She was thirty-four years old. She had once cured a neighbor's child of a fever with willow bark and warm milk, and that was the whole of the evidence against her.

# The Unsewing at Molliger Fen

The pit had been dug in haste eleven years ago, and haste has a smell.

Vaunt Ederick knelt at its lip in three inches of standing water and let the cold climb his shins. Below him the fen had done its slow work: four hundred men of the Ash Company, tipped in with their boots still on, pressed down by their own weight and the weight of the peat until they had become one thing. Not bodies. A stratum. A seam of men.

He could see the topmost of them where the winter rain had scoured the covering soil away. A shoulder, grey-green and swollen tight as a sausage casing. A hand with the skin sloughed loose so that it lay in the mud beside its own bones like a discarded glove, fingernails still attached, still faintly ridged where the man had bitten them. The peat had pickled some of them and let others go soft. Where the two conditions met, along the flank of a man whose face was pressed into another man's ribs, the flesh had gone to grave-wax — that pale, crumbling, candle-coloured substance the body makes of itself when it drowns slowly in its own fat. It looked like cheese. It smelled like a butcher's floor in August, and under that, sweeter, like the black water at the bottom of a flower vase.

Ederick had smelled worse. He had *made* worse. He set down his lamp, and he began.

There is a way the world is stitched. Most people never feel the seams; they walk on the surface of the cloth their whole lives and die on it. Ederick had found the hem when he was nine years old and grieving, and he had been picking at it ever since, and the trouble with picking at a hem is that the thread comes out easier every time.

He spoke the first name. Not a word — names are not words. It came out of him wrong, the way a thing comes out of you when you are sick, and it did not travel outward through the air. It travelled *backward*, into the pit, arriving before he had finished uttering it.

The water in the pit stopped moving.

Not froze — the cold had teeth but no ice in it. The rain kept falling and the surface kept accepting it and each drop made its ring, but the rings did not spread. They stood there, four hundred perfect circles held open like little mouths, waiting.

"Coel Hardwyn," Ederick said, in the other way, "sergeant, forty-one years, dead of a spear through the liver on the ninth of Frost, buried without your rings because someone took them, *come up*."

Something in the seam moved.

The wrongness was worst at the beginning, always, and he had never grown used to it because it was not a thing the body was built to become used to. It was the sensation of a word being spoken in a language your mouth has no shape for, and finding that your mouth is changing. It was the feeling of standing in a room and knowing, with perfect animal certainty, that the room had one more corner than it should. His eyes watered. His lamp guttered, and the flame leaned *toward* the darkness rather than away from it, and the shadow of his own kneeling body fell across the water in the direction of the light.

Coel Hardwyn came up.

He came up wrong-side first, one arm rotating in its socket past where a shoulder ends, the humerus grinding out of the sodden meat with a sound like a boot pulled from clay. His chest broke the surface and the gas came with it — eleven years of it, held under pressure in the cavity, released in one long shuddering belch that fluttered his ribs. The skin of his torso had gone to a dark marbling, green and purple and that particular bronze that means the blood has settled and set like a stain. When he sat up, the loose sheet of his back came away and stayed in the peat, and Ederick could see the ladder of his spine and the peat-black shrivelled knots that had been his kidneys, and the small white cave of him where the rot had eaten out and left a room.

Hardwyn turned his head. The neck did not so much bend as *fold*. And here was the thing that made Ederick's hands shake, though he had done this ninety times: the beetles came out of the man's throat and died. All of them, instantly, a small dry rain of carapaces spilling down his sternum. The maggots in the eye-sockets went still and grey. Every living thing that had made a home in Coel Hardwyn's body could not endure what was now in it.

Even the rot refused. That was the wrongness. Ederick had known scholars who said necromancy was the imitation of life, and they were fools, they were children. Life he could have respected. This was the imitation of *obedience*. He had not given Hardwyn back his warmth or his breath or his name; he had taken the name and sewn it, with his own stolen thread, to the outside of a thing that was no longer a man, the way you tie a label to a crate. And the crate stood up. And it looked at him with the two dry stones in its face, and it *waited*, and there was nothing behind the waiting, and the horror was not that it was empty — the horror was that it was empty *and it remembered*. It lifted the loose glove of its own skin from the mud and began, patiently, methodically, to try to put it back on the wrong hand.

"Stop that," Ederick said, in his own voice, which cracked.

The thing stopped. Somewhere beneath it, the seam shifted, and the whole pit sighed at once — four hundred chests compressing, a great wet exhalation that rolled out across the fen and set the reeds hissing.

He worked until dawn. He worked until his gums bled and his fingernails came away soft and he had lost the feeling in the last two fingers of his left hand, permanently, one more coin paid into the black.

They came up in ones and threes and then in slabs, tearing free of each other, taking each other's flesh with them, standing in the shallow water with their heads canted at angles that had nothing to do with looking. Some had no legs and hauled themselves upright on their fists. Some had been so pressed together that they came up as a single lurching architecture of four men, and Ederick let them; he had not the strength to be delicate, and armies are not made of individuals anyway. The rain resumed its spreading rings. The false cold went out of the air and left only the honest cold of a Molliger morning, and the smell — released, unlidded, four hundredfold — settled over the fen like a weather.

He stood, at last, with his hand pressed to the small of his back like an old man, and he counted them, because a man should always count what he owes.

He counted four hundred and one.

He counted again.

Out at the pit's far edge, past the last of the Ash Company, something small was standing very straight in the water with its arms at its sides, and it had not been called, and it was looking at him with an attention that none of the others had, and Vaunt Ederick understood, with the calm of a man watching his own house burn, that the hem he had been picking at for thirty-one years had finally begun to unravel from the other side.
