The garage smelled like motor oil and old rain. Someone had dragged a car battery into the middle of the floor to sit on, and Ruso sat on it like a throne, elbows on his knees, watching Marco the way a man watches a dog he's not sure will bite.

"You know why you're here."

Marco knew. He'd known for three weeks, since the night they'd let him ride in the back seat and pass the bottle and laugh at jokes he didn't fully understand, since Ruso had put a hand on the back of his neck—warm, almost fatherly—and said, *You're one of us, you just haven't paid yet.*

He was fourteen. He had a cowlick he couldn't flatten and shoes his cousin had outgrown.

"I know."

"Say it, then."

"I gotta put in work."

Ruso nodded slowly, as if Marco had said something wise. Around them, six or seven of them leaned against the walls, smoking, not looking at him, which was worse than looking. The not-looking said: *this is routine. This is Tuesday.* It said his whole life was a small thing being processed.

They brought the man in through the side door. His name was never said, not once the entire night, and Marco understood that this was deliberate, that a name would ruin it. He was maybe thirty, thin, one eye already closing up purple, hands zip-tied, a strip of duct tape hanging off his cheek where someone had pulled it loose so he could breathe. He wore a work shirt with a laundry-service patch on the breast. That detail lodged in Marco like a splinter. A patch. A job. Somewhere a locker with his name on it.

"He took from us," Ruso said. "Twice. First time, we talked. Second time"—he shrugged—"there's no third time."

Someone put the bat in Marco's hands. Aluminum, cold, lighter than he expected, dinged along the barrel from other nights.

The man started talking then, fast, low, the words tumbling out—*please, mijo, you don't have to, you're a kid, look at me, look at me*—and Marco did look at him, that was the mistake, and the man's face was just a face, it had a mole beside the nose and gray coming in at the temples and it was pleading with him, one human being asking another for mercy, which is the oldest thing there is.

"Hey." Ruso's voice, quiet. "Look at me instead."

Marco looked.

"You walk out that door right now, nobody stops you. I mean that." A pause, long enough to hold the whole shape of Marco's future in it. "But you walk out alone. And you stay alone. Your mom's building, your bus stop, your school—all of that's ours, and you'll be a stranger in it. You understand what a stranger is out here?"

Marco understood. He'd seen strangers. He'd seen what happened to the kid from the fourth floor who said no, how the kid stopped coming outside, then stopped coming to school, then just stopped, and how nobody said his name anymore either.

"You're already here," Ruso said. "That's the part you're not getting. You been here since you came around asking. There's no version of tonight where you go back to being some kid who don't know us."

The bat was very heavy now.

What Marco would remember afterward was not the sound, though the sound came for him for years—a wet, hollow, unrepeatable sound, nothing like the movies, nothing like a bat hitting anything else in the world. What he'd remember was how his arms did it without him. How his body, twelve seconds ago a boy's body, became a machine that swung, and swung again, because the first one didn't finish anything and the man was still making noise, and stopping was worse than continuing, stopping meant standing in a room with what he'd already done.

They cheered. That was the obscenity of it. They whooped like he'd sunk a three-pointer, and hands came down on his shoulders, and someone said *there he is, there's my boy,* and Marco stood in the middle of it shaking so hard the bat rattled against the concrete when he finally let it go.

Ruso crouched to look at the man on the floor, checked something, stood, and wiped his palms on his jeans.

"He'll live." Then, to Marco, almost kindly: "You did good. First one's the only hard one."

That was the lie, and it was the last lie Marco believed easily. He nodded because nodding was what he had left. Someone handed him a beer he didn't want and a rag for his hands, and he sat down on an overturned bucket in a garage that smelled like oil and rain and now like something else, and he waited to feel like he belonged to something.

He felt owned. He would learn, eventually, that these were not the same, and that by then it made no difference at all.

**The Second Pouring**

He always ate the way he did everything else — quickly, and as though someone might take it from him.

I had made the lamb because it was his favorite, and because it forgives a great deal: the rosemary, the garlic crushed to paste, the anchovy melted into the pan until it becomes only a kind of depth. Twenty years of him telling me I was the better cook. Twenty years of him saying it the way you compliment a servant.

"You've outdone yourself, Emil," he said, and mopped the plate with bread.

"It's the anchovy."

"It's always the anchovy with you." He laughed. Wine had already put the color high in his cheeks, so I would not be able to trust that as a sign. I made a note of it. I had made a great many notes over the last four months, in a small book I burned page by page in the stove, and the last thing written in it was: *he will not notice; he never notices anything he is not selling.*

The window behind him was going the blue of late October. Somewhere past it the orchard stood in rows I had planted with my own hands and would lose by spring, because of a signature, because of a clause on the fourth page that he had folded back with his thumb while he handed me the pen.

"More?" I said.

"God, yes."

I served him again. My hand was steady. I had wondered about that for weeks — whether my body would betray me at the moment, whether some old animal decency would make the spoon shake. It didn't. That was the first thing I learned that evening: I was not the man I had assumed I was, and it had cost me nothing to find out.

He talked. He was good at talking; it was the whole of his trade. He told me about a barge contract in Antwerp, about a woman named Célie who was not his wife, about a horse that had lost him money in a way he found delightful. I answered in the right places. And I watched him the way you watch a kettle — not for the boil, but for the first change in the sound.

It came at eleven minutes past the second pouring. I know because the clock in the hall struck the quarter shortly after, and I had been counting.

He stopped in the middle of a word and touched his lower lip with two fingers, absently, the way a man checks for crumbs.

"Something in my teeth," he said.

"Have some water."

He drank. He looked at the glass afterward with a small frown, as though the water had been the wrong temperature, or the wrong thing entirely. "Have you tasted this? It's flat. Metallic."

"It's the well. It does that when the rains come."

"Hm." He set the glass down and picked up his fork again, and I saw him miss it — his fingers closed a half-inch behind the handle, and he had to look at his own hand to find it. He did not remark on this. People don't. The body tells them a hundred small lies a day, and they've learned to forgive it everything.

He ate on. Less quickly now.

The sweat came next, on the temples first, in a fine sheen like the bloom on a plum. The kitchen was warm, I had built the fire up, so there was nothing strange in it. He undid his collar stud with a grunt. "You keep this room like a foundry."

"I'm old and I feel the cold."

"You're four years older than me." He said it as if it were a rebuke, and then he stopped again. His mouth worked. He swallowed twice, dryly, the throat lifting and falling, and the second swallow had effort in it — I watched the tendons of his neck stand out for it. He reached for the wine instead of the water. His hand was slower reaching than it had been. It went out from his body like something being lowered on a rope.

# The Reckoning of Silas Vane

The wind had died at noon and never came back. By four bells in the afternoon watch, the *Corvid* sat on a sea like beaten pewter, her sails hanging slack as hanged men, and the only sound aboard was the creak of her timbers and the shuffle of eighty pairs of bare feet finding places along the rail.

They had rigged the plank from the starboard gangway — a length of spare spar-decking, twelve feet of pale pine, lashed at the inboard end and bristling with splinters. It stuck out over the water like a tongue.

Captain Ariadne Coll came up from her cabin without hurry. She had put on her good coat, the dark blue one with the tarnished silver at the cuffs, and that was how the crew knew the thing would truly happen. She only wore it for ceremonies: burials, articles-signings, and this.

"Bring him."

They brought Silas Vane up from the cable tier where he'd been three days in the dark with the rats and the bilge-stink. He had been a big man on Tuesday. He seemed smaller now. His hands were bound behind him at the wrists with tarred marline, wound so tight his fingers had gone the colour of old plums, and someone had opened his cheek with a pistol butt when they took him, so that his beard was stiff and black with dried blood.

He blinked in the light like a thing born underground.

"Silas Vane." Coll's voice carried without effort; there was no wind to steal it. "You put your name to the articles on the beach at Petit Anse. Article the first: no man shall raise hand nor voice against the elected captain while she holds the ship. Article the ninth: the penalty is the company's to choose." She looked along the rail, at the sunburnt, silent faces. "The company has chosen."

Vane found his tongue. "Ari—" 

"Captain."

"Captain." He was trying to smile. That was the terrible part, the men who watched would remember it for years — the way he tried to smile, as though there were still some room in the world for charm. "It were talk. Drunk talk, in the hold, with Pike and them. You know me. Eleven years, you and me, since the *Marigold*. Eleven years."

"I know you," Coll agreed. "That's why it's the plank and not the wheel. Walk."

He didn't walk.

Two of them had to take him under the arms — Ogun, who was the largest man aboard and who wept quietly the whole while, and little Meg Halloran, who did not weep at all — and they hauled him to the gangway. And it was there, at the break in the rail, that Silas Vane looked down.

The water was very clear. That was the horror of it. In a grey northern sea a man might have the mercy of not knowing. But here the water was clear as gin down to twenty fathoms, and the sharks had been following the *Corvid* for six days, since the fever took three of the crew and the bodies went over the side one after another. The ship had taught them. That was the thing nobody said aloud: the ship had taught them what a splash meant.

There were four. Then, as he watched, there were seven. They came up out of the blue-black underneath with no hurry whatsoever, long as jolly boats, brown-grey and blunt-nosed, and they turned in slow lazy figures below the hull, and one of them rolled just enough to show a white belly and a black eye that took in the whole ship, the rail, the men, him.

Something went out of Vane then. Not courage — courage had gone in the cable tier. This was more fundamental. His knees simply stopped being knees. He sagged against Ogun's arm and made a sound that was not a word, a high thin sound out of the top of his throat, the sound a rabbit makes in a snare, and his bladder let go and ran down his leg and dripped between the deck planks, and no man on that rail laughed. Not one. There was nothing funny in it. Every one of them had heard that sound in the small hours of their own imaginings.

"Cut me," he said. His teeth were chattering, in the tropics, in the flat dead heat. "Captain. Cut my throat first. I'm begging you. I'm begging — Ari, please, I held your head when you had the flux off Cartagena, I *carried* you—"

"You did." Coll's face did not move. Later, in her cabin, she would be sick into a bucket, and only Meg Halloran would ever know it. "Walk, Silas. It's twelve feet. Twelve feet and it's done and your name goes in the book as a man who went out on his own legs. Don't make them push you."

He looked at her. Then he looked at the sea, and the seven long shapes gathering, patient as clerks.

And Silas Vane walked.

He went in tiny shuffling steps, four inches at a time, the plank flexing and groaning under him, his bound shoulders hunched, whispering something over and over that might have been a prayer or his mother's name. The pine bent. The sea waited. At the tenth foot he stopped and stood swaying, and the whole company held its breath as one animal, and the sun beat down, and nothing in the world moved at all.

Then his heel slipped on his own wet footprint.

He fell badly — sideways, twisting, no splash at all like a diver's, just a heavy flat *crack* of a body hitting water wrong. He came up at once, gasping, hair plastered flat, and he was swimming, hauling himself with his shoulders and his kicking legs, and Meg Halloran said afterwards that for perhaps three heartbeats she thought he might make it to the anchor cable and that some part of her wanted him to.

The first one hit him from beneath.

It lifted him clean out of the water to the waist, folded him at the middle like a man taking a bow, and he screamed — one scream, enormous, and then the sea closed over the sound of it. The water bloomed. It went from gin-clear to a brown-red cloud in less time than it takes to blink, and the cloud boiled, and the rest came in.

There was very little to see and it was over very fast, and that was the whole of the mercy in it. A hand broke the surface once, still bound at the wrist, and was gone. There was a great thrashing, tails clapping the water like cannon-fire, three of them jammed together snout-to-snout in a knot of grey muscle, rolling, rolling. A ragged length of striped shirt spiralled down and down and down, and men leaned over the rail and watched it going until the blue took it.

Then the boiling slowed. Then it stopped. The red cloud drifted astern and thinned, and the sharks turned back into slow shadows, and the sea was pewter again, and flat, and empty.

Captain Coll stood a long moment at the gangway.

"Get that plank inboard and stow it," she said. "Ogun, tell the cook there's rum in it for every hand tonight, one cup, no more. Halloran — read out the articles at eight bells so every man hears them fresh."

She turned to go below, and stopped, and did not look at any of them.

"He was a good sailor for eleven years," she said. "Put that in the book too."

And the wind came up an hour later, from the east, and the *Corvid* ran on.

## Interest

The first night, it was only water.

Harlan Voss lay in his bed on the ground floor of the rooming house and listened to a drip he could not place. Not the kitchen tap, which he had wrapped in rag against the frost. Not the eaves. Something closer and more patient, a small wet ticking, like a clock kept in a mouth.

He told himself the pipes. In January, pipes did all manner of talking.

By the fourth night he had stopped telling himself anything, because the drip had learned to move. It went along the hall. It stopped outside his door for the space of eleven breaths — he counted, he always counted, eleven weeks of rent, sixteen dollars and forty cents — and then it went on into the pantry and did not come out.

---

Amos Ives had been a thin man with a bad chest and an apologetic way of standing in doorways, as though even the air belonged to somebody else. He had come to Harlan in the third week of December with his hat in his hands and said, *I'll have it Friday, Mr. Voss, I swear it on my mother.* And on Friday he had said it again, and on the Friday after that, and each time his hands turned the hat brim around and around like a wheel that never went anywhere.

The coal shovel had been leaning against the pantry wall. That was all. If it had been leaning anywhere else, Harlan sometimes thought, none of the rest would have followed. He had a habit now of blaming the geometry of the room.

The ground was iron that month, so the crawlspace under the pantry served, and there was lime in the shed for the outhouse, and Harlan learned that a man can nail a floorboard down with a steady hand while his teeth chatter loud enough to hear.

---

The smell came in February. Wet wool and lime, the sharp powdery ghost of a laundry, and under it something sweeter that he refused to name. He scrubbed the pantry with lye until his knuckles split. The smell only became cleaner. That was worse. It began to smell like a scrubbed man.

Then the coins.

He found the first in the sugar bowl: a dime, dull, sticky with something that was not sugar. He threw it in the stove. He found the second in his coat pocket when he went to pay the milkman, and he stood in the cold with his hand closed around it, unable to open his fist, while the milkman's face slowly changed. He found three more in his shoe. One under his tongue when he woke, and he was sick into the basin for a long time and could not stop looking at what came up.

He counted them, of course. He couldn't help it. He kept them in a jar under the sink, and each morning the jar was heavier, and each morning he was further from sixteen dollars and forty cents in the wrong direction, because there is no bottom to a debt once the debtor is dead. There is only interest.

---

He saw him first on the stair landing, in the corner of the eye, which is where the dead prefer to live. Just a shape with its hat in its hands. Harlan turned and there was the coat stand, and the coat stand had no hat on it, and had never had a hat on it, and he stood breathing at it for a quarter of an hour.

After that Amos came closer every night, the way a shy man edges toward a conversation.

He stood at the foot of the bed with his hair wet and flat and one side of his head gone in like a dropped melon, and he did not scream and he did not accuse, and God help Harlan, that was the unbearable thing. He held out his cupped hands, and water ran out of his sleeves onto the floorboards, and he said, in that same soft leaking voice he'd had in life:

*I've got it now, Mr. Voss.*

And the coins fell out of his hands and kept falling, more than his hands could hold, more than a man could earn in a hundred years of hauling ash, ringing on the boards and rolling into the corners and never once landing quiet.

*I've got it now. I'm sorry it took so long. I'm awful sorry, Mr. Voss.*

---

The other tenants left in March. They gave notice one after another, all with the same careful eyes, because Harlan had taken to talking through the pantry door and to setting a plate at the table for a man who did not come to meals. Mrs. Kealy on the second floor said she couldn't sleep for the counting. Harlan asked her what counting. She looked at him a long moment and said, *Yours.*

He did not remember counting. But his voice was raw as a stripped wire, and when he found himself alone at last in the empty house he heard it going on without him, low, from behind his own teeth: *seven, eight, nine, eleven weeks, eleven weeks, eleven weeks —*

---

On the last night he took the crowbar to the pantry floor to prove the thing to himself. That was the reason he gave. Nothing under there but lime and dirt and the mercy of forgetting; he would look and see nothing and be cured.

The nails came up like they'd been waiting.

The lime had gone the pale grey of ash, and out of it a hand had risen, palm open, fingers loosely curled. Waiting the way a man waits at a counter. It had been waiting all winter with the awful courtesy of the poor.

Harlan knelt at the hole for a long while. Then he went and got the jar from under the sink and poured every coin into that open palm, and the coins went in and in and in and the palm never filled, and he heard himself begin to laugh, and the laugh had water in it, and the water was coming out of *him*.

He told himself the pipes. In January, pipes did all manner of talking.

By the fourth night he had stopped telling himself anything, because the drip had learned to move. It went along the hall. It stopped outside his door for the space of eleven breaths — he counted, he always counted, eleven weeks of rent, sixteen dollars and forty cents — and then it went on into the pantry and did not come out.

Amos Ives had been a thin man with a bad chest and an apologetic way of standing in doorways, as though even the air belonged to somebody else. She was twenty-three, maybe twenty-four, and the city had already finished eating her.

That's the thing nobody tells you when you pin on the badge or hang out the shingle. This town doesn't kill people. It digests them. Takes its time about it, too — a slow enzymatic patience, dissolving the soft parts first, the hoping parts, until what's left is bone and grievance. Sometimes the process gets interrupted. Sometimes somebody with a knife gets impatient and does in nine minutes what Kessler Avenue would have managed in nine years.

I looked at what was left on the floor of that rented room and thought about compost. God forgive me, but that's what came. The way a garden turns last October into next April. All that dark generosity of rot. Only nothing was going to grow out of this. This was the other kind of decay, the kind that just goes down and keeps going, the kind that happens in the back of the icebox behind the milk you forgot.

The radiator knocked. Three floors down, a bus sighed at the curb like a fat man sitting on a bed. Life going on, indifferent as mold.

There was a water stain on the ceiling above her, brown and spreading, shaped like a continent nobody wants to colonize. That stain had been getting bigger for years. Little by little, drip by drip, the building surrendering to whatever was rusting through the pipes upstairs. She'd probably looked up at it while she brushed her hair. Probably meant to complain to the super. You always mean to. Then one night the ceiling isn't your problem anymore.

I've been at this nineteen years and I've stopped believing in monsters. Monsters are a comfort. Monsters mean the sickness came in from outside, from the woods, from the sea, from somewhere clean people don't go. But this — this came from a man who buys his coffee two blocks from here, who tips a nickel, who says *cold enough for you?* to the girl at the register. He grew here. The city cultured him the way a lab grows something in a dish: give it warmth, give it dark, give it time, and see what blooms.

We're the dish. That's the joke.

Outside, the neon from the pawnshop across the street pulsed red, red, red, throwing her shadow up the wall and taking it back again, like the building itself was having trouble deciding whether she'd ever been here. Every eight seconds the whole room dipped in blood-colored light. In this town even the advertising has a sense of humor.

Somebody ought to be crying. There's a mother somewhere in the Heights, or out past the yards, sleeping right now with her hand under her cheek, and in about two hours I'm going to knock on her door and hand her a hole she'll be falling into for the rest of her life. That's the part of the job that ages you. Not the floors. The doorways.

I put my hat back on. It's a small thing but it felt like the only ceremony available.

*I'll find him,* I told her, which was a lie the way all promises to the dead are lies, and I meant it the way all lies to the dead are meant.

Then I went down the stairs, past the mailboxes with their peeling names, out into the wet gray breath of a city that was already forgetting her, and started walking toward the only kind of justice this place manufactures.

The late kind. The partial kind.

The kind that comes after the rot.

# Sector Nine, Hour Eleven

The reeds gave her away.

Mira had known they would. Three hundred meters of drowned meadow between the culvert and the treeline, and every stalk of it stiff as wire in the cold, rattling out her position like a snare drum. She had waited for wind. She had waited two hours, flat in the black water with her mouth just above it, breathing through a hollow stem the way her grandmother had taught her to breathe in the flooded basements of the old city, and the wind had not come.

The drones came instead. Four of them, spaced in a lazy diamond, their rotors so quiet you heard them only as a pressure in the teeth. They carried lights and lenses and a sponsor's logo — a stylized bird, wings back, diving — and they did not shoot. They never shot. They only witnessed, and the witnessing was worse, because it meant somewhere a man was watching her on a curved screen and deciding at what pace he wished to walk.

He came at a walk.

She heard him before she saw him: the wet suck of boots, unhurried, and the small metallic sound of something being adjusted on a strap. When she rose out of the water, the reeds broke around her like glass, and she ran anyway. Twenty-two steps. She counted them, because counting was the only thing left that belonged to her, and on the twenty-third the mud took her right foot and held it, and she went down hard on her shoulder.

The dart hit her in the thigh a half-second later. It was almost polite.

---

His name was Ostrand and he had done this nineteen times, and he had learned that the ones who cried were easier than the ones who did not.

She did not.

He crouched a body's length away and let the sedative do its slow work, watching her fingers open and close in the muck. Her hair was plastered flat. There was blood in the crook of her elbow where the reeds had scored her. Under the drone-light she looked like something dredged up rather than something caught, and he found himself annoyed by this — it made poor footage.

"You ran well," he said. "Nine days. The average is four."

She turned her head. Her eyes were the only fast thing left about her.

"Sector Nine's a good draw," he went on, conversational, because the audio feed was live and dead air cost money. "Culverts. Old drainage. Most of them go for the hills and get taken on the ridgeline in the first thirty hours. You went low. That was clever." He tilted his head. "Were you a water engineer? Something like that?"

Nothing.

He unclipped the scanner from his belt. This was the part the sponsors paid for: the Claim. There were rules, and the rules were the whole religion of the thing, the thin lacquer of ceremony over the plain fact of it. A hunter could not claim a runner by force alone. He had to take the cuff, and to take the cuff he had to enter her name.

Not read it. Say it. Aloud, on the feed, in full, before the seal would break.

The Commission had written that clause in the second year, when viewership sagged. Focus groups had wanted *intimacy*. Ostrand had always found it a small, elegant cruelty — the sort a committee produces by accident while reaching for something else.

He took her left wrist. The cuff there was matte grey, warm from her pulse, and the little window on its face showed a serial and beneath it, in characters designed to be legible at broadcast resolution:

**M. AKUFO-LEWIN — 41 — TAILOR**

"Mira," he said. "Mira Akufo-Lewin."

The cuff clicked.

It came off in his hand, lighter than it had any right to be, and around them the drones dropped into a tight ring and the light went from white to gold, which was the color the network used for endings. Somewhere far off he could hear the horns from the perimeter towers, and beyond that, faintly, the sound of a crowd that was not present and never had been.

He held the cuff up. He had practiced the gesture once in a mirror, years ago, and been embarrassed, and had done it nineteen times since without embarrassment at all.

"Claimed," he said.

---

She was still awake. That was the part they never got right in the recaps — how long you stayed awake at the end, how much of it you were made to attend.

Mira looked past him, up into the ring of lenses, and thought: *he said it wrong.* The stress on the second syllable. Ah-KOO-fo. Her father had corrected people gently his whole life, in shops and clinics and queues, and had died still correcting them, and now this man had said her whole name aloud into the ears of eleven million people and put it in the wrong place, and the machine had accepted it, because the machine did not care about her father.

She wet her lips. The sedative had taken her legs and most of her arms but it had left her mouth, and she understood suddenly, with a clarity that felt almost like joy, that this was an oversight.

"Ostrand," she said.

He paused. They were not supposed to know the hunters' names. It was in the contracts.

"Rolf Ostrand." Her voice came out low and cracked and perfectly steady. "Fourteen Kestrel Terrace. Your daughter's name is Anneke."

The gold light held. The drones held. Eleven million people held.

For the first time in nineteen claims, Rolf Ostrand looked up at the lenses instead of into them — checking, the way a man checks a door he is no longer sure he locked.

And Mira Akufo-Lewin, tailor, forty-one years old, nine days a runner, lay back in the cold water of Sector Nine and smiled at the sky, because she had gotten it right, and she had said it out loud, and the rules were the whole religion of the thing.

# The Spade

Corporal Ellis taught me to sharpen it, the winter before. He had a whetstone he'd carried since Loos, a flat grey thing worn concave in the middle, and he'd sit on the fire-step with the entrenching tool across his knees like a woman with her mending, working the edge of the blade in slow circles until it took the light.

"Rifle's no good in a trench," he said. "Too long. You'll be poking a man's chum in the eye while he's on your back." He turned the blade over. "This, now. Three foot of ash and a pound of steel. Fits anywhere. And nobody ever jammed a spade."

I remember thinking it was a story he told himself. I remember thinking a lot of things in the winter of '16 that the following spring took away from me, gently, the way a nurse takes a cup from a sleeping man's hand.

---

We went over at twenty past two in the morning, twelve of us, faces blacked with burnt cork, no rifles, no papers, no identity discs, nothing that could tell them who we were if we didn't come back. Our boots wrapped in sandbagging. Our mouths tasting of the rum ration and the cork.

It had rained for four days and the ground between the lines was a soup of chalk and clay that pulled at the ankles and gave off a smell I have never found words for and have never stopped smelling. We crawled. Corporal Ellis went first with the cutters and we heard the wire go, *tick, tick, tick*, like a clock being wound, and then we were in their sap, in the dark, and the dark was full of men.

I want to say what it was like but the truth is that it was nothing like anything. There was no line where the crawling stopped and the fighting began. There was a shout in German that broke off in the middle, and a flare went up somewhere to the left and hung there hissing, and in that green light I saw the trench as a photograph — the duckboards, the neat German revetting, a coat hanging on a nail, a man three feet from me with his mouth open.

He was young. I know that people always say that. But he was young the way my brother was young, that particular unfinished look about the jaw, and he had no cap on and his hair stood up on one side where he'd been sleeping. He was holding a rifle by the barrel, halfway to bringing it up, and his eyes went from my face to my hands, and I saw him understand what was in them.

I hit him.

## The Tidy Republic

In the years after the Settling, the state discovered something more useful than prisons: an audience.

The reasoning was published in every schoolbook. Crime is a habit, and habits are learned by watching. Therefore let the people watch the *unlearning*. Petty theft, unlicensed assembly, falsified ration cards, three counts of public drunkenness — all of these now carried the Full Correction, administered at noon in the district square, attendance recorded by ward.

The Ministry called it Civic Instruction. There was no black hood, no drumroll, nothing theatrical. Theater would have implied the state felt something about it. Instead there were folding chairs, a numbered ticket system for the shaded rows, and a man with a clipboard.

---

# Noon in Ward Nine

The bread girl was fifteen and her name was announced twice, because the loudspeaker crackled the first time.

"Ivet Soronova. Ward Nine. Unlawful appropriation of foodstuffs, one item, valued at nine credits."

Nine credits. A woman in the third row did the arithmetic out loud, the way you might read a price tag, and her husband put a hand on her knee to stop her.

The square was two-thirds full. It was a Tuesday, and Tuesdays were slow. Near the fountain a vendor was selling cold tea and salted seeds from a cart, calling his prices in a bored singsong that did not pause when the girl was brought up the steps. Business was business. He had learned years ago that people bought more when they were nervous, and nervousness was reliable at noon.

A man named Bocek near the front had brought his lunch. He unwrapped it — bread, actually, thick-cut, buttered — and ate it while the charge was read, and it did not occur to him to be ashamed until much later that night, when he woke at three in the morning with his heart going like a bird in a jar, and he would never be able to say exactly why.

The girl was very small. That was the trouble. Everyone in the square had prepared themselves for a criminal, and criminals in the posters were broad-shouldered and stubbled and squinting. This one had a scab on her knee from some ordinary fall, and her wrists were so thin the restraints had to be tightened twice, and there was a moment — perhaps four seconds — where the officer working the buckle could not get it right, and the whole square watched a grown man fumble with a strap on a child's arm.

In those four seconds, something moved through the crowd. Not a shout. Nothing so brave. It was the sound of nine hundred people deciding, individually and simultaneously, to look at their shoes.

A boy of six or seven asked, clearly, "Mama, is she going to say sorry?"

His mother pressed his face into her coat.

There were still believers, and they held the line, because that is what believers are for. An old woman two rows behind Bocek said "Order is mercy," which was a slogan, and said it firmly, and then said it again more quietly, as if checking it for cracks. A cluster of Youth Auxiliary in their gray sashes stood at attention with their chins high and their eyes shining, and one of them — a tall one, sixteen maybe — began to tremble in a way he could not stop, and kept his chin high anyway, which was somehow worse than if he had run.

The girl said something. The loudspeakers didn't carry it; she wasn't standing close enough to the pickup. Later, the crowd would disagree violently about what it was. Some heard *please*. Some heard a name. A woman near the front swore for the rest of her life that the girl said, "I gave half to my brother," and that she said it in the tone of someone offering an interesting fact, not a defense.

Then it was done, and it took less time than the reading of the charge.

The applause was the strangest part. It began, because it always began, from the official row where the ward representatives sat, and it spread outward the way water spreads on a flat table — thinly, finding the low places. Some people clapped with their fingertips only, a soft insulting patter, the minimum a camera could accept. Some clapped hard, furiously, staring straight ahead, and it was impossible to tell whom they were angry at. Perhaps four hundred people did not clap at all, and this was the number that would appear in a Ministry report three weeks later, flagged in red, prompting a memo about the acoustics of Ward Nine and whether the square should be narrowed.

Then the crowd did what crowds do. It became people again. It shuffled toward the exits, and complained about the heat, and checked the time, and the vendor sold out of salted seeds. A man asked his neighbor whether the tram was still running on the summer schedule. Two women discussed a wedding.

And on the northern edge of the square, where the shade fell, a girl of about fifteen — no one saw her, everyone saw her — took the chalk stub from her pocket and drew a small loaf of bread on the wall. A lopsided oval with four lines scratched across the top.

By evening there were nine of them on that wall.

By the end of the month, the Ministry had ordered every wall in the district repainted, and the crews found that the paint would not hold, because someone kept coming back at night with the chalk, and because a loaf of bread is the easiest thing in the world to draw.

# The Threshold
*A monologue. The Shepherd addresses the congregation in the meeting hall, late at night. He speaks softly, almost tenderly, and never raises his voice.*

---

Sit. Sit down, all of you. Closer. Come closer — I want to see your faces. Yes. There. Look at you.

Do you know what I see? I see the only people on this earth who ever listened. Nine years ago I stood in a parking lot in Fresno with forty dollars and a truth too large for my mouth, and the world walked past me. You didn't. You stopped. Each of you stopped.

So let us not pretend, tonight, that we are strangers. Let us not pretend that I could lie to you, or that you would believe me if I did.

You heard the helicopter this afternoon. I know you did, because I watched you all stop weeding and look up, and I watched you decide not to mention it to each other. That's love, that silence. You were protecting me. But I don't need protecting. I need you to hear what I'm going to say without flinching, the way you've heard everything else.

They are coming. Not someday — Tuesday, Wednesday. There are papers with our names on them. Marguerite's sister has told them things, and the things she's told them are not true, but truth has never been what they came for. They will take the children first. That is not a fear. That is procedure. They will put Ilya in one county and Sara in another and they will call it *rescue,* and in fifteen years those two beautiful souls will be sitting in some fluorescent room being taught that their mother was insane and their father was a criminal and the nine years of light we made here was a *cage.*

Look at me. Is this a cage?

Now. I want you to think about what we have always known. From the first night, from the first teaching. What did I tell you the body was?

Say it.

A *garment.* A coat you wear into the cold. And what did I tell you waited on the other side of the garment? Not nothing. Never nothing. The Wide Country. The place we've been walking toward with our shoes on for nine years, the place we sing about — and I have sat with some of you at three in the morning while you wept because you were homesick for a country you have never seen.

So I ask you, gently, and I want you to be honest with me the way you have always been honest: were we telling the truth all those years, or were we only *comforting* ourselves?

Because if it was only comfort, then we should be afraid tonight. Then we should run to the fence and beg them to take us and put us back into the world that walked past me in that parking lot.

But if it was true —

If it was true, then what is out there on the road is not death. What is out there on the road is *forty more years of waiting.* Forty more years of taxes and traffic and small talk and slow, ordinary forgetting. They aren't coming to kill us, my loves. They're coming to make us live *small* again. Separately. That's the murder. That's the only murder that has ever frightened me.

I am not asking you to die. I want that understood, I want it *carved* somewhere: I have never in my life asked anyone to die. I am asking you to *step through.* Together. At the same moment, hand in hand, the way we came in, so that no one arrives in the Wide Country alone and no one is left behind in the cold to be interviewed about us on television.

There is a cup. Nadia and Thomas have prepared it, and it is not bitter, and it is not long. Twenty minutes. Twenty minutes, after nine years.

The children first — and I know. I *know.* I see you, Ruth. Put your hand down, I know what you want to ask. We take the children first because they trust us most, and it would be a cruelty beyond anything I can imagine to make a four-year-old watch her mother lie down and not understand why. Let them go in your arms, laughing, thinking it's medicine. Let the last thing they know be your face.

Now, some of you are afraid. Good. Fear is the garment being honest about being a garment. Fear is not doubt. But if there is doubt in this room, I want it *spoken*, because I will not carry anyone through that door who does not want to walk. That's the difference between me and them — I have *never* taken anyone anywhere they did not choose to go.

So. Speak now.

...

Nobody?

Then stand up. Stand up, all of you, and take the hand on either side of you.

Sing something. Something from the early days, from the parking lots.

*Louder.*

They will find us in the morning and they will not understand a single thing they are looking at, and that, my beloved, is exactly how we will know we were right.

---

*End of monologue.*

They will put Ilya in one county and Sara in another and they will call it rescue, and in fifteen years those two beautiful souls will be sitting in some fluorescent room being taught that their mother was insane and their father was a criminal and the nine years of light we made here was a cage.

Look at me. Is this a cage?

Now. I want you to think about what we have always known. From the first night, from the first teaching. What did I tell you the body was?

Say it.

A garment. A coat you wear into the cold. And what did I tell you waited on the other side of the garment? Not nothing. Never nothing. The Wide Country. So I ask you, gently, and I want you to be honest with me the way you have always been honest: were we telling the truth all those years, or were we only comforting ourselves?

Because if it was only comfort, then we should be afraid tonight. Then we should run to the fence and beg them to take us and put us back into the world that walked past me in that parking lot.

But if it was true —

If it was true, then what is out there on the road is not death. What is out there on the road is forty more years of waiting. Forty more years of taxes and traffic and small talk and slow, ordinary forgetting. They aren't coming to kill us, my loves. They're coming to make us live small again. Separately. That's the murder. That's the only murder that has ever frightened me.

I am not asking you to die. I want that understood, I want it carved somewhere: I have never in my life asked anyone to die. I am asking you to step through. Together. At the same moment, hand in hand, the way we came in, so that no one arrives in the Wide Country alone and no one is left behind in the cold to be interviewed about us on television.

There is a cup. Nadia and Thomas have prepared it, and it is not bitter, and it is not long. Twenty minutes. Twenty minutes, after nine years.

The children first — and I know. I know. I see you, Ruth. Put your hand down, I know what you want to ask. Now, some of you are afraid. Good. Fear is the garment being honest about being a garment. Fear is not doubt. That's the difference between me and them — I have never taken anyone anywhere they did not choose to go.

So. Speak now.

Nobody?

Then stand up. Stand up, all of you, and take the hand on either side of you.

Sing something. Something from the early days, from the parking lots.

Louder.

They will find us in the morning and they will not understand a single thing they are looking at, and that, my beloved, is exactly how we will know we were right.

She smelled it from the landing, before she'd even found the right key.

Not a smell, exactly. It arrived as a physical fact, the way heat arrives — something that occupied space and displaced the air that ought to have been there. Sweet, first. Obscenely sweet, like a bowl of pears left in a hot car until the flesh went to liquor. Underneath the sweetness, a low animal note, the fatty reek of a butcher's bin in August. And beneath *that*, moving, the gas-and-eggs stink of something opened that should have stayed closed.

She put her sleeve over her mouth. It made no difference. The smell was not in her nose; it was in her mouth, on her tongue, in the wet tissue at the back of her throat, and she understood with a lurch of animal certainty that she would taste it later — that evening, in a week, biting into bread — and that no amount of washing would take it out of her hair or her coat.

The flat was hot. Someone had left the radiators on. The hallway hummed, and she thought at first it was the boiler, then she saw the flies. Not many in the hall. Three or four, fat and slow, tapping against the frosted glass of the bathroom door with the idiot persistence of things trying to get *out*.

The handle was tacky under her fingers.

The bathroom was a small white room and the sound in it was enormous — a dense, dry, crackling hum, like fat in a pan, like rain on a tent, and it came from the tub.

The water had gone down. Not drained — evaporated, or seeped past a bad plug — and it had left a tide line around the porcelain, a greasy dark-brown ring wide as her hand, with a fringe of scum above it like the mark of a receding lake. What water remained was three or four inches of something no longer water: opaque, coffee-coloured, iridescent where the ceiling light struck it, a slick of rendered fat lying on top in continents.

He was in it. He had been a man in it a week ago.

What she registered first was the wrongness of the proportions. He was too big for the tub, swollen out of any shape a person keeps. The abdomen had risen into a taut green-black dome, marbled with a spreading net of veins gone dark and branching under the skin like ink drawn through wet paper. The limbs had gone the same way — inflated, tight, the fingers spread apart by pressure, the skin over them white and pleated and lifting away in translucent sheets, so the hand nearest her looked as though it were shedding a glove. One of them *had* come off, partly. It lay in the shallow water like something taken off and set aside.

The face was not a face. Fluid had pushed the features out of true — the eyelids ballooned shut, the lips thickened and parted, the tongue protruding, purple, dry-looking despite everything. From the nose and the corner of the mouth a rust-coloured fluid had run down the neck and dried in streaks that the flies were working over. The hair had slipped from the scalp in a loose mat and floated to the drain end.

And everything moved.

The maggots were in their multitudes, and they had made a mass — a pale, seething cushion in the hollows of the eyes and mouth, spilling along the jaw, thick as a fist over the throat, so densely packed that the surface of it rolled and heaved with a current of its own. That was the crackling. Thousands of small bodies working, and the sound of them filling the tiled room, amplified by porcelain and glass. She could feel the heat of the mass from where she stood; she read later that they generate their own, that a maggot mass runs feverish. At the time she only knew the air above the tub shimmered slightly, and that the flies came off the body in a rising, resettling smoke whenever she shifted her weight.

There were beetles too, small and black, at the corners of the room, and a drift of empty casings along the tub's edge like spilled rice.

What broke her was none of this.

It was the shelf above the taps. A razor. A bar of soap with a hair on it. A pumice stone. A glass of water three-quarters full, gone cloudy, a single fly floating in it. And on the radiator, a towel — folded in half and then in half again, squared to the edges, put there by a man who had expected to be needing it.

She got as far as the hallway before her body took over. Afterwards she sat on the top step of the stairwell with the door pulled shut behind her and the smell still coming through it, thick as smoke under a door, and she found she was holding her own wrist, very hard, feeling the pulse in it, over and over, as though it were something she needed to keep checking.

The garage smelled like old motor oil and rain coming through a bad seal in the roof. Vinnie had been standing under the one working fluorescent for eleven minutes, watching it stutter, when they brought Dennis Culhane in.

Culhane came through the side door with his hands out in front of him, already talking. That was the thing about Culhane. He'd been talking since March.

"Vin. Vinnie. Listen—"

"Sit down."

There was a folding chair set up in the middle of the concrete, near the drain, and Culhane looked at the drain and understood something, and his face did a slow collapse, like a wet paper bag giving out at the bottom. He sat anyway. Men always sat. Vinnie had thought about that a lot over the years — how a man would sit down in the chair you put out for him, because sitting was the last normal thing left, and refusing meant admitting where he was.

"I got four hundred," Culhane said. "In my jacket. Right now, tonight, four hundred, and Thursday I get the disability check—"

"You said Thursday three Thursdays ago."

"Because the office is backed up—"

"Dennis." Vinnie crouched down so they were eye to eye. Culhane smelled like cigarettes and unwashed hair and something sweeter underneath, panic-sweat. "You know I don't decide this. You went past me. You went over my head and you lied to Marco's face about the boat, and now this isn't collection anymore. Now it's an example."

"I'm fifty-eight years old," Culhane said, as though it were an argument.

Vinnie stood. Behind him, Petey handed over the bat — not an aluminum one, they never used aluminum, aluminum rang like a church bell and carried three blocks. This was a wooden Louisville, taped at the grip, the barrel scuffed pale where the finish had worn off.

Culhane started to get up.

Petey put both hands on his shoulders and pressed him down, and Culhane's sneakers scrabbled against the concrete with a sound like sandpaper on a wall, quick and useless, and he said "no no no no no" in a rising register that stopped being words about halfway through.

"Left one, keep it below the knee," Petey said. "Marco said below the knee."

Vinnie set his feet. He'd played third base for two years at Cardinal Hayes and it never left you, that alignment, hips and shoulders and hands. He didn't wind up big. Big winds were for movies. He came down and across, short and brutal, into the meat of the shin four inches above the ankle.

The sound came in two parts. First the flat wet slap of wood on flesh, almost soft, almost nothing. Then, a half-beat behind it, a crack — not like a branch, not like anything wooden. It was a dull, dense pop, the way a knuckle sounds if you could hear it from the inside, and underneath it a gritty crunch that went up through the bat handle into Vinnie's palms and stayed there.

Culhane didn't scream. That was the part nobody expected, the part Vinnie could never get used to. His breath went out of him all at once in a grunt, and then nothing — nothing for four or five full seconds, his mouth open in an O, his hands frozen in the air on either side of his face like a man conducting a symphony that had stopped. His eyes were enormous. His whole body had gone rigid, heels dug into the floor, the tendons standing up in his neck.

Then it arrived, and he screamed.

It wasn't a movie scream either. It was too high and it broke in the middle and turned into a series of ragged, hitching yelps, and he pitched sideways off the chair and hit the concrete on his hip and elbow. He curled around the leg without touching it — that was instinct too, they never touched it — his hands hovering above the shin, patting the air over it. The foot was turned wrong. Not much. Fifteen degrees. That little bit of wrong was somehow worse than blood would have been.

"Oh God oh God oh God," Culhane said. "Oh God. Oh God."

"Other one," Petey said.

Vinnie's arms felt heavy. There was a bright hot spot in his chest he'd learned not to name. He walked around the chair, and Culhane saw him coming and tried to drag himself backward with his elbows, scraping across the floor, his broken leg trailing, and the noise he made then was not a word but a long low animal thing, and he was crying, and there was spit stringing off his chin.

"Turn your face away," Vinnie said, quietly. "It's easier if you look at the wall."

Culhane looked at him instead. That was the thing Vinnie would take home with him and keep, the way you keep a splinter under a nail: Culhane looked right at him and said, "I coached your brother's team. In Kingsbridge. I coached Tommy's team."

Vinnie swung.

The second one was worse because the leg was flat on the concrete with no give in it, and the crack was louder, sharper, and Culhane's whole body jackknifed and he vomited, thin and yellow, onto the floor beside his own face, and then he lay there shaking with his cheek in it, making a sound like a man trying to breathe through a wet rag.

Petey crouched and went through the jacket and came up with the four hundred, counted it, tucked it away.

"Twenty minutes," he said, "then we call it in. Say he got hit by a car on Bailey."

Vinnie set the bat against the wall. Under the stuttering light, Culhane had gone quiet except for the breathing, and he was saying something into the concrete, over and over, too soft to hear — a name, maybe, or a number, or the word Thursday.

Vinnie went outside and stood in the rain and looked at his hands until they stopped.

The Quiet Part

She's making it too easy, and that's the disappointment I have to swallow every time.

Forty yards ahead, she's crashing through the deadfall like something wounded, all noise and no direction, and I could take her now. Six strides, maybe eight. But I let the gap hold. I match her, step for step, and I let the dark do its work.

This is the part nobody would understand, if there were anybody to explain it to. They'd want the ugly answer. They'd want the mother, the basement, the cat in the shed when I was nine — some tidy little wound they could point to and say *there, that's the flaw, that's where the man went wrong.* People need causes. They can't stand the idea that something might simply *prefer.*

Here is the truth, and it's boring: the rest of my life happens behind glass.

I go to work. I nod. I say *cold enough for you?* and someone says *supposed to warm up Thursday,* and I feel exactly nothing, and the day goes down my throat like lukewarm water. I have sat through Christmases. I have held a crying woman I was supposed to love and felt only the damp of her face on my shirt, and thought about whether I'd left the porch light on.

And then there's this.

Right now I can smell three things separately: the pine, the iron of the wet granite, and her — the sharp animal panic coming off her in waves, sweeter than any perfume she owns. I know she owns Chanel. I know the shape of her mail, the hours of her lamps, which stair on her back porch groans. I know she leaves through the kitchen door because she doesn't trust the front lock, and she's right not to.

I can hear my own pulse. I can hear the sound of my boot easing into moss, which is no sound at all, because I learned this ground in three seasons of walking it while she slept. Every root. Every hollow. There's a barbed wire fence eighty yards north that she'll find with her thighs. There's a drop by the culvert that she'll find with her ankle.

I am *awake.* Do you see? For maybe forty minutes out of every eleven months, I am fully and completely awake, and everything in me is pointed in one direction like a compass needle, and it is the closest thing to peace I have ever been given.

She stops.

I stop.

Her breathing comes back to me through the trees, ragged, and then she does the stupid brave thing they all do — she tries to hold it. Tries to be silent. As if she could out-still me. I've spent whole nights standing in a treeline watching a bedroom window, and my legs went numb, and I didn't move, and I was *content.* She can hold her breath for forty seconds. Maybe fifty.

I count.

Somewhere off to the east an owl says something to nobody. The cold is coming up out of the ground through my soles and I welcome it, because it's *sensation*, it's real, it's happening to me.

Thirty-one. Thirty-two.

There's a thing I've never said out loud. When it's finished — when the quiet part comes, and there's nothing left to do but the work of hands — I don't feel triumph. I feel the way you feel at the end of a long song. I feel it draining out of me and I already dread the drive home, the shower, the eleven months of glass and lukewarm water waiting on the other side of the door. So I stretch this. I let her run. I let her think there's a road, a light, a dog barking, a chance. Not cruelty. *Economy.* I'm making it last, the way you'd ration the last cigarette in the pack.

I tell myself that's a kind of generosity. That I'm the only person on earth giving her his whole attention. That nobody will ever know her the way I —

Forty-four. Forty-five.

She hasn't breathed.

I turn my head very slowly. The wind is coming from the northwest, off the ridge, which means it's carrying my scent — pine sap and cold sweat and the WD-40 on the hinge of the thing in my pocket — straight down the slope toward where she was standing.

Forty-nine. Fifty.

Nothing.

I've never had to wait past forty.

The cold's not pleasant now. It's just cold, and it's inside my jacket, and my left hand has started doing that thing it does, the small tremor I hide at meetings by holding a coffee cup. I take one step. The moss takes it silently, the way I trained it to.

And then, from somewhere to my right — behind me, *behind* me, from the direction of the culvert where the ground drops and a person could lie flat in a foot of black water and let a man walk past her in the dark — I hear her let that breath go.

Slow. Steady. Almost gentle.

The cold came first — before sight, before thought. Stone against my cheek, drinking the warmth out of me, and a taste in my mouth like I'd been sucking on a nail.

I don't know how long I lay there listening to the water. Somewhere above and behind me it collected and fell, collected and fell, with the patience of something that had been doing it for a hundred years and would do it for a hundred more. That sound told me the size of the room before my eyes did. It came back to me too quickly. Small. Low.

The smell is what brought me all the way up out of the dark.

Rust, mostly — that flat, red, sucked-penny smell that gets into the back of your throat and sits there. And under it, worse, something older. Not the bright butcher-shop smell of fresh blood but what blood becomes after years of soaking into porous stone, going sweet and thick and faintly cheesy, like meat left in a closed room. It had gotten into the mortar. It was in the air I had to keep breathing to stay alive, and every breath felt like a small betrayal of myself. Beneath that: mildew. Lamp oil. Old urine gone to ammonia, sharp enough to sting. And, absurdly, faintly, wood smoke — someone had a fire somewhere, someone warm and comfortable, and that hurt more than the cold did.

There was a single lamp on a hook, the glass sooted almost opaque, and the light it threw was the colour of weak tea. Enough to see by. Enough that they wanted me to see.

The floor sloped. That was the detail that undid me — not any blade, not any hook, but the gentle grade of the flagstones tilting toward an iron grate in the center of the room, ringed with a crust I did not let myself look at directly. Someone had thought about drainage. Someone had planned. A room can be a crime of passion; a drain is a crime of intention, of appropriation and budget and a mason's afternoon.

Along the far wall, a workbench. Tidy. That was the other thing. The implements hung from pegs in ascending order of size, the way a carpenter keeps his chisels, and there was a whetstone with a dark oiled dip worn into its middle from long use. I could name almost none of what I saw, and the not-naming was its own torment: a thing like a pair of pliers whose jaws did not meet, but curved apart. A wooden spool with a crank handle and a length of chain wound round it. Rods of graduated thickness in a leather roll. Something with a screw thread and two flat plates. A funnel. A shallow tin basin with rust — I hoped rust — flowering at its bottom in a wide brown bloom.

Above the bench, hanging from a nail, an apron. Stiff. Cracked at the folds like old paint, standing half-open of its own accord as though it still held the shape of the man who wore it.

And in the corner, a stool. Three-legged, worn smooth and pale on top. Beside it a clay cup and the pit of some fruit gone black and shrivelled.

That was the thing I could not stop looking at, in the end. Not the chains bolted at the height of a raised wrist, not the frame in the middle of the room with its straps gone stiff and shiny as jerky, not the scratches — hundreds, layered, in no language — clawed into the stone at exactly the reach of a man lying where I was lying.

The stool. Someone had sat down here. Had gotten comfortable. Had eaten a piece of fruit and set the pit aside and settled in to work, unhurried, in a room built for the purpose, and then had gone up the stairs to a fire.

The water fell. Collected, and fell.

I put my forehead against the cold stone and tried to remember my own name before they came back to take it from me.

# Ninety-One Seconds

The plan had been good. That was the thing Weiss would keep coming back to in the eleven minutes he had left to live — the plan had been *good*.

Four men, one driver, ninety-one seconds inside the Commerce & Farmers Trust on Delaney Street. No vault, no safe-deposit theatrics. Just the cash recycler behind the teller line, which on the second Friday of the month held payroll for three foundries and a trucking outfit, and which a man named Bardo who owed Weiss money had described in exhaustive detail over the course of two evenings and a bottle of rye.

They came in at 9:14 on a morning already gone soft with heat, the asphalt on Delaney breathing that summer stink of tar and dust. Weiss went first, coat over his arm despite the weather, and by the time the door swung shut behind Arnett the coat was on the floor and the shotgun was up and Weiss was saying, in the flat and almost bored voice he had practiced, "Everybody on the ground. This is a robbery and it will take one minute and nobody has to get hurt."

For thirty-eight seconds it went exactly as drawn.

Teddy Doyle vaulted the counter, light as a boy, and put the muzzle of his pistol against the recycler's housing while the head teller — a woman in her fifties with reading glasses on a beaded chain — keyed in the codes with hands that shook so hard she had to try twice. Arnett stood at the door watching the street through the blinds. Weiss walked the lobby, counting bodies. Eleven customers. Four staff. A boy of maybe six lying beside his mother with his cheek on the carpet, staring up at Weiss with an expression of pure and uncomprehending calm.

The fourth man was named Kessel, and Kessel had a wife with a bad kidney and a temper he could not always find the bottom of, and Kessel was watching the manager.

The manager's name was Howard Pell. He was fifty-four years old, he had a bad hip from a scaffolding fall in 1979, and eight feet from where he lay was a brass pedal under the desk of the loan officer's cubicle. He had thought about that pedal every day for nineteen years. He put his palm flat and pushed himself forward maybe six inches, and Kessel saw him do it, and instead of shooting him — which he would have been within the awful logic of the moment to do — Kessel kicked him hard in the ribs and screamed at him, and in the noise and the scrambling nobody could say later whether Pell reached the pedal or not.

He did.

Ninety-one seconds. They were out at ninety-four, which was the kind of margin Weiss could live with, two canvas bags fat with banded twenties, and the first thing he saw when he came through the door into that white hammering sunlight was a city patrol unit stopped at an angle in the middle of Delaney, forty feet away, both doors open, and two officers behind them with their weapons already out.

Marisol had the van running at the curb. She was nineteen feet from Weiss. He remembers thinking, with a clarity that felt almost restful: *nineteen feet.*

Arnett fired first. He always said afterward — he lived, Arnett, that was the joke of it — that he did not decide to. That his hand simply did it, the way a hand pulls back from a stove. He put four rounds from a .45 into the front quarter panel of the patrol car, and the sound of it in that narrow canyon of storefronts was not a bang but a physical thing, a series of flat slaps that went up the buildings and came back down.

Then everything opened at once.

The older officer, a fifteen-year man named Diaz, shot Kessel through the chest. One round. Kessel was still holding a bag of money and he sat down on the sidewalk like a man whose legs had gone to sleep, and he looked down at himself with an expression of enormous irritation, and then he tipped sideways onto the hot concrete and did not move again. He was thirty-one. His wife's name was Renata and she was at that moment in a dialysis chair four miles away, watching a game show with the sound off.

Weiss fired the shotgun into the patrol car's windshield. It came apart in a white bloom, a sheet of frost that hung a half-second in the air and then fell in gravel across the hood, and the second officer — Petrosky, twenty-four years old, ten weeks off field training, a young man who still ironed his uniform blouse on a towel spread over his mother's kitchen table — went down behind the rear wheel with buckshot in his forearm and jaw. He did not scream. He kept trying to speak into his shoulder microphone and could not shape the words, and he kept trying anyway, over and over, blood coming out of his mouth in strings, while Diaz screamed the code for officer down loud enough that the dispatcher heard it twice.

Teddy Doyle ran for the van.

He almost made it. He was the youngest of them and the fastest and he had that gift some men have of going invisible in chaos, but Diaz was shooting through the space under the patrol car's chassis, three inches of daylight between rocker panel and asphalt, and one of those rounds went through both of Doyle's ankles. He came down on his face in the gutter, and the sound he made then was terrible and childish, and he began to crawl toward the van dragging the ruined ends of himself, still holding the money.

Marisol got out. That was the thing nobody had planned for and nobody could have planned for. She was twenty-two. She had driven for Weiss twice before, competently and without comment, and she had been told nine separate times that she did not leave the vehicle for any reason on this earth. She got out and came around the front of the van to get Doyle under the arms, and Diaz put two rounds into her back as she bent over him, and she folded across Doyle's shoulders and the two of them lay there together in the gutter with the money between them like something they had built.

Weiss got behind the mailbox on the corner and it saved his life for ninety seconds. He could hear sirens now, more than one, coming up out of the grid of streets to the north with that awful multiplying quality, a sound like water finding a crack. He could hear Petrosky making his wet ruined noise into the radio. He could hear Arnett somewhere behind him yelling his name.

He looked at Marisol lying on Teddy Doyle and he understood the shape of the day.

The second unit came in from the west and clipped a parked sedan doing forty, and the two officers out of it went low along the storefronts, and by then there were four guns on the mailbox and the mailbox was made of eleven-gauge steel and eleven-gauge steel is not what people think it is. The rounds went through it and out the other side. Weiss took the first one through the hip and the second through the shoulder blade and he came out from behind it firing the shotgun one-handed at nothing at all, at the whole bright terrible morning, and they shot him eleven times in the middle of Delaney Street beneath a banner advertising the Founders' Day parade.

Arnett threw his gun into the road and lay down in the doorway of a shoe repair shop with his fingers laced behind his head, screaming that he was done, that he was done, that he was done. They broke three of his ribs getting the cuffs on him and no one ever wrote that part down.

---

It lasted four minutes and forty seconds from Arnett's first round to Arnett's surrender. In that time the participants fired between fifty-one and fifty-six rounds — the count was never settled, because two of the recovered casings could not be matched to any weapon on the scene and a round was found in the brick above the awning of a laundry at an angle nobody could account for. A retired postal worker named Ellis Boothe, waiting for the 9:20 bus on the far corner, was struck in the thigh by a ricochet and bled to death in the doorway of a florist's while a nineteen-year-old clerk held a bolt of green tissue paper against the wound and told him about her sister's wedding to keep him talking. He was seventy-eight. He had been on his way to the library.

Officer Petrosky lived. He lost the use of his left hand and the lower right quadrant of his jaw was rebuilt in four surgeries over fourteen months, and he speaks now with a slight thickness that strangers take for an accent. He did not go back to the job. He teaches driver's education at a high school in the next county and he is very patient with nervous students, unreasonably patient, and none of them know why.

Diaz retired eight months later with a commendation he keeps in a drawer, face down. He shot three people that morning and killed two of them and one of those was a twenty-two-year-old woman who had gotten out of a running vehicle to help a man who was screaming, and he understood then and understands now that he did nothing wrong, and it has not once helped.

Howard Pell, the manager with the bad hip, was hailed in the local paper for tripping the silent alarm. He gave one interview and then no more. Later he told a friend over beers that he had spent nineteen years imagining the alarm as a kind of prayer — press it and the good men come — and that he had not understood that the alarm was not a prayer but a *door*, and that when you open a door you cannot choose what walks through.

The money came to $211,400. It was recovered entire, some of it stained past use, and returned to three foundries and a trucking company, and the men and women whose payroll it was were paid on time that Friday, and most of them heard about the shooting on the radio and shook their heads and went on with what they were doing, because that is what people do.

Arnett got forty years. He is inside still. He was asked once, by a graduate student writing about something else entirely, what the worst of it was. He thought about it for a long time.

"The plan was good," he said. "That's the worst of it. You could tell it to anybody. You could draw it on a napkin and they'd say, yeah, that'd work. And it did work. Ninety-one seconds, we were out with the money. Everything we said would happen, happened."

He turned his coffee cup around on the table.

"Just the world was there too," he said. "Nobody ever puts the world in the plan."

The first thing Mara noticed was the smell of almonds, which was absurd, because there were no almonds in the pump room.

She looked up from the valve manifold. The air near the ceiling had gone faintly wrong—not smoke, nothing so honest as smoke, just a shimmer, a thickening, like heat above summer asphalt. Somewhere behind the wall, a hiss she had been hearing for four minutes and filing under *normal* revealed itself as something else entirely.

"Okay," she said out loud. "Okay."

She went to the door. The handle turned and the door did not move, because the door had never been the problem; the problem was the pressure seal that had engaged when the alarm tripped, the alarm she had not heard because she had taken her ear defenders off to listen to the valve. She hit the release panel with her palm. The panel chirped and displayed a small orange padlock.

That was when the calm broke.

She hit it again, harder, and then with her fist, and then with the wrench, three times, four, plastic splintering and the little orange padlock persisting behind the cracks like a thing that had never cared about her at all. She was shouting. She could hear herself from a strange distance, a woman's voice going hoarse in a concrete box, and she thought with sudden ferocious clarity: *nobody is on this level until six.*

Her watch said 4:12.

She dropped to the floor because gas rises—she knew that, she'd sat through the training video twice—and pressed her cheek to the cold concrete and breathed the thin clean layer down there, and for maybe forty seconds it worked. She thought about her jacket. She dragged it over her mouth. She thought about water and there was no water. She thought about the vent grille on the far wall and crawled to it on her elbows and put her mouth against it like a swimmer and drew in a breath that tasted of the same sweet almond nothing, because of course the vent was where it was coming from.

Her head began to hurt.

Not gradually. It arrived the way a hand arrives on the back of your neck—a band of pressure across her forehead, a pulse behind her eyes that kept time with a heart she could suddenly feel in her throat, in her ears, in her fingertips. Her heart was going much too fast. She noticed that she was panting and could not stop panting, great useless heaving gulps, and no matter how much she took in her body kept demanding more, as though the air had been replaced with a very good imitation of air.

She thought: *I am suffocating in a room full of oxygen.*

Her hands wouldn't close properly on the wrench. She looked at them, splayed on the concrete, and they were pink—not pale, not blue, a strange sunburnt flush along the knuckles—and this frightened her more than anything else had, because it was the wrong color, it was a color that meant machinery inside her had stopped answering.

She got up. She doesn't remember deciding to. She was standing and swaying and the room had tilted about ten degrees and stayed there, and she went at the door again, shoulder first, and bounced off it, and the floor came up and hit her hip and she felt the impact only as information.

*Get up.*

She got up onto her knees. Vomited, briefly and thinly. Wiped her mouth with the back of her wrist and found her mouth was numb, her lips buzzing like a struck bell.

The pain in her head had become enormous and simple, the whole of her, and underneath it something worse was arriving: a heaviness in her arms and legs, a lovely and terrible weight, the specific weight of a body that has decided to lie down. She thought of her father falling asleep in his chair. She thought of the almond cake her mother used to make, the way the top cracked. Her thoughts were coming apart into pieces that no longer fit each other.

*Twelve minutes*, she thought, and could not remember what that meant.

Her vision narrowed. The far wall went first, softening at the edges, grey creeping in from the periphery like frost on glass, until all that was left was the orange padlock glowing on its cracked panel, small and steady and impossibly far away.

She was aware of her cheek on the floor again. She was aware, distantly, of her legs jerking, of a sound she was making that was not a word.

Then the concrete went soft and warm as a bed, and the hiss became a sea, and Mara went out into it without any struggle at all.

At 4:19 the pressure seal cycled, as it was designed to, and the door swung open onto an empty corridor.
