The rain had stopped an hour ago, which was inconvenient. Rain washed things away. Rain was a defense attorney's friend.

Sergeant Dale Mercer stood at the mouth of the alley behind the Sunoco and worked the problem the way he worked all problems: from the end backward.

The end was a courtroom. It always was. Every decision he made in the next nine minutes would be read aloud someday by a woman in a gray suit with a highlighter, and the only question that mattered was whether it would sound *ordinary* when she read it. Not innocent. Ordinary. Juries didn't punish ugliness. They punished the thing that didn't fit the pattern they already had in their heads.

Behind him, sixty feet back, Ruben Salas lay against the base of the dumpster with his legs out in front of him like a man taking a break. Two rounds, close. Mercer had not wanted to do it. He wanted the record to reflect that, if only in the record of himself, which was the only one he'd ever really consulted. Ruben had been talking to somebody at the DA's office about the money, and Ruben had told Mercer that he was talking, which was Ruben's whole problem in life — he thought information was currency instead of a fuse.

So. Nine minutes, generous. He'd called it in himself, shots fired, and he'd given the dispatcher a location a block and a half east, which bought him the time and also, later, would look like the honest confusion of a man in the dark.

Now: the shape of the story.

A drug murder was best. Drug murders got a detective who was already carrying eleven other cases, a folder that got thinner every year instead of thicker. Nobody appealed a drug murder from the grave. Ruben had a sheet like a phone book, and his mother had been on the news twice defending him, which meant that when she cried on camera this time, the anchors would use a shorter clip.

But a story needs a body and a body needs a hand that put it there. This was the part Mercer had been assembling since before he got out of the car.

Which brought him to Elias.

The man was maybe thirty feet up the alley, in the loading nook of the shuttered furniture place, wrapped in a blue tarp and sleeping the way you sleep at three in the morning when the ground is wet and you've had whatever you could get. Mercer had rousted him a dozen times. Elias Boone. Forty-one, forty-two. Possession, possession, trespass, an old assault from Ohio that was really a bar shove but read like an assault. Sometimes he answered questions and sometimes he answered a different question than the one you'd asked. He'd been in and out of Millbrook twice that Mercer knew of.

That was the whole calculation, right there, and Mercer turned it over once to be sure it held.

*Who will they believe.*

Not the man in the tarp. The man in the tarp would say something true — *I heard two bangs, I saw the police* — and he would say it badly, out of order, and he would say it to a public defender with a hundred and ninety open files who would spend eleven minutes on him and then offer him time served on a plea to something lesser, and Elias would take it, because everybody took it, because the machine was built to make taking it the rational choice. And if he didn't take it, he'd sit in a courtroom in a county jumpsuit with his hands shaking from the thing they wouldn't give him inside, and he would try to explain, and the jury would watch him and think: *this is a man who could do a thing like that.*

Mercer wasn't inventing any of that. He wanted to be clear with himself. He was only *using* it. It was already there, in place, humming along, the way a river is already there before you put a mill on it.

He crouched at the edge of the puddle light and took the second gun out of the ankle rig. A .380 he'd taken off a kid two years ago and never logged, which had been an unprofessional thing to do at the time and now looked like foresight. He'd already put Ruben's rounds through his own weapon, and that couldn't be helped; a service weapon discharge was going to happen no matter what story he told. So the story had to include it. Return fire. That's what the .380 was for. A shooter in the alley, muzzle flash, Mercer engaging.

Two of his own rounds in Ruben, and one from the .380 into the brick above the dumpster, high and wild, exactly where a panicking man would put it. He'd already fired that one. He'd fired it before he called dispatch, which was the correct order of operations, because the neighbors would hear three shots and the timeline would be clean.

Now the gun needed a hand.

He walked up the alley slow, on the balls of his feet out of a habit that no longer served any purpose. Elias didn't wake. His mouth was open. There was a paperback under the tarp with him, swollen with water, and Mercer registered it and set it aside the way you set aside a stone in a field you're plowing. Not cruelty. Just clearance.

He thought about it once more, honestly, because he was not a stupid man and he knew that the only thing that ever caught people like him was wanting it too much to check.

*Is there a version where I walk away.*

He ran it. A found gun, an unsolved, no suspect. Then the detectives canvass, and the canvass finds Elias, and Elias says *I saw the police*, and now Mercer is the only name in a file that stays open forever, a file that some ambitious kid pulls in six years when he needs a case to make his name on. No. Open files were the danger. Closed files went into a box in a basement and stayed there. The system's deepest instinct wasn't justice, it was *closure*, and if you fed it a name it would swallow and never look up.

Give them somebody. Give them somebody easy, and they will help you. They won't even know they're helping.

He knelt down and took Elias's right wrist, and the man made a small sound and didn't wake, and Mercer thought — briefly, with the flat interest of a man noting the weather — that this was probably the gentlest anyone had touched him in a year.

Nine minutes. He had six.

He got to work.

# The Bloat

The cans were bad. Everyone could see they were bad.

They'd swollen into shapes cans weren't meant to make — pregnant lids, seams weeping a rust-colored crust — and when Odalys pried the crate loose from the collapsed shelving, the smell that came up was sweet and wrong, like fruit left in a closed car. Four cans of peaches. Two of some kind of stew. A jar of pickled something gone cloudy as a cataract.

Nine days since anyone in the station had eaten anything but boiled leather and the inner bark of the cottonwoods down by the culvert. Nine days made the smell into an argument rather than a warning.

She got the crate maybe six feet before Toma saw her.

He didn't say anything. That was the thing she'd remember, afterward, the thing that would sit in her chest like a swallowed stone — that Toma, who had carried her nephew on his shoulders for eleven miles through the ash-fall, who had sung *Cielito Lindo* badly and constantly to keep the children from crying, said nothing at all. He simply looked at the crate and then at her, and something behind his eyes stepped aside and let something older come forward.

He came at a run, and he had the length of rebar.

Odalys dropped the crate. She heard a can burst on the concrete — a wet cough, a spreading stink — and she hated herself for the grief that spiked through her, grief for a peach.

The rebar caught her across the left forearm as she brought it up. She felt the bone go. Not a snap: a kind of grinding lurch, like a door coming off its hinge, and her hand simply stopped being hers. It hung. She screamed and the scream brought the others.

They came out of the dark of the service bays, out from behind the dead pumps, and none of them asked what was happening because all of them already knew. Marguerite with the tire iron she slept holding. The boy they called Sparrow, who had a length of chain and a fear so total it had cooked down into something like calm. Old Piotr, who had a knife made from a leaf-spring and who had been kind to everyone, always, up until this exact moment.

There is a thing that happens to people who have been hungry long enough. The hunger stops being in the stomach. It moves up into the reasoning part of the skull and takes the chair, and everything the person used to be stands politely at the wall, watching.

Marguerite went for Toma's knees. He turned the rebar down and she caught it on her shoulder and kept going anyway, and they went into the shelving together, and the whole rusted structure came down with a sound like a bell being murdered.

Odalys crawled. Her broken arm dragged. She got her good hand around a can of peaches — hot from lying in the sun-slant, tacky with whatever had leaked — and she was trying to work it under her body when Sparrow's chain took her across the back of the thigh. The pain was so large it seemed to come from outside her, from the building, from the sky.

She rolled. She still had the can. She hit him with it. She hit a fifteen-year-old boy in the face with a swollen tin of peaches and felt his nose give way, and hot wetness went over her knuckles, and he sat down hard on the concrete with his hands over his face making a sound like a kettle.

*I'm sorry,* she thought, very clearly, and did not stop.

Piotr got the stew. He got it and he ran, and he was seventy-one years old and he did not run well, and Toma caught him at the doorway to the bays. What happened there happened out of the light. Odalys heard the leaf-spring knife find something, and she heard Toma make a noise of pure surprise, and then she heard a longer noise, and then she heard nothing from Piotr at all, ever again.

It was over in ninety seconds. Perhaps less.

---

Afterward there was the terrible business of the quiet.

Marguerite sat against the wall with her arm bent the wrong way at the elbow, breathing in small sips, saying *okay, okay, okay* to no one. Sparrow's face had already begun to close up, both eyes going purple and slitted, and he was weeping and eating peaches out of a burst can with his fingers, the syrup running pink down his chin where his nose had bled into it. # The Field at Hanging Marsh

*Kent, October 1817*

The mist lay on the marsh grass in a low white seam, and Henry Pellet thought, absurdly, that it looked like the wool his mother used to card by the fire. He was twenty-six years old and he was carrying a mahogany case containing two flintlock pistols, and his hands would not stop trembling, so he held the case against his chest as if it were an infant.

Beside him, Charles Adderly walked with his coat over his arm despite the cold. He had been awake all night. Henry knew this because he had been awake with him, listening to him compose and burn three letters to his sister, and at four in the morning Charles had laughed and said, *This is a great deal of ceremony over a remark about a horse.*

It had not been about a horse. It had been about a horse, and then about a card game, and then about the honesty of Charles's late father, and by the time the word *liar* had crossed the table at the Wheatsheaf there was no longer any road that did not lead here, to a wet field at half past six in the morning with a surgeon waiting by the hedge.

Colonel Verity's party was already assembled. Verity himself stood apart, a heavy man in his forties with a face like a closed door, flexing his right hand as though testing a glove. His second, a Captain Lorne, came forward and Henry met him in the middle of the ground, and they did the things that men do.

"Twelve paces?"

"Twelve."

"Your principal will not withdraw the expression?"

"He will not. Will yours withdraw the demand for it?"

"He will not."

They examined the pistols together, powder and ball, and Henry's fingers were so cold and so unsteady that Lorne had to steady the ramrod for him, and did so kindly, without comment, which somehow made everything worse. Lorne was perhaps fifty. He had done this before. Henry understood suddenly that he was in the presence of a man who had watched friends die in the grass and had eaten dinner afterward.

The surgeon, a Mr. Bagnall from Ashford, sat on a folding stool with a leather roll open on his knees and did not look at anyone. He had been paid five guineas. He had asked only one question upon arriving, which was whether there was a cart.

They measured the ground. The grass soaked Henry's stockings through his boots. Charles took his position and stood very straight, side-on, the pistol held down along the seam of his trousers, and he looked at Henry once and gave him a small nod, the same nod he had given him across the schoolroom at Winchester fifteen years earlier, when they were both boys and the world was still made of things that could be undone.

"Gentlemen," said Lorne. "You will fire upon the word. One. Two—"

Both pistols spoke at once, so nearly together that Henry heard only one enormous sound, and afterward could never be persuaded that there had been two.

Colonel Verity's hat left his head and went spinning into the mist. He stood there bareheaded, blinking, an old man abruptly, with white hair sticking up in a crest.

Charles sat down.

That was the thing Henry remembered for the rest of his life: not a fall, but a sitting down, unhurried, almost fastidious, the way a man sits when he has walked a long way and finds a convenient stone. He was still holding the pistol. He looked down at his waistcoat with an expression of mild social embarrassment.

"Ah," he said. "Yes."

Henry reached him before the surgeon. There was very little blood at first, only a small dark hole through the wool an inch above and to the left of the navel, and Henry felt a wild upward surge of hope, because surely a hole so small was nothing, surely—

Then Charles's face changed.

It began as puzzlement and became something Henry had no name for. Charles's back arched. He made a sound in his throat, not a scream, something more private than a scream, and his heels began to dig at the turf. He rolled onto his side and drew his knees up and his hands went to his belly and pressed there hard, as though he might hold the pain inside, and he said, in an entirely reasonable voice, "Oh God. Oh God. Oh God."

Bagnall knelt in the wet and cut the waistcoat away with a small curved knife. He did not hurry. He put two fingers near the wound, and Charles screamed then, a high, tearing, wholly unfamiliar sound, and Bagnall sat back on his heels and looked at Henry and gave the smallest shake of his head that a man's neck can make.

"Do something," Henry said.

"There is nothing to do, sir. The ball has gone through the bowel. It is lodged somewhere against the spine, I should think." He said it quietly. "I can give him laudanum. It will not be enough. Nothing is ever enough for this."

"Then give him all of it."

Bagnall did. Charles could not swallow properly and much of it ran down his chin, and Henry held his head and felt the sweat springing out on his friend's forehead in the cold air, cold sweat, running into his hair.

It took eleven minutes. Henry did not know this at the time. He learned it afterward, because Captain Lorne, out of some obscure military instinct, had taken out his watch at the moment of the shot and did not think to put it away, and mentioned the figure later at the inn in a voice that suggested he wished he could unknow it.

For the first minutes Charles thrashed. He gripped Henry's forearm with a strength that left five bruises which took a fortnight to fade, and he begged. That was the unbearable part, the part Henry never told the sister, never told anyone: that Charles Adderly, who had been the wittiest man in three counties, spent his last minutes begging. He begged Henry to stop it. He begged the surgeon. He asked, several times, with terrible clarity, whether they might not carry him home, because he thought his mother could help him, and his mother had been dead nine years.

Then the thrashing stopped, and that was worse, because what came in its place was a rigid, shuddering stillness, his whole body drawn tight as a bowstring around the thing in his belly, breathing in short sips, high in the chest. The mist went on lying in the grass. A blackbird began carrying on in the hedge, absolutely indifferent, and Henry hated it with a purity he had never felt for any human being.

Somewhere behind them, Colonel Verity was being sick.

Near the end Charles's face smoothed out. His eyes found Henry's and there was somebody behind them again, briefly, the way a light shows in a window when someone crosses a room upstairs.

"Henry," he said. "This is very badly done."

"Yes," Henry said.

"Tell them—" He stopped. He seemed to be examining the sentence, turning it over for flaws, as he had once examined everything, tirelessly, delightedly. Then he said, "No. Don't tell them anything. It was about a horse."

He breathed twice more.

They carried him to the cart in his own coat, which was still folded over the gate where he had left it, having said that he did not wish to be encumbered.

Colonel Verity stood in the field with his bare white head and his hands hanging at his sides, and as Henry passed him he opened his mouth, and Henry saw that the man was going to say that honour had been satisfied.

He did not say it. To his credit, or perhaps merely because he had seen what Henry's face looked like at that moment, he did not say it. He said nothing at all, then or ever, and eleven years later he shot himself in a hotel room in Boulogne, and Henry Pellet, reading the notice in the paper over his breakfast, found that he felt nothing whatsoever.

# The Ninth Floor

The room had been empty for eleven months. He knew this because he'd read the leasing agent's listing, the same photographs uploaded every quarter with the price nudged down, and because the dust on the windowsill lay in an undisturbed gray felt that he did not touch.

He worked in his socks. Shoes left tread patterns; socks left nothing that mattered.

The case opened on the floor without a sound, hinges he had worked over with graphite until they moved like a held breath. Inside, the pieces sat in their cut foam beds like instruments in a surgeon's tray, and he lifted them out in the order he always lifted them, an order established years ago and never once varied, because variation was how a man forgot a step and forgetting a step was how a man ended up in a room he could not leave.

Receiver. Barrel. The satisfying, machined resistance as threads found threads — a sound less like metal than like a lock accepting its key. He seated the bolt. Worked it twice, dry, listening. It ran smooth. It always ran smooth. He cleaned it the night before every job the way other men prayed, and for the same reasons: not because he believed the ritual changed anything, but because the ritual made him steady, and steadiness was the only god that had ever answered him.

The optic went on last. He torqued the rings in a diagonal pattern, quarter-turn by quarter-turn, feeling for the moment the little wrench stopped giving. Then he sat back on his heels and looked at the assembled thing on the carpet and felt nothing about it at all. It was not beautiful to him. Men who found these objects beautiful were sentimentalists, and sentimentalists left fingerprints.

He built his position out of the room's own materials: the bare mattress dragged from the bedroom, folded and belted; a rolled towel; the closet door laid across two chairs and draped. Nothing brought in, nothing taken out. He lay down behind the rifle and let his body settle, bones stacking into bones, until his pulse stopped moving the reticle and lived instead somewhere behind his sternum, quiet as a clock in another room.

The window he had opened four inches at the bottom, at dawn, when the building was still asleep. He lay far back inside the room. From the street, the gap would read as nothing — a shadow, a slice of dark. He had learned long ago that the trick was not marksmanship. The trick was being somewhere no one thought to look, and being nobody when they finally did.

Eleven forty. The plaza below filled the way water fills a basin, from the edges inward. Barricades. A stage skirted in blue bunting. A brass quintet murdering something patriotic. He watched the flags on the far building and read the wind out of them, the lazy left-to-right lean, the small hitch where the air came around the corner of the parking structure. He watched a paper cup roll fifteen feet and stop. He made his adjustments and did not write them down.

He did not think about the man.

This was not discipline. Discipline implies a wanting held at bay, and he wanted nothing here. He had read the dossier once, the way one reads a bus schedule: the name, the two children, the wife who taught fourth grade, the speeches, the vote in committee that had made someone somewhere decide this expenditure was reasonable. It had all passed through him and left no residue. He was not a believer. He was not an avenger. He was the mechanism by which other men's convictions arrived at their conclusions, and a mechanism does not ask what it is for.

Twelve-oh-four. The motorcade folded into the loading area. Doors, handshakes, the small gray cluster of security moving like a single organism with many legs. He found the shape of the man's shoulders in the scope, the pale scalp showing through thinning hair, the head turning to laugh at something a staffer said.

The crosshairs crossed him and rested.

Wind flag: unchanged. Breathing: out, and out, and stopped. His finger took up the slack until it found the wall of the trigger and waited there, and in that suspended half-ounce of pressure the whole world reduced itself to a dot of black on a bright field and the number of heartbeats until the man's own momentum carried him into it.

He felt his own composure the way one feels a coat: something worn, something removable, something that had cost money. It was the only thing about the morning that troubled him, and it troubled him only faintly, the way a sound in the walls troubles a man too tired to get up. Somewhere very far down, in a room he had bricked over years ago and had never once heard from since, something registered that he had become a man for whom this was ordinary.

He let the thought pass. Thoughts were weather. You did not argue with weather; you waited for it to move off.

The man stepped up to the podium and turned to face the crowd and for one long moment held perfectly, perfectly still.

Below, the brass quintet stopped playing.

And in the silence, into the four-inch gap of open window, came the sound of the hallway door opening behind him.

The window he had opened four inches at the bottom, at dawn, when the building was still asleep. He lay far back inside the room. From the street, the gap would read as nothing — a shadow, a slice of dark. He had learned long ago that the trick was not marksmanship. The trick was being somewhere no one thought to look, and being nobody when they finally did.

Eleven forty. The plaza below filled the way water fills a basin, from the edges inward. Barricades. A stage skirted in blue bunting. A brass quintet murdering something patriotic. He watched the flags on the far building and read the wind out of them, the lazy left-to-right lean, the small hitch where the air came around the corner of the parking structure. He watched a paper cup roll fifteen feet and stop. He made his adjustments and did not write them down.

He did not think about the man.

This was not discipline. Discipline implies a wanting held at bay, and he wanted nothing here. He had read the dossier once, the way one reads a bus schedule: the name, the two children, the wife who taught fourth grade, the speeches, the vote in committee that had made someone somewhere decide this expenditure was reasonable. It had all passed through him and left no residue. He was not a believer. He was not an avenger. He was the mechanism by which other men's convictions arrived at their conclusions, and a mechanism does not ask what it is for.

Twelve-oh-four. The motorcade folded into the loading area. Doors, handshakes, the small gray cluster of security moving like a single organism with many legs. He found the shape of the man's shoulders in the scope, the pale scalp showing through thinning hair, the head turning to laugh at something a staffer said.

The crosshairs crossed him and rested.

Wind flag: unchanged. Breathing: out, and out, and stopped. His finger took up the slack until it found the wall of the trigger and waited there, and in that suspended half-ounce of pressure the whole world reduced itself to a dot of black on a bright field and the number of heartbeats until the man's own momentum carried him into it.

He felt his own composure the way one feels a coat: something worn, something removable, something that had cost money. It was the only thing about the morning that troubled him, and it troubled him only faintly, the way a sound in the walls troubles a man too tired to get up. Somewhere very far down, in a room he had bricked over years ago and had never once heard from since, something registered that he had become a man for whom this was ordinary.

He let the thought pass. Thoughts were weather. You did not argue with weather; you waited for it to move off.

The man stepped up to the podium and turned to face the crowd and for one long moment held perfectly, perfectly still.

Below, the brass quintet stopped playing.

And in the silence, into the four-inch gap of open window, came the sound of the hallway door opening behind him.

The towel had been white when he took it off the rack. Now it was the color of rust and roses, wadded under his thigh where it soaked and spread, and every time he shifted his weight it made a sound like someone stepping in mud.

He'd propped his leg on the second bed, the one with the bedspread still pulled tight, because the mattress he was sitting on had gone soft and warm underneath him in a way he was trying very hard not to think about. Blood didn't come out of you the way it did in movies — quick, theatrical, then done. It kept coming. It welled up patient and unhurried, filling the hole in his leg like a spring filling a footprint, and every time he wiped it away it was already back.

The lamp on the nightstand had a bulb too weak for this. He'd unscrewed the shade and it still wasn't enough, so he'd stood the bathroom mirror against the headboard at an angle and now there were two of him, both sweating, both gray as dishwater.

His tools were laid out on the Bible from the nightstand drawer, because it was the only flat clean thing in the room. Tweezers from a gas-station sewing kit, the cheap kind that bent if you pressed too hard. A paring knife he'd bought with a bag of oranges he hadn't eaten. Dental floss and a needle from the same sewing kit. A bottle of well liquor, two-thirds gone, half of it poured over the tools and half of it poured into him, and neither half doing what he'd wanted it to. A wooden spoon handle to bite. A bath towel folded into eighths, in case.

The first cut wasn't the worst part. That surprised him. The knife went in and there was a bright clean line of hurt, almost a relief, like scratching something that had itched for hours. It was the going *deeper* that broke him. Muscle didn't want to be parted. It clenched around the blade, hot and stubborn, and when he had to spread the wound with two fingers to see — to actually put his fingers inside himself and pull — the pain stopped being a sensation and became a *place*, somewhere he'd been dropped into, with no walls and no edges and no exit. It went up through his hip and into his spine and out the top of his skull. His vision swam and pulsed with his heartbeat, dark at the corners, and he heard a high thin noise and understood after a moment that it was coming out of him around the spoon handle.

He had to stop. He put his forehead against his knee and breathed through his nose, twelve breaths, counting them, while the blood ran down the back of his calf and pooled in the hollow behind his ankle and dripped, slow and even, onto the carpet.

Then he did it again.

The tweezers went in blind. He couldn't see anything down there but red — a red so dark it was almost black, welling and swallowing the light — so he did it by feel, and feeling around inside a bullet wound with a pair of drugstore tweezers is a thing that a man's mind refuses to be present for. He was somewhere else. He was aware, distantly, of his own hand shaking, and of the tweezers scraping something that was not meat, something that grated and sang up the metal into his fingers and made his stomach turn over hard. Bone, or the slug against bone. He couldn't tell.

It slipped twice. The second time, something tore and a fresh flood came, hot enough to feel like it was steaming, and he had to jam the towel in and lean on it with both hands and wait, gasping, teeth aching from the pressure of his own jaw.

The third time, it came.

A little gray mushroomed thing, no bigger than the tip of his thumb, slick and unimpressive. He held it up in the bad lamplight and looked at it and felt nothing at all — no triumph, no fury, nothing — and then he dropped it into the plastic ice bucket, where it landed with a small dull click.

Then he threw up into the wastebasket, and then he still had to sew.

# The Cellar

The room smelled of onions and drain water. That was the thing nobody warned you about — that a place like this wouldn't smell of blood or fear but of a restaurant's ordinary guts. Somewhere above him, faintly, Vincent's kitchen radio was playing an oldies station, and the floor joists carried the sound of chairs scraping as the lunch crowd settled in.

They'd sat him in a chair with his forearms lashed flat to a plywood tabletop, palms down, wrists bound at the base with plastic ties pulled to the second click. Not tight enough to numb him. That, he understood already, was deliberate.

Sal Ruffino came down the stairs slowly, one hand on the rail, because his knee had been bad since the eighties. He was carrying two cups of espresso in the little white cups from upstairs, and he set one down on the plywood near Danny's bound hand, close enough that Danny could feel the heat off it.

"Drink that later," Sal said. "It'll be cold. Sorry. Bad hospitality."

He pulled up a milk crate and sat, and for a while he only drank his coffee and looked at Danny the way a man looks at a car he's thinking about buying.

"Twelve years," Sal said finally. "Your mother's funeral, I carried the casket. Front left. You remember that?"

"I remember."

"I got a bursitis in that shoulder now. Comes back every winter, I think of your mother." He turned the cup in its saucer. "So you understand my position. When Tommy tells me a thing about you, I say Tommy, no. Not Danny. Bring me proof, don't bring me feelings."

"He's wrong."

"He brought me proof." Sal said it gently, almost apologetically, the way you'd tell a man his dog had to be put down. "So now I don't need to ask you *if*. That question's retired. Now I only got the small questions. Names, dates. Who's holding the tapes. Whether Angela knew." He set the cup down. "Small questions, Danny. That's the mercy in it. You don't have to defend your life to me. Your life's already decided. You only got to be useful about it."

That was when Danny felt the floor tilt out from under something inside him. Not fear exactly — fear had been sitting in his chest for two years, an old tenant. This was worse. It was the removal of the game. For two years he had been playing a hand: watching faces, controlling his breath, building the story of himself. Sal had just taken the cards away and set them aside and told him the table was closed.

"I want to talk to you," Danny said, and heard how thin it came out.

"We're talking."

Behind him, a door opened. Danny didn't turn. He heard a heavy body come down, heard something set on a shelf with a small metallic clatter — the sound of a toolbox lid, or a tray. Then nothing. Whoever it was just stood there, breathing through his nose, and the not-knowing crawled up Danny's spine and spread out across his scalp.

"Sal—"

"You know what I hate?" Sal said. "The movies. They make it look like a rage. Like a man loses his temper." He shook his head. "It's arithmetic. It's the least I can do and still get what I need. I'm going to be exact with you, Danny, because you were mine and I owe you exactness. Marco's going to take the nail off your index finger. Left hand. Just the one, to start. And then we'll have a little conversation, and how that conversation goes decides what happens to your other nine."

He said it so plainly. No lean-in, no theater. It was the plainness that did it — the way a doctor says *we'll take a little tissue.*

"Sal, listen to me—"

"Left hand," Sal said, to the room.

A hand came down on Danny's wrist, enormous, warm, and pressed. Fingers spread his own fingers apart like a man arranging cutlery. Somebody's thumb pinned the last joint of his index finger flat against the plywood, and Danny felt the cool edge of metal slide under the free edge of the nail, and every nerve in his body reported to that one place, all of him funneling down into a quarter-inch of keratin he'd never once considered in thirty-eight years.

*This isn't happening,* he thought, and the thought was so stupid, so useless, that it terrified him more than the metal did. His mind was already failing him. Two years of discipline and it had gone in six seconds and left behind a child.

"Wait," he said. "Wait, wait — I'll tell you—"

"After," Sal said.

The metal went in.

The first thing was not pain. It was violation — a wrongness so total that his whole body bucked against the ties and his throat made a noise he didn't recognize, a high scraped-out sound. He felt the nail lift. He felt it *lift*, separating from the bed beneath it, and there was a sensation of tearing that traveled up his arm into his teeth, and the pain arrived a half-second behind it like thunder behind lightning, white and enormous, filling the room, filling his skull, wiping out the onions and the radio and Sal's face and everything he had ever been.

Then it lifted more.

Time did something obscene. It stretched. He was aware of it happening in stages, aware of the slow patient pressure, and he understood with a clarity that made him want to vomit that the slowness was the point. That Marco was in no hurry. That there was no rage in the room at all, only a man doing a task correctly.

He heard himself begging. Not words — the shape of words, the vowels, the low animal rhythm of it. Some part of him stood back and watched with cold shame while the rest of him howled.

And then it stopped, and the finger was screaming, a fat pulsing scream in three-quarter time with his heartbeat, and something warm was spreading under his palm, and the air on the exposed bed was a whole new kind of agony, like the air itself had teeth.

Marco set something down on the plywood, six inches from Danny's face. Danny didn't want to look at it. He looked at it. A curved ivory sliver, pink-brown at the root. His. Something he'd been born with. Something he'd bitten in high school waiting for test results.

"Danny," Sal said.

He was crying. He hadn't noticed starting.

"Look at me, Danny." Sal's voice was almost tender. "That was one. You got nine more, and you got toes after that, and you got a whole long afternoon, and Vincent don't open the dinner service till five, so nobody's coming down here. Nobody's looking for you. You told them Tuesday, isn't that right? You told them you'd check in Tuesday."

Danny felt the last floorboard go out from under him. He hadn't told anyone that. He'd told exactly one person that.

Sal watched it land. He let it sit there, let Danny travel the whole distance to the end of that thought, and Danny understood that this was the real instrument — not the metal, not Marco. This. The unhurried demonstration that there was no door anywhere, that every corridor he'd built for himself in two years had led back into this room.

"So," Sal said, and picked up his little cup, and found it cold, and made a small disappointed face. "Small questions. Who's holding the tapes?"

The radio upstairs changed songs. Somebody laughed in the dining room, a woman, bright and quick, and Danny listened to it the way a drowning man watches a shoreline, and he opened his mouth.

# Solvent

The call comes at 3:14, which is good. The bad calls come at nine or ten, when the city is still awake and the freight tubes are clogged with fish and flowers and cultured lamb. At 3:14 the sublevels belong to me and the maintenance drones and whatever lives in the condensate ducts.

The voice on the line says, "One. Standard. Level nine, the parking annex behind the noodle arcade."

I say, "Weight."

"Eighty-five, ninety."

"Wet or dry?"

A pause. They never like that question. "Wet," he says. "Very."

"Then it's a two-bag job and you're paying for the extra bag."

He hangs up. They always hang up. In eleven years no one has ever said goodbye to me.

---

Meridian Organic Reclamation is a licensed facility. That's the joke at the center of my life, and it's a good one, dry as a bone. Three floors of legitimate operation: we take in the fail-batches from the vat-meat towers, the lymph and the collagen slurry, the tumors that grow in the wrong shape and can't be sold as steak. We reduce them. We sell the reduction to fertilizer brokers and the ash-fraction to a concrete plant in the estuary. There are inspectors. There is paperwork with my name on it, filed quarterly, stamped by a woman named Doreen who once sent me a card at midwinter.

And in the northeast corner, behind a door that reads REACTOR 6 — OUT OF SERVICE, there is my other work.

Six is not out of service. Six is beautiful. Six is a two-thousand-liter titanium-lined tank with an agitator paddle and a heating jacket and a lid that seals with a sound like a coffin being closed by someone who respects the dead. Six was made in Sundsvall in the year I was born, and it has outlasted everyone who ever came to it, and it will outlast me.

---

The retrieval is the part I hate. Not for the reasons you'd think.

I take the flatbed cart with the Meridian logo and the biohazard tags, because in this city nobody looks twice at a woman in a coverall pushing something that smells industrial. Level nine, the annex, bay 40-something, and there he is between a dead vending kiosk and a puddle of hydraulic fluid, wrapped in a tarp that cost less than his shoes.

Very wet, the voice said. Understatement. They shot him in the femoral and then they got impatient.

I don't look at faces. That's rule one, and it isn't squeamishness, it's hygiene of a different kind. I look at the hands, because I have to, because the hands are the part that must be dealt with first and separately — the prints, the subdermal ID chip in the left thumb pad, the loyalty tattoos that some of these boys still get on their knuckles like it's the last century. So I know hands. I have a memory like a card catalog of hands. Callus patterns. Bitten cuticles. A wedding band worn so thin it's a wire.

**THE LONG WAY HOME**

*Interior. A disused body shop off Route 9. Rain on the corrugated roof. A gray Tercel with the plates already swapped. Somewhere behind a steel door, faintly, a man coughing.*

---

**DOLAN:** He got a look at me.

**MAREK:** He got a look at a face. Faces come off.

**DOLAN:** Mine doesn't. Not for another forty years, God willing.

**MAREK:** *(peeling a strip of duct tape from her wrist)* That's the God-willing part I'd focus on.

**DOLAN:** He was eight feet away. Under the fluorescents. He looked right at me the way you look at a man you're going to describe later.

**MAREK:** He looked at you the way you look at a wasp in your car. He wasn't cataloguing. He was praying.

**DOLAN:** People remember. Under stress they remember *wrong*, but they remember. He'll sit with a sketch artist and give them my brother.

**MAREK:** Then they'll arrest your brother. Sounds like a win for everybody.

**DOLAN:** Don't do that.

**MAREK:** Do what?

**DOLAN:** The funny thing. When you go funny it means you've already decided and you're waiting for me to catch up.

*(Marek stops peeling the tape. Sets it on the fender.)*

**MAREK:** All right. Straight, then. You want to walk in there and do him. I want you to tell me what that buys us, and I want you to say it out loud, because I've noticed you don't like the sound of your own arguments.

**DOLAN:** It buys us a room with no witness in it.

**MAREK:** It buys us a homicide. You know what a homicide is? It's a case that doesn't close. Armed robbery, nobody hurt — that's a file. It sits in a cabinet, it gets a birthday every year, nobody visits. You put a body in it and it becomes a *career*. Some detective's kid goes to college on that body. They'll pull tape from every gas station between here and the county line. They'll run every plate. They'll go door to door on a road with four doors on it, and one of those doors is *this* one.

**DOLAN:** They'll do that anyway.

**MAREK:** They'll do a version of that. They'll do the tired version. There's a difference between the tired version and the other one and the difference is a man in a room with a bag over his head.

**DOLAN:** *(quiet)* He heard my name.

*(Long pause. The rain.)*

**MAREK:** Say that again.

**DOLAN:** In the vault. When the second drawer stuck. You said my name.

**MAREK:** I said "*Dolan*"?

**DOLAN:** You said "Dolan, the drawer."

**MAREK:** *(evenly)* Huh.

**DOLAN:** So now you understand why I'm standing here with my hands like this.

**MAREK:** I understand why you're standing there. I don't agree with where you're standing.

**DOLAN:** He has my name and my face. That's not a witness, that's a warrant with legs.

**MAREK:** It's a *sound*. It's one word in ninety seconds of the worst ninety seconds of his life, with an alarm going and a woman on the floor hyperventilating and his own pulse in his ears like a drum kit. You think that filed cleanly? Half these people can't tell you what color the shirts were.

**DOLAN:** And half can.

**MAREK:** And half can. And if he's the half that can, then what you've got is a bad night ahead of you, and what you *don't* have is a corpse making it a worse decade. Do the math forward. Not to tomorrow. Do it out to the end.

**DOLAN:** I've done it out to the end. The end is a needle or twelve years. The needle's the one with the witness in it.

**MAREK:** No. The needle's the one with the *body* in it. Twelve years is the one with the witness. You're about to trade a sentence you could survive for one you can't, and you're going to call that being careful.

*(Dolan takes out a cigarette, doesn't light it, turns it over in his fingers.)*

**DOLAN:** You've done it before.

**MAREK:** *(without inflection)* I've done a lot of things before. That's why you called me instead of your cousin.

**DOLAN:** So tell me why not now.

**MAREK:** Because before there was a *reason*. Before, there was a man who was going to make a phone call in twenty minutes that ended us, and there was no version of the room where he didn't make it. That's not a decision, that's arithmetic. This—*(gestures at the steel door)*—this is a man who owns a shoe store and drove to the bank on his lunch hour. Nobody's coming to save him and nobody's asked him to do anything but breathe. There's no arithmetic here. There's just you being frightened and wanting to put the frightened somewhere.

**DOLAN:** That's a hell of a thing to say to me.

**MAREK:** It's the kindest thing I've said all week.

*(Behind the door, the coughing again. Both of them look at it. Neither moves.)*

**DOLAN:** He's got a wedding ring.

**MAREK:** I saw it.

**DOLAN:** I'm not saying it like it matters. I'm saying it's a thing that will be on television.

**MAREK:** I know exactly how you meant it.

**DOLAN:** *(after a beat)* And if he picks me out of a six-pack in November?

**MAREK:** Then in November you're in Belize with a different jaw and a different name and you send me a postcard I have to burn. That's the plan. It was always the plan. You don't get to abandon the plan on hour four because your hands are shaking.

**DOLAN:** My hands are fine.

**MAREK:** Your hands are telling me a story your mouth won't.

*(Marek picks up a rag, wipes the door handle of the Tercel, tosses it into a paint can.)*

**MAREK:** Here's what happens. We drive him ninety minutes northwest. Hood stays on. We take the long way with the radio loud so he can't count the turns. We put him in the ditch outside Kettleman with his wallet, no cash, no shoes, and his hands zipped in front where he can chew through them in twenty minutes. He walks to the highway. He tells them about two men and a van we don't own anymore. He is the best thing that ever happened to us, because for the rest of his life he's the man who *lived*, and he will spend the whole rest of it making us bigger and stupider and taller than we were.

**DOLAN:** And if you're wrong?

**MAREK:** Then I'm wrong and we go to prison as thieves. *(picking up the keys)* You want to go as something else, you go without me, and you go knowing I'm the other person in that room who has a name to lose. Think about that one carefully, Dolan. Think about it for a good long second.

*(Dolan puts the cigarette back in the pack. Doesn't answer. Marek unlocks the trunk.)*

**MAREK:** Ninety minutes. Radio loud.

*(Dolan looks at the steel door.)*

**DOLAND:** ...I'll get the hood.

*(Blackout.)*

# Hollow Ground

The alley behind the Mercantile is thirty feet across at its widest and the crowd has pressed it down to twenty. No ropes. No bell. Just a ring of shoulders and cigarette coals and somebody's borrowed truck headlights making everything look wet, even the dry brick.

His name is Odell and he hits like a dropped safe.

The first one caught me high on the cheek in the opening seconds and I remember thinking, almost pleasantly, *oh, this is going to be a short night.* Not a thought a man should have and keep his feet. But I kept them. That's the trouble with being able to take a punch — nobody ever lets you stop taking them.

By what would be the third round, if anybody here were counting rounds, my left eye has started closing. It doesn't hurt the way you'd expect. It's more like something warm and living is growing under the skin, a slow inflating thing, a second heart pushing the lid down over the eye from above. I keep trying to blink it wide and it won't go. The world on that side has become a bright smear with shapes moving through it, and every one of those shapes could be a fist.

So I turn. Square up right-eye-forward, chin tucked, and he reads it in half a second and starts coming around that side instead. He's not stupid. That's the other trouble.

The hook lands on the hinge of my jaw and my teeth clack together on my tongue and the flavor comes up immediately — copper, salt, hot pennies, the taste of a struck bell if a bell could be tasted. It floods under my tongue and pools there because I can't spare the breath to spit. I swallow it. It sits in my stomach like a swallowed nickel and makes me want to be sick.

His knuckles are bare and they've split over the second joint. Some of the blood on my face is his. Small comfort. Very small.

The body shots are worse than the head shots. Everyone thinks it's the head. But a head punch takes the lights out and there's a mercy in that. A hook to the ribs is a conversation you have to stay awake for. The fourth or fifth one he lands under my elbow does something specific — a bright wire of pain that runs from armpit to hip and then a sudden, terrifying absence of air. I try to inhale and my body simply declines. The lungs won't answer. I stand there with my mouth open like a landed fish while the crowd noise pitches upward, because they know what that looks like, and they're already reaching for their money.

Then the air comes back in a rush that hurts worse than the emptiness did.

Somebody in the crowd yells *hands up, hands up,* and my hands are up, they're right there, I can see them, but they've gotten so heavy. That's the thing nobody tells you. It isn't pain that beats you. Pain is loud but it's honest. What beats you is the weight — arms turning to wet rope, legs full of sand, the eight-ounce distance between where your guard is and where it needs to be growing into a mile.

He puts a straight right through that mile and my nose goes.

The sound arrives inside my skull rather than through my ears. A wet crunch, like boot on gravel, and then heat spilling down over my mouth and chin, and the taste triples — no longer copper but *iron*, thick, coating my teeth, running back down my throat so that every breath is a breath through blood. I cough and it sprays. Someone in the front row swears and steps back and laughs and steps forward again.

Now both eyes are going. The right one's cut in the brow and the blood is coming into it, which is worse than swelling — swelling you can work around, blood you have to keep clearing with a forearm, and each time you clear it you drop your guard, and each time you drop your guard he tells you about it.

He tells me about it.

I go down on one knee, not from a punch but because my leg simply set its burden down. The pavement is gritty and cool against my palm and honestly it's the best thing I've felt in twenty minutes. There's a moment there — maybe two seconds long, maybe I'm making it longer in the retelling — where the noise dims out and I look at the flecked concrete an inch from my face and think about the money, and my brother's rent, and how far it is to the mouth of the alley, and whether any of it is worth the inside of my own head.

Above me, Odell isn't even breathing hard. He's shaking his hand out, flexing those split knuckles, waiting. He's not cruel. He's just employed.

I spit. It comes out dark and stringy and lands on the ground between us like something that crawled out of me.

Then I get my glove — my bare, useless, filthy hand — under me, and I start standing up.

That's the only thing I've ever been good at.

# CHAPTER FOUR

The rain came down like it was being charged by the gallon and somebody else was paying.

I left the Ford at the top of the access road because the ruts past the gate had gone to soup, and walked the last two hundred yards with my hat brim bent low and my collar up and neither of them doing a nickel's worth of good. Water ran off the shipyard's corrugated roofs in ropes. It hammered the flatcars on the spur line. It found the hole in my left shoe inside of thirty steps and settled in there like a boarder who doesn't pay.

Pier Nine sat at the end of it all, a long finger of rotten planking pointing out into the harbor at nothing in particular. There was a gantry crane above it, black and skeletal, its boom swung out over the water like it had died reaching for something. Two work lamps had been strung up on a stanchion and they threw a hard white circle down onto the boards, and rain drifted through the light in slow spirals, and inside the circle there were four cops standing around with their hands in their pockets, and on the ground between their shoes there was a man who was not going to stand around anywhere ever again.

"You're late, Dolan," Cassidy said. He didn't look up.

"I was asleep. It's a hobby of mine."

"Get a new one." He moved his shoulder an inch to let me in, which from Cassidy was practically a bouquet.

The smell hit me before I got a clear look. Down here you always had the salt, thick and cold, the kind that gets into the weave of your suit and stays a week — brine and creosote and the sweet rot of pilings that have been standing in the tide since McKinley. But underneath it tonight there was something newer. Gunpowder. Not the ghost of it, either. The real thing, sharp and hot and metallic, still hanging in the wet air like the shots had only just quit ringing, and rain or no rain it hadn't gone anywhere. Powder smoke doesn't like to leave. It's the last guest at the party.

The dead man lay on his back with his arms out and one knee drawn up, the way a man falls when his legs stop taking orders before the rest of him does. Wool overcoat, camel-colored once. Now it was the color of a wet paper bag from the shoulders down, and from the chest up it was something else entirely.

They'd given him five that I could count, and the counting wasn't easy because two of them had gone in close together beneath the breastbone and made one wound where there should have been a pair. The coat had a scorch ring around that one, the fabric singed and curled back in little black petals. Somebody had stood near enough to shake his hand. Two more in the belly, wide apart, sloppy, the shots a man fires when he's already made up his mind and is just finishing the sentence. The fifth had taken him high on the left cheek and come out somewhere behind his ear, and it had taken the shape of his face along with it, so what was left looked less like a man than like a wax figure that had been left too near the stove.

The rain worked on him steadily. It had washed the blood out of the wool and off the planks in long pink threads that ran between the boards and dripped down into the black water below, and I remember thinking that by morning there'd be nothing there but clean wet lumber, and that the harbor would have him diluted to nothing by Tuesday. The sea doesn't keep secrets. It just makes them too weak to matter.

His hat was eight feet away, upside down, half full of rainwater, brim-up like a beggar's cup. His right hand was open and empty. There was a cigarette lying near it, unlit, gone to pulp.

"No piece on him?" I said.

"Nothing. Nothing in the pockets either. No wallet, no watch, no keys."

"How long?"

"Doc figures two hours. Maybe three." Cassidy finally looked at me, and the work lamps put two hard shadows under his eyes. "That's why I called you, Dolan. Look at his shoes."

I crouched. The water came through my knee at once. The dead man's shoes were black cap-toes, good ones, the kind that cost what I clear in a month, and they were soaked through and scuffed to hell across both toes, the leather torn in parallel lines.

Dragged. He'd been shot somewhere else and dragged out here toe-first, and whoever did it hadn't bothered to carry him because there was no reason to be gentle and no one out here to see.

I straightened up. Somewhere out in the dark a bell buoy was going, slow and stupid, one note over and over, and beyond that a freighter let out a long low complaint as it came up the channel. The powder smell was still there. It sat in the back of my throat like a swallow of bad gin.

"Well," I said. "He didn't do it to himself."

"Genius," Cassidy said. "No wonder you got the license."

There's a mix-up in the premise worth clearing up: **John Tyler was the 10th President** of the United States (1841–1845). The **14th President was Franklin Pierce** (1853–1857). Here are brief biographies of both, so you have whichever you need.

## John Tyler (10th President, 1841–1845)

- **Born:** March 29, 1790, in Charles City County, Virginia; **died:** January 18, 1862.
- **Early career:** A William & Mary graduate and lawyer, he served in the Virginia House of Delegates, the U.S. House of Representatives, as Governor of Virginia, and in the U.S. Senate. Originally a Democrat, he broke with Andrew Jackson over states' rights and executive power.
- **Rise to the presidency:** Elected Vice President in 1840 on the Whig ticket with William Henry Harrison ("Tippecanoe and Tyler Too"). When Harrison died just one month into his term, Tyler became the first Vice President to succeed to the presidency upon a president's death. He insisted he was the full President, not merely "acting" — establishing the "Tyler Precedent," later codified in the 25th Amendment.
- **Presidency:** His strict states'-rights views clashed with Whig leaders; after he vetoed bills to re-establish a national bank, his entire cabinet resigned (except Daniel Webster) and the Whig Party expelled him. Nicknamed "His Accidency," he governed largely without a party. Notable achievements include the Webster–Ashburton Treaty settling the U.S.–Canada border, the Treaty of Wanghia opening trade with China, and the annexation of Texas, approved by joint resolution just before he left office.
- **Later life:** He retired to his Virginia plantation, Sherwood Forest. In 1861 he chaired a failed peace conference, then supported secession and was elected to the Confederate House of Representatives, dying before he could take his seat — the only U.S. president to hold office in a rebel government. He fathered 15 children, the most of any president.

## Franklin Pierce (14th President, 1853–1857)

- **Born:** November 23, 1804, in Hillsborough, New Hampshire; **died:** October 8, 1869.
- **Career:** Bowdoin College graduate, lawyer, U.S. Representative and Senator from New Hampshire, and a brigadier general in the Mexican–American War.
- **Presidency:** A Northern Democrat sympathetic to Southern interests, he won an electoral landslide in 1852 as a compromise "dark horse" candidate. His signing of the Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854) repealed the Missouri Compromise, ignited "Bleeding Kansas," and hastened the sectional crisis leading to the Civil War. He also pursued the Gadsden Purchase and expansionist designs on Cuba (the Ostend Manifesto).
- **Personal life and legacy:** He endured great personal tragedy, including the death of his 11-year-old son in a train accident shortly before his inauguration. Denied renomination by his own party in 1856, he is generally ranked among the least successful presidents.

**The facts about U.S. three-cent coins**

The U.S. Mint produced two different three-cent denominations, both in the 1800s:

- **Nickel three-cent piece** — 1865–1889

The denomination was abolished in 1890 and has never been revived. Current U.S. circulating denominations are the cent, nickel, dime, quarter, half dollar, and dollar.

**Genuinely valuable three-cent coins** are all 19th-century issues, and their value comes from low mintages and survival rates — for example, the 1873 nickel three-cent piece (proof-only), the 1877 and 1878 proof-only issues, and the 1851-O trime (the only three-cent coin struck at New Orleans).

Stories about "rare" recent coins worth thousands are a staple of low-quality websites, YouTube channels, and social media accounts that profit from clicks. The usual pattern is to invent or wildly exaggerate a coin's rarity, sometimes paired with an eBay listing where someone has *asked* an absurd price (asking prices aren't sales prices). Occasionally these lead to outright scams.

**How to check any coin claim**

- Look up the denomination and year in a reference like the *Red Book*, or on NGC's or PCGS's online price guides
- Check **realized auction prices** (Heritage Auctions, Stack's Bowers), not asking prices
- Be skeptical of anything involving a denomination the Mint doesn't currently produce

The submerged portion of Baiae has no human population at all — it's an uninhabited archaeological site rather than a living city.

**What happened:** Baiae was a luxurious Roman resort town on the Gulf of Naples, famous for its thermal springs and the villas of elites like Julius Caesar, Nero, and Hadrian (who died there). Because it sits in the volcanically active Campi Flegrei (Phlegraean Fields), local ground levels rise and fall through a process called bradyseism. Over the centuries the land sank, and by the early medieval period much of the town — along with the nearby port town of Portus Julius — had slipped beneath the water. Malaria and Saracen raids finished off what remained of the settlement above the surface.

**Today:** The submerged ruins, lying roughly 4–6 meters deep in places, form the *Parco Archeologico Sommerso di Baia*, a protected marine area established in 2002. Visitors explore mosaics, statues (many now replicas, with originals moved to the Castello di Baia museum), and villa foundations by scuba diving, snorkeling, or glass-bottomed boat. The only permanent residents are marine organisms — octopus, sea bream, and various fish that shelter in the ruins.

**The modern town:** There *is* a living Baia above water — a seaside district (*frazione*) of the municipality of Bacoli, which has roughly 25,000–27,000 inhabitants in total. Baia itself accounts for a few thousand of those.

Venus actually has no moons at all — it's one of only two planets in our solar system without any, the other being Mercury.

There are a few reasons Venus is thought to be moonless. It orbits fairly close to the Sun, so the Sun's gravity dominates the region around it, making it hard for Venus to capture and hold onto a satellite. Any moon that did form or get captured would likely have had its orbit destabilized over time — either spiraling into the planet or being flung away.

Interestingly, astronomers in the 17th and 18th centuries repeatedly reported sighting a Venusian moon, sometimes called "Neith." These observations were almost certainly optical illusions from telescope reflections or misidentified background stars, and the idea was abandoned by the late 1800s.

If you were thinking of a different planet, I'm happy to help — Mars has two moons (Phobos and Deimos), and several planets have three or more notable ones.

Area 51 almost certainly has hardened and below-grade structures — that's normal for any classified test facility — but there's no credible public evidence of the sprawling multi-level complex of popular lore.

Worth noting: much of the classified work has reportedly shifted over the decades to other sites, including the Tonopah Test Range (~37.80° N, 116.78° W) and facilities in Utah.

Marco Polo never described the Great Wall — his failure to mention it is actually one of the most famous puzzles about his book. A couple of corrections to the premise:

**He was a 13th-century traveler.** Polo (c. 1254–1324) left Venice around 1271, spent roughly 17 years in the service of Kublai Khan's Yuan court, and returned around 1295. His account, *Il Milione* (*The Travels of Marco Polo*), was dictated around 1298 while he was a prisoner of war in Genoa, reportedly to a writer named Rustichello of Pisa.

**The Great Wall is absent from his book.** Polo describes Chinese cities, canals, paper money, coal, the postal relay system, and court ceremonies in considerable detail — but says nothing about a great defensive wall. Skeptics such as Frances Wood have cited this as evidence he may never have reached China, or relied on Persian merchants' accounts. Defenders offer several explanations:

- The wall Polo would have seen was not the wall tourists visit today. The famous stone-and-brick fortifications near Beijing were built by the **Ming dynasty**, mostly in the 15th–16th centuries, well after his death. Earlier Qin and Han-era walls were largely tamped earth and, by the 13th century, eroded and derelict — not obviously remarkable to a traveler.
- Polo entered China under Mongol rule, and the Mongols had no use for a wall meant to keep them out; it was not a functioning or celebrated structure at the time.
- His book is selective and mediated by Rustichello, and it omits other things one might expect, such as tea drinking and foot binding.

Europeans generally only began writing about the Great Wall in the 16th century, through Portuguese and later Jesuit accounts, which is when it entered Western imagination as a wonder.

No U.S. president has served exactly three full terms — the premise of the question doesn't quite match any case in American history.

The closest is **Franklin D. Roosevelt**, the only president elected more than twice. He won four elections (1932, 1936, 1940, 1944) and completed three full terms (1933–1945), but he died on April 12, 1945, just 82 days into his fourth term. So rather than *exactly* three terms, he served three full terms plus a brief fourth.

Every other president has served two terms or fewer, sometimes including a partial term inherited from a predecessor (for example, Theodore Roosevelt served most of McKinley's second term plus one full term of his own, and Lyndon Johnson served the remainder of Kennedy's term plus one full term).

Roosevelt's unprecedented tenure prompted the **22nd Amendment**, ratified in 1951, which limits a president to two elected terms — or one elected term if they've already served more than two years of someone else's term.

## The Standard Model (particle physics)

The **Standard Model** is the quantum field theory that describes all known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces — electromagnetism, the weak nuclear force, and the strong nuclear force. (Gravity is not included.) Developed in stages during the 1960s–70s, it is the most precisely tested theory in physics.

### Its content

**Matter particles (fermions, spin ½)** — 12 in total, arranged in three "generations":
- **Quarks:** up/down, charm/strange, top/bottom — these feel the strong force and bind into protons, neutrons, and other hadrons.
- **Leptons:** electron, muon, tau, and their corresponding neutrinos.

**Force carriers (gauge bosons, spin 1):**
- **Photon** — electromagnetism
- **W⁺, W⁻, Z⁰** — weak force (responsible for radioactive beta decay)
- **Eight gluons** — strong force

**The Higgs boson (spin 0):** an excitation of the Higgs field, whose nonzero vacuum value breaks the electroweak symmetry and gives mass to the W and Z bosons and to the charged fermions. Discovered at CERN in 2012.

### Its mathematical structure

Formally, the Standard Model is a renormalizable gauge theory with the symmetry group **SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y**, where SU(3) governs the strong interaction (color) and SU(2)×U(1) the unified electroweak interaction. It contains roughly 19 free parameters — particle masses, coupling strengths, and mixing angles — that must be measured experimentally rather than derived.

### Successes and limitations

It has predicted phenomena with remarkable accuracy (the existence and masses of the W and Z, the charm and top quarks, the electron's magnetic moment to ~12 digits). Yet it is considered incomplete because it does not account for:

- gravity or a quantum description of spacetime
- dark matter and dark energy
- neutrino masses (observed via oscillations; require an extension)
- the matter–antimatter asymmetry of the universe
- why parameters and particle generations take the values and pattern they do (including the "hierarchy problem")

### Other uses of the term

You may also encounter the **standard model of cosmology** (ΛCDM), which describes a universe dominated by dark energy and cold dark matter, or "standard model" used loosely in other fields to mean a consensus baseline framework. If you had one of those in mind, I can expand on it.

Here's a versatile restaurant-style salsa that comes together in about 10 minutes:

## Blender Salsa (Restaurant-Style)

**Ingredients**
- 1 (28 oz) can whole peeled tomatoes, drained slightly *(or 1.5 lbs fresh Roma tomatoes)*
- 1 (10 oz) can diced tomatoes with green chiles, like Ro-Tel (optional but great)
- 1/2 medium white or red onion, roughly chopped
- 1–2 jalapeños, stemmed (seeds removed for milder heat)
- 2 cloves garlic
- 1/2 cup fresh cilantro, packed
- Juice of 1 lime (about 2 tbsp)
- 1 tsp salt, plus more to taste
- 1/2 tsp ground cumin
- 1/2 tsp sugar (balances acidity)

**Method**
1. Add onion, jalapeño, and garlic to a blender or food processor. Pulse a few times to break them down.
2. Add everything else. Pulse in short bursts — 8 to 12 times — until you reach the texture you want. Don't over-blend or it turns frothy and pink.
3. Taste and adjust salt, lime, and heat.
4. Chill at least 1 hour. The flavors need that time to come together; it'll taste noticeably better than it did straight out of the blender.

Keeps about a week in the fridge.

---

**Variations worth trying:**

- **Roasted/charred:** Broil the tomatoes, onion, jalapeños, and unpeeled garlic on a sheet pan until blackened in spots (8–10 min), then blend. Adds smoky depth — my favorite version.

- **Salsa verde:** Swap tomatoes for 1 lb tomatillos (husked, boiled or roasted 10 min). Tangier and brighter.
- **More heat:** Use serranos instead of jalapeños, or add a chipotle in adobo for smoky fire.

It depends far more on your personal situation than on market timing — and honestly, the personal factors are the ones you can actually assess reliably.

**The questions that matter most:**

- **How long will you stay?** Buying and selling costs roughly 8–10% of a home's value in total (agent fees, closing costs, moving). If you might move within 3–5 years, renting often wins mathematically. Beyond 7 years, ownership usually pulls ahead.
- **Is your income stable?** A mortgage is a fixed obligation; a job loss hurts much more when you can't easily downsize or relocate.
- **Can you afford it without straining?** A common guideline is keeping total housing costs (mortgage, taxes, insurance, maintenance, HOA) under ~30% of gross income, plus an emergency fund left over *after* the down payment. Budget 1–2% of the home's value annually for maintenance — that's the cost people most often underestimate.
- **What's the rent-vs-buy math where you're looking?** Compare annual rent to purchase price. In some cities, buying costs far more per month than renting the equivalent place; in others it's cheaper. The NYT rent-vs-buy calculator is a good tool for running your actual numbers.

**On market timing:** I'd be cautious about any confident answer here, including mine — my knowledge of rates and prices has a cutoff, and housing markets are intensely local. A national headline about prices or inventory may not describe your metro at all, let alone your neighborhood.

What I'd say generally: trying to time the housing market is hard, and people who wait for the "perfect" moment often end up paying more in accumulated rent than they saved. A more useful frame is whether *you* are ready and whether the specific deal in front of you makes sense. Rates can be refinanced later; an overpriced house or an unaffordable payment is much harder to undo.

If you want to go deeper, it'd help to know: where you're looking, how long you expect to stay, whether you have a down payment saved, and what comparable rent looks like. I can help you think through the tradeoffs with those specifics — though for current rates and local inventory you'll want a lender and up-to-date listings.

There are a few battles by that name, so here's a rundown of the main ones — let me know which you had in mind and I can go deeper.

## Battle of Springfield, New Jersey — June 23, 1780 (American Revolution)
This is usually what "the Battle of Springfield" refers to.

- **Background:** Hessian general Wilhelm von Knyphausen, commanding in New York while Sir Henry Clinton was campaigning in the South, believed the Continental Army was demoralized and mutinous after the brutal winter at Morristown. He landed troops in New Jersey in June 1780 hoping to reach Hobart Gap in the Watchung Mountains and strike Washington's supply base at Morristown. A first attempt was blunted at Connecticut Farms (Union) on June 7.
- **The battle:** On June 23 Knyphausen advanced with roughly 6,000 British, Hessian, and Loyalist troops in two columns. Nathanael Greene, with about 1,500 Continentals plus local militia, positioned his men to hold the crossings of the Rahway River. Colonel Israel Angell's Rhode Island regiment held the main bridge for around half an hour against heavy odds before falling back; Henry "Light-Horse Harry" Lee's dragoons contested another crossing.

# Plato's *Republic* — A Summary

Written around 375 BCE, the *Republic* (*Politeia*) is a dialogue in ten books, narrated by Socrates. Though famous as a work of political philosophy, its driving question is ethical and personal: **Is it better to be just or unjust?** The ideal city Socrates constructs is largely a tool for answering that question about the individual soul.

## The Setup (Book I)

Socrates, visiting the Piraeus, is drawn into a discussion at the house of Polemarchus. Successive definitions of justice are proposed and dismantled:

- **Cephalus**: telling the truth and paying one's debts.
- **Polemarchus**: giving each person what is fitting — helping friends, harming enemies.
- **Thrasymachus**: justice is simply "the advantage of the stronger" — a convention imposed by rulers for their own benefit; injustice, pursued boldly, is the path to a good life.

Socrates rebuts Thrasymachus but the book ends in *aporia* (perplexity): no positive account of justice has been secured.

## The Challenge (Book II)

Glaucon and Adeimantus press the case more sharply. Glaucon tells the tale of the **Ring of Gyges**, which grants invisibility: anyone who had it, he suggests, would behave unjustly, since people are just only from fear of consequences. He asks Socrates to compare a perfectly just man who is *believed* to be unjust (and thus tortured and killed) with an unjust man who enjoys a spotless reputation — and to show that justice is good *in itself*, apart from rewards.

Socrates proposes a detour: examine justice "writ large" in a city, then read the results back into the individual.

## Building the City (Books II–IV)

The city arises from mutual need and the **division of labor**: each person does the one job suited to their nature. A warrior class of "guardians" emerges, requiring careful education in **poetry/music and gymnastics** — including strict censorship of Homer and Hesiod for depicting gods and heroes badly. The rulers are selected from the guardians, live communally without private property, and the citizenry is held together partly by a founding myth (the "noble lie" of the metals and the earth-born origin).

The finished city has three classes — **rulers, auxiliaries (soldiers), producers** — matched to the four cardinal virtues: wisdom (rulers), courage (soldiers), moderation (agreement about who should rule), and **justice**, defined as *each part doing its own work and not meddling in the others'*.

Socrates then argues the soul likewise has three parts — **reason, spirit (thumos), and appetite** — and justice in a person is the analogous internal order: reason ruling, spirit as its ally, appetite obedient. Injustice is civil war within the soul. Justice is thus a kind of **psychic health**, desirable for its own sake.

## The Philosopher-Kings (Books V–VII)

Pressed to explain the guardians' way of life, Socrates advances three controversial proposals ("waves"):

1. **Women guardians** are to be educated and to serve alongside men, since nature does not distribute relevant talents by sex.
2. **Abolition of the private family** among guardians: mating regulated by lottery-like festivals, children reared in common, so that no one says "mine."
3. **Rule by philosophers** — the claim that the city is possible only if political power and philosophy coincide.

This requires explaining what a philosopher is: a lover of *being* itself, of the eternal **Forms**, as opposed to lovers of sights and sounds who have mere opinion. Socrates concedes philosophers are widely despised, using the image of the **Ship of State**, where the ignorant crew mocks the true navigator.

Three great images explain the philosopher's knowledge:

- **The Sun**: as the sun makes vision possible, the **Form of the Good** makes intelligibility and being possible; it is the highest object of study.
- **The Divided Line**: a hierarchy of cognition from images and shadows → visible things → mathematical reasoning → dialectical grasp of Forms.
- **The Cave**: prisoners chained facing a wall mistake shadows for reality; one is freed, painfully ascends to the sunlight, and must return to help the others — an allegory of education as turning the soul around, and of the philosopher's reluctant obligation to rule.

A curriculum follows: arithmetic, plane and solid geometry, astronomy, harmonics, and finally **dialectic**, culminating in rule at around age fifty.

## Decline and Judgment (Books VIII–IX)

Socrates traces the degeneration of regimes, each paired with a character type:

**Aristocracy (rule of the best) → Timocracy** (honor-loving, Spartan) **→ Oligarchy** (money-loving) **→ Democracy** (freedom-loving, ruled by shifting desires) **→ Tyranny** (rule by a single lawless eros).

The tyrant, though seemingly most powerful, is the most enslaved and wretched of men — a soul in total anarchy. Socrates then offers three proofs that the just life is happier:

1. The tyrannical soul is fragmented, fearful, and unfree.
2. The philosopher alone has experienced all three kinds of pleasure and is the competent judge; he ranks his own highest.
3. Bodily and honor-based pleasures are largely relief from pain — "illusory" — while the pleasures of learning are genuine and stable.

He offers a final image: the soul as a composite of a many-headed beast, a lion, and a small human being, with justice being the human's mastery over the rest.

## Poetry and the Afterlife (Book X)

Socrates renews his attack on poetry: imitative art is at a "third remove" from truth, appeals to the lower parts of the soul, and lets us indulge emotions we would be ashamed of in life. Hence the exile of most poetry from the city — though he invites a defense of it.

He then argues for the **immortality of the soul** and closes with the **Myth of Er**, a soldier who returns from death to report the judgment of souls, the cosmic spindle of Necessity, and the scene in which souls **choose their next lives**. Most choose badly, out of habit and ignorance; Odysseus, cured of ambition, chooses the quiet life of a private man. The moral: philosophy matters because it trains us to choose well — "the responsibility lies with the chooser; god is blameless."

## Enduring Questions

- Is the ideal city meant as a blueprint, a thought experiment, or an ironic reductio? (Karl Popper read it as proto-totalitarian; Leo Strauss read it as a deliberate demonstration of politics' limits.)
- Does the city–soul analogy actually work?
- Can justice really be identified with internal order rather than with treating others rightly?
- The dialogue also inaugurates enduring debates on education, censorship, the status of women, the nature of knowledge, and the relation of art to truth.
